chapters.title: The Window · 1
paragraphs: “Yes, of course, if it’s fine tomorrow,” said Mrs. Ramsay. “But you’ll have to be up at the crack of dawn,” she added.

To her son these words brought an extraordinary joy. It was as if the trip were settled and bound to happen, as if the wonder he had looked forward to for years and years, it seemed, were now within reach, after just one night of darkness and one day’s sail. He belonged, even at the age of six, to that great clan who cannot keep one feeling separate from another, but must let their hopes for the future, with all its joys and sorrows, cloud what is actually in front of them. For people like this, even in earliest childhood, any turn of the wheel of sensation can crystallize and fix the moment on which its gloom or radiance falls. So James Ramsay, sitting on the floor cutting pictures out of the illustrated catalogue of the Army and Navy Stores, a London department store, gave the picture of a refrigerator a heavenly bliss as his mother spoke. It was fringed with joy. The wheelbarrow, the lawnmower, the sound of poplar trees, leaves whitening before rain, rooks cawing, brooms knocking, dresses rustling—all these were so colored and so distinct in his mind that he already had his own private code, his secret language. Yet he looked the very image of stark, uncompromising severity, with his high forehead and his fierce blue eyes, flawlessly candid and pure, frowning slightly at the sight of human weakness. So his mother, watching him steer his scissors neatly round the refrigerator, pictured him all in red and ermine as a judge on the Bench, or directing some stern and momentous undertaking in a crisis of public affairs.
“But,” said his father, stopping in front of the drawing-room window, “it won’t be fine.”

If there had been an axe within reach, or a poker, or any weapon that could have gashed a hole in his father’s chest and killed him, there and then, James would have grabbed it. Such were the extremes of feeling that Mr. Ramsay stirred in his children just by being there. He stood, as he stood now, lean as a knife, narrow as the blade of one, grinning sarcastically. He was pleased not only to disillusion his son and make fun of his wife, who was ten thousand times better than he was in every way (James thought), but also, secretly, to be vain about how accurate his judgment was. What he said was true. It was always true. He was incapable of untruth. He never tampered with a fact, never softened an unpleasant word to suit the pleasure or convenience of any living being, least of all his own children. They, born of his body, ought to know from childhood that life is difficult; that facts don’t bend; and that the passage to that fabled land where our brightest hopes are put out, where our frail boats go down in darkness (here Mr. Ramsay would straighten his back and narrow his little blue eyes at the horizon), is one that needs, above all, courage, truth, and the power to endure.

“But it may be fine—I expect it will be fine,” said Mrs. Ramsay, impatiently giving some little twist to the reddish-brown stocking she was knitting. If she got it done tonight, and if they went to the Lighthouse after all, it would be a present for the Lighthouse keeper’s little boy, whose hip was threatened with tuberculosis. It would go along with a heap of old magazines and some tobacco—really anything she could find lying around that nobody wanted and that only cluttered up the room. Those poor men must be bored to death, sitting all day with nothing to do except polish the lamp, trim the wick and rake about on their patch of garden; this would give them something to amuse them. Because how would you like being shut away for an entire month at a stretch, perhaps longer when the weather was stormy, on a rock no bigger than a tennis lawn? she would ask. With no letters, no newspapers, no one to see; if you had a wife, not seeing her, not knowing how your children were—whether they were sick, whether they had fallen and broken an arm or a leg; watching the same dreary waves break week after week, and then a dreadful storm rolling in, spray over the windows, birds flung against the lamp, the whole place shaking, and you unable to put your nose outside in case you were swept into the sea? How would you like that? she asked, turning especially to her daughters. And so, she went on, in a somewhat different tone, you must take them whatever comforts you can.

“It’s due west,” said Tansley the atheist, spreading his bony fingers so the wind blew between them; he was keeping Mr. Ramsay company on his evening walk, up and down, up and down the terrace. In other words, the wind was coming from exactly the worst direction for a landing at the Lighthouse. Yes, Mrs. Ramsay granted, he did say disagreeable things; it was nasty of him to press the point and make James more disappointed than ever. And yet she would not allow the children to laugh at him. “The atheist,” they called him; “the little atheist.” Rose made fun of him; so did Prue; so did Andrew, Jasper and Roger; even old Badger, who hadn’t a tooth left in his head, had bitten him, because he was (in Nancy’s words) the hundred-and-tenth young man to chase them all the way up to the Hebrides, when it was so much nicer to be left alone.

“Nonsense,” said Mrs. Ramsay, very sternly. Setting aside their habit of exaggerating, which they had inherited from her, and the suggestion (a true one) that she invited too many people to stay and had to lodge some of them in the town, she simply could not stand rudeness to her guests—especially to young men, who were poor as church mice, “exceptionally able,” according to her husband, great admirers of his, and who had come for a holiday. In fact the whole of the other sex was under her protection. Her reasons she could not have explained: their chivalry and bravery; the fact that they negotiated treaties, governed India, ran the world’s money; and lastly a certain attitude toward herself which no woman could fail to sense or to enjoy, something trusting, childlike, reverent, which an old woman might accept from a young man without any loss of dignity. And woe to the girl—please heaven it was none of her daughters!—who did not feel the value of it, and everything it implied, right down to the marrow of her bones.
She turned sternly on Nancy. He had not chased them, she said. He had been invited.

They must find some way out of it all. There might be a simpler way, a less exhausting way, she sighed. When she looked in the mirror and saw her gray hair and sunken cheek, at fifty, she thought that perhaps she could have handled things better—her husband; money; his books. But for her own part she would never for one second regret the choice she had made, run away from difficulties, or cut corners on her duties. She was a formidable sight just now. Only in silence, lifting their eyes from their plates after she had spoken so sharply about Charles Tansley, did her daughters—Prue, Nancy, Rose—dare to toy with the heretical ideas they had cooked up for themselves of a life unlike hers: in Paris, maybe; a wilder life; not forever looking after some man or other. For all of them silently questioned deference and chivalry, the Bank of England and the Indian Empire, ringed fingers and lace. And yet all of them also found in it something that was the very essence of beauty. It roused the manliness in their girlish hearts, and made them, sitting at the table under their mother’s gaze, respect her strange severity and her extreme courtesy—like a queen lifting a beggar’s dirty foot from the mud and washing it—when she reproached them so very sternly about that wretched atheist who had chased them to—or, strictly speaking, been asked to stay with them on—the Isle of Skye.

“There’ll be no landing at the Lighthouse tomorrow,” said Charles Tansley, clapping his hands together where he stood at the window with her husband. Surely he had said enough by now. She wished the two of them would go on with their talk and leave her and James in peace. She looked at him. The children said he was such a wretched specimen, all humps and hollows. He was no good at cricket; he poked about; he shuffled. A sarcastic brute, Andrew called him. They knew what he liked most: pacing endlessly up and down, up and down, beside Mr. Ramsay, discussing who had won this prize and who had won that, who was a “first-rate man” at Latin verse, who was “brilliant but I think fundamentally unsound,” who was beyond question the “ablest fellow in Balliol,” the Oxford college. Or who had hidden his light for the moment at Bristol or Bedford, but was sure to be heard of later, once his Prolegomena to some branch of mathematics or philosophy was published—Mr. Tansley happened to have the first pages in proof with him, if Mr. Ramsay cared to look at them. That was the kind of thing they talked about.

She couldn’t help laughing herself sometimes. The other day she had said something about “waves mountains high.” Yes, Charles Tansley agreed, it was a bit rough. “Aren’t you soaked right through?” she had asked. “Damp, not wet through,” Mr. Tansley replied, pinching his sleeve and feeling his socks.

But that wasn’t what bothered them, the children said. Not his face; not his manners. It was him—the way he saw things. Whenever they talked about something interesting—people, music, history, anything at all—or simply said what a fine evening it was, why not sit outside, their complaint about Charles Tansley was that he could never rest until he had twisted the whole subject round so that it somehow reflected on himself and made them look small. Somehow he set all their nerves on edge with that acid way he had of stripping the flesh and blood off everything. And he would go to art galleries, they said, and then ask you whether you liked his tie. God knows, said Rose, you didn’t.

The moment the meal was over, the eight sons and daughters of Mr. and Mrs. Ramsay slipped away from the dinner table as stealthily as deer and made for their bedrooms. These were their strongholds in a house where there was no other privacy, places to debate anything, everything: Tansley’s tie; the passing of the Reform Bill, the great voting reform of 1832; seabirds and butterflies; people. Meanwhile the sun poured into those attics, which were divided from each other by a single plank, so that every footstep could be clearly heard, and the Swiss girl sobbing for her father, who was dying of cancer in a valley of the Grisons, in Switzerland. The sun lit up bats, flannels, straw hats, inkpots, paint pots, beetles, and the skulls of small birds, and drew from the long frilled strips of seaweed pinned to the wall a smell of salt and weeds, which was in the towels too, gritty with sand from swimming.

Strife, divisions, differences of opinion, prejudices twisted into the very fiber of their being—oh, that they should start so early, Mrs. Ramsay lamented. They were so critical, her children. They talked such nonsense. She went out of the dining room, holding James by the hand, since he would not go with the others. It seemed such nonsense to her—inventing differences, when people, heaven knows, were different enough without that. The real differences, she thought, standing by the drawing-room window, are enough, quite enough. What she had in mind at that moment was rich and poor, high and low. The well-born received some respect from her, half grudging, for didn’t she have in her own veins the blood of that very noble, if slightly mythical, Italian house, whose daughters, scattered about English drawing rooms in the nineteenth century, had lisped so charmingly and stormed so wildly? All her wit and her bearing and her temper came from them, and not from the sluggish English or the cold Scots. But more deeply she brooded on the other problem, of rich and poor, and the things she saw with her own eyes, weekly, daily, here or in London. She would visit this widow or that struggling wife in person, with a bag on her arm and a notebook and pencil, and write down wages and spending, employment and unemployment, in columns carefully ruled for the purpose. She hoped that in this way she would stop being a private woman whose charity was half a sop to her own indignation, half a relief to her own curiosity, and would become what, with her untrained mind, she greatly admired: an investigator, shedding light on the social problem.

They were questions with no answer, it seemed to her, as she stood there holding James by the hand. That young man they all laughed at had followed her into the drawing room. He was standing by the table, fiddling awkwardly with something, feeling left out, as she could tell without turning round. Everyone had gone—the children; Minta Doyle and Paul Rayley; Augustus Carmichael; her husband—everyone had gone. So she turned with a sigh and said, “Would it bore you to come with me, Mr. Tansley?”

She had a dull errand in the town; she had a letter or two to write; she would be ten minutes perhaps; she would put on her hat. And there she was again, ten minutes later, with her basket and her parasol, giving off a sense of being ready, equipped for an outing. She had to interrupt it for a moment, though, as they passed the tennis lawn, to ask Mr. Carmichael if he wanted anything. He was basking there with his yellow cat’s eyes half open, so that, like a cat’s, they seemed to reflect the branches moving or the clouds passing, but gave no hint of any inner thoughts or feelings whatsoever.

For they were making the great expedition, she said, laughing. They were going to the town. “Stamps, writing paper, tobacco?” she suggested, stopping beside him. But no, he wanted nothing. His hands clasped themselves over his ample belly and his eyes blinked, as if he would have liked to answer her coaxing kindly (she was charming but a little nervous) but could not. He was sunk in a gray-green drowsiness that took them all in, without any need for words, in a vast and kindly lethargy of goodwill: the whole house; the whole world; all the people in it. For at lunch he had slipped a few drops of something into his glass, which explained, the children thought, the vivid streak of canary yellow in a mustache and beard that were otherwise milk-white. He wanted nothing, he murmured.

He ought to have been a great philosopher, Mrs. Ramsay said as they walked down the road toward the fishing village, but his marriage had been an unlucky one. Carrying her black parasol bolt upright, and moving with an air of expectation that was hard to describe, as though someone might be waiting for her just round the corner, she told him the story: a love affair at Oxford with some girl; marrying young; poverty; going out to India; translating a little poetry, “very beautifully, I believe”; being ready to teach the boys Persian or Hindustani, but honestly, what good was that?—and then ending up lying on the lawn, the way they had just seen him.

It flattered him. After being snubbed, he found it soothing that Mrs. Ramsay should confide this to him. Charles Tansley perked up. She suggested, too, how great a man’s intellect was, even as it declined, and how every wife was subordinate to her husband’s work—not that she blamed the girl, and the marriage had been happy enough, she believed—and this made him more pleased with himself than he had been so far. He would have liked, say, if they had taken a cab, to be the one to pay. And her little bag—might he carry it? No, no, she said, she always carried _that_ herself. And she did, too. Yes, he could sense that about her. He sensed a great many things, one thing especially that excited and unsettled him for reasons he could not put into words. He wanted her to see him in academic cap and gown, walking in a procession. A fellowship, a professorship—he felt he could do anything, and pictured himself—but what was she looking at? A man pasting up a poster. The enormous flapping sheet smoothed itself flat, and every sweep of the brush uncovered more legs, hoops, horses, gleaming reds and blues, beautifully sleek, until half the wall was taken up by a circus advertisement: a hundred horsemen, twenty performing seals, lions, tigers. … Leaning forward, because she was shortsighted, she read aloud that it … “will visit this town.” What terribly dangerous work, she exclaimed, for a man with one arm to stand at the top of a ladder like that—he had lost his left arm in a reaping machine two years ago.
“Let’s all go!” she cried, walking on, as though all those horses and riders had filled her with a child’s delight and driven her pity from her mind.

“Let’s go,” he said, echoing her, but he clipped the words out so self-consciously that she winced. “Let us go to the Circus.” No. He couldn’t say it properly. He couldn’t feel it properly. But why not? she wondered. What was the matter with him? Just then she felt real warmth toward him. When they were children, she asked, hadn’t they been taken to circuses? Never, he replied, as though she had asked exactly the question he wanted to answer; as though for days he had been longing to tell her how they never went to circuses. It was a big family, nine brothers and sisters, and his father was a working man. “My father is a pharmacist, Mrs. Ramsay. He keeps a shop.” He had supported himself since the age of thirteen. Many winters he went without an overcoat. At college he could never “return hospitality” (those were his dry, stiff words). He had to make everything last twice as long as other people did; he smoked the cheapest tobacco, shag, the kind the old men smoked down on the docks. He worked hard—seven hours a day; his subject at present was the influence of something on somebody—they were walking along, and Mrs. Ramsay didn’t quite catch the sense, only a word here and there … dissertation … fellowship … readership … lectureship. The ugly academic jargon rattled off so smoothly that she could not keep up with it. But she told herself she understood now why the circus had knocked him off his perch, poor little man, and why he had burst out straight away with all that about his father and mother and his brothers and sisters; and she would see that nobody laughed at him any more; she would tell Prue. What he would have liked, she imagined, was to be able to say he had gone to an Ibsen play with the Ramsays. He was a terrible prig—oh yes, a bore past bearing. Because even though they had reached the town now, and were walking along the main street with carts grinding by over the cobbles, he kept on talking, about settlement houses, and teaching, and working men, and helping our own class, and lectures, until she gathered that his self-confidence was entirely restored, that he had got over the circus, and that he was about (and once more she felt warmly toward him) to tell her—but here the houses dropped away on either side, they came out onto the quay, and the whole bay lay open in front of them, and Mrs. Ramsay couldn’t help crying out, “Oh, how beautiful!” For the great plateful of blue water lay before her; the hoary Lighthouse, far off and austere, stood in the middle of it; and to the right, as far as she could see, the green sand dunes faded and fell away in soft low folds, with wild, streaming grasses on them, which always seemed to be running off into some moon country that no human being lived in.
That was the view, she said, stopping, her eyes turning grayer, that her husband loved.

She paused a moment. But now, she said, artists had come here. And there indeed, only a few steps away, stood one of them, in a Panama hat and yellow boots, gazing seriously, softly, absorbedly, though ten little boys were watching him, with a look of deep contentment on his round red face. He gazed, and then, when he had gazed, he dipped, steeping the tip of his brush in some soft mound of green or pink. Ever since Mr. Paunceforte had been there, three years before, all the pictures were like that, she said: green and gray, with lemon-colored sailboats, and pink women on the beach.

But her grandmother’s friends, she said, with a discreet glance as they went by, had gone to enormous trouble. They mixed their own colors to begin with, then ground them, and then covered them with damp cloths so they would stay moist.

So Mr. Tansley supposed she meant him to see that the man’s picture was skimpy—was that what you said? The colors weren’t solid? Was that what you said? Under the influence of that extraordinary emotion which had been growing all through the walk—it had begun in the garden when he wanted to carry her bag, and grown stronger in the town when he wanted to tell her everything about himself—he was coming to see himself, and everything he had ever known, gone slightly crooked. It was awfully strange.

There he stood in the front room of the cramped little house she had brought him to, waiting while she ran upstairs for a moment to see a woman. Above him he heard her quick step; heard her voice, bright, then quiet; looked at the mats, the tea caddies, the glass domes; waited with real impatience; looked eagerly ahead to the walk home, set on carrying her bag. Then he heard her come out; close a door; tell someone to keep the windows open and the doors shut, and to ask at the house for whatever they needed (she must be speaking to a child). And then, all of a sudden, in she came and stood silent for a moment (as though she had been playing a part up there, and now for a moment let herself simply be), stood perfectly still for a moment against a picture of Queen Victoria wearing the blue ribbon of the Garter; and all at once it came to him that it was this: it was this:—she was the most beautiful person he had ever seen.

With stars in her eyes and veils in her hair, with cyclamen and wild violets—what was this nonsense he was thinking? She was fifty at least; she had eight children. Walking through fields of flowers and gathering to her breast broken buds and fallen lambs; with the stars in her eyes and the wind in her hair—He took her bag.

“Goodbye, Elsie,” she said, and they set off up the street, her parasol held upright, and she walking as though she expected to meet someone round the corner. And Charles Tansley, for the first time in his life, felt an extraordinary pride. A man who was digging in a drain stopped his digging and looked at her; let his arm hang down and looked at her. Charles Tansley felt an extraordinary pride; he felt the wind and the cyclamen and the violets, because for the first time in his life he was walking with a beautiful woman. He was holding her bag.

chapters.title: The Window · 2
paragraphs: “No going to the Lighthouse, James,” he said, as he stood by the window. He spoke awkwardly, but out of respect for Mrs. Ramsay he was trying to soften his voice into at least some semblance of friendliness.
Hateful little man, thought Mrs. Ramsay, why keep on saying that?

chapters.title: The Window · 3
paragraphs: “Perhaps you’ll wake up and find the sun shining and the birds singing,” she said tenderly, smoothing the little boy’s hair. She could tell that her husband, with his biting remark that it wouldn’t be fine, had crushed his spirits. Going to the Lighthouse was a passion of his, she saw. And then, as though her husband had not said enough with his biting remark that it wouldn’t be fine tomorrow, this hateful little man had to go and rub it in all over again.
“Perhaps it will be fine tomorrow,” she said, smoothing his hair.

The only thing she could do now was praise the refrigerator and leaf through the Stores catalogue, hoping to come upon something like a rake or a mowing machine, whose prongs and handles would take the utmost skill and care to cut out. All these young men were parodies of her husband, she reflected: he said it would rain; they said it would be a full-blown tornado.

But here, as she turned the page, her search for the picture of a rake or a mowing machine was suddenly interrupted. There had been a gruff murmur, broken now and then as pipes were taken out and put back in, which had kept assuring her, though she could not hear what was said (sitting as she was in the window), that the men were talking happily. This sound had gone on for half an hour now, and had taken its soothing place in the scale of sounds pressing in on her, such as the tap of balls on bats, and the sharp, sudden bark now and then, “How’s that? How’s that?” of the children playing cricket. And it had stopped. That left only the monotonous fall of the waves on the beach. For the most part the waves beat a measured and soothing rhythm to her thoughts, and seemed to repeat comfortingly over and over, as she sat with the children, the words of some old lullaby, murmured by nature: “I am guarding you—I am your support.” But at other times, suddenly and unexpectedly, especially when her mind lifted itself a little from the task actually in hand, they had no such kind meaning. Instead, like a ghostly roll of drums, they beat out relentlessly the measure of life, made you think of the island being destroyed and swallowed by the sea, and warned her, whose day had slipped past in one quick task after another, that it was all as fleeting as a rainbow. Now this sound of the waves, which had been muffled and hidden under the other sounds, suddenly thundered hollow in her ears and made her look up with a rush of terror.

They had stopped talking; that was the explanation. In a single second she fell from the tension that had gripped her to the opposite extreme, which, as if to repay her for the feeling she had wasted, was cool, amused, and even faintly malicious. Poor Charles Tansley, she concluded, had been dropped. That mattered little to her. If her husband needed sacrifices (and indeed he did), she cheerfully offered him Charles Tansley, who had snubbed her little boy.

For one moment more she listened, her head raised, as if she were waiting for some habitual sound, some regular mechanical sound. And then she heard something rhythmical, half spoken, half chanted, starting up in the garden as her husband paced up and down the terrace, something between a croak and a song. She was soothed once more, reassured that all was well, and looking down at the book on her knee she found the picture of a pocketknife with six blades, which could only be cut out if James was very careful.
Suddenly a loud cry, like a sleepwalker’s, half awake, something about
Stormed at with shot and shell

shouted out with the fiercest intensity right in her ear, made her look round anxiously to see whether anyone had heard him. Only Lily Briscoe, she was relieved to find; and that didn’t matter. But the sight of the girl at the edge of the lawn, painting, jogged her memory: she was meant to be holding her head as still as she could for Lily’s picture. Lily’s picture! Mrs. Ramsay smiled. With her little Chinese eyes and her puckered-up face she would never marry; nobody could take her painting very seriously; but she was an independent little creature, and Mrs. Ramsay liked her for that. So, remembering her promise, she bowed her head.

chapters.title: The Window · 4
paragraphs: Indeed, he nearly knocked her easel over, bearing down on her with his hands waving and shouting out “Boldly we rode and well.” But mercifully he turned sharply and rode off, to die gloriously, she supposed, on the heights of Balaclava, like Tennyson’s Light Brigade. Never was anybody at once so ridiculous and so alarming. But as long as he kept on like that, waving and shouting, she was safe; he would not stand still and look at her picture. And that was what Lily Briscoe could not have endured. Even while she looked at the mass, at the line, at the color, at Mrs. Ramsay sitting in the window with James, she kept a feeler out on her surroundings, in case someone should creep up and she should suddenly find her picture being looked at. But now, with all her senses sharpened as they were, looking and straining until the color of the wall and the clematis beyond burned into her eyes, she became aware of someone coming out of the house and coming toward her. Somehow she guessed from the footstep that it was William Bankes. So although her brush quivered, she did not turn her canvas face down on the grass, as she would have done if it had been Mr. Tansley, Paul Rayley, Minta Doyle, or practically anybody else. She let it stand. William Bankes stood beside her.

The two of them had rooms in the village, and so, walking in and walking out and parting late on doormats, they had exchanged little remarks about the soup, about the children, about one thing and another, and these had made them allies. So now, when he took up his position beside her in his judicial way (he was old enough to be her father too: a botanist and a widower, who smelled of soap and was very scrupulous and clean), she just stood there. He just stood there. Excellent shoes, he observed of hers. They let the toes spread out naturally. Since they lodged in the same house, he had also noticed how orderly she was—up before breakfast and off to paint, alone, he believed. Presumably she was poor, and she certainly lacked Miss Doyle’s complexion and allure; but she had a good sense which, in his eyes, put her above that young lady. Take now, for instance: when Ramsay came bearing down on them, shouting and waving his arms, Miss Briscoe understood, he felt certain.
Someone had blundered.

Mr. Ramsay glared at them. He glared at them without seeming to see them. That did make them both vaguely uncomfortable. Together they had seen something they were not meant to see. They had intruded on a privacy. So, Lily thought, it was probably an excuse to move, to get out of earshot, that made Mr. Bankes say almost at once something about its being chilly and suggest they take a walk. She could come, yes. But it was hard for her to take her eyes off her picture.

The clematis was a bright violet; the wall was a staring white. Since that was how she saw them, she would not have thought it honest to tamper with them, even though it had been the fashion, ever since Mr. Paunceforte came, to see everything as pale, elegant, half-transparent. And then, beneath the color, there was the shape. When she looked, she could see it all so clearly, so commandingly. It was when she picked up her brush that everything changed. In that moment’s flight between the picture and the canvas the demons fell on her—the demons who often brought her close to tears, and made this passage from idea to work as frightening as a dark corridor is to a child. That was often how she felt: fighting against terrible odds to keep her courage up, to say, “But this is what I see; this is what I see,” and so to hug to her breast some miserable scrap of her vision, while a thousand forces did their best to tear it away. And it was then too, as she started to paint, in that chill and windy way, that other things pushed in on her: how inadequate she was, how insignificant, keeping house for her father off the Brompton Road. She could barely control the impulse to throw herself (thank Heaven she had always resisted so far) at Mrs. Ramsay’s knee and tell her—but what could anyone tell her? “I’m in love with you?” No, that wasn’t true. “I’m in love with all this,” with a wave of her hand at the hedge, the house, the children? It was absurd; it was impossible. Nobody could say what they meant. So now she put her brushes neatly side by side in the box and said to William Bankes:

“It suddenly gets cold. The sun seems to give less heat,” she said, glancing around, for it was still bright enough. The grass kept its soft deep green; purple passionflowers starred the greenery on the house; and from the high blue, rooks let fall their cool cries. But something moved and flashed; a silver wing turned in the air. It was September, after all—mid-September—and it was past six in the evening. So they wandered off down the garden the usual way, by the tennis lawn and the pampas grass, to the gap in the thick hedge. Red-hot pokers guarded it like braziers of clear burning coal, and between them the blue water of the bay looked bluer than ever.

They came there regularly every evening, drawn by some need. It was as if the water floated off and set sailing thoughts that had grown stagnant on dry land, and even gave their bodies some kind of physical relief. First the pulse of color flooded the bay with blue, and the heart expanded with it and the body swam, only to be checked and chilled the next instant by the prickly blackness on the ruffled waves. Then, from behind the great black rock, almost every evening, a fountain of white water spurted up at irregular moments, so that you had to watch for it, and it was a delight when it came. And while you waited for that, you watched wave after wave on the pale half-moon of the beach, smoothly shedding a film of mother-of-pearl again and again.

They both smiled, standing there. They both felt a shared hilarity, stirred up by the moving waves, and then by the swift, cutting race of a sailboat, which sliced a curve in the bay and stopped; shivered; let its sail drop. And then, with a natural instinct to complete the picture after this swift movement, both of them looked at the dunes far away, and instead of merriment they felt a sadness come over them—partly because the thing was finished, and partly because distant views seem to outlast the person gazing at them by a million years (Lily thought), and to be communing already with a sky that looks down on an earth entirely at rest.

As he looked at the far-off sandhills, William Bankes thought of Ramsay. He thought of a road in Westmorland, and of Ramsay striding along it on his own, wrapped in that solitude which seemed to be the air he naturally breathed. But then, William Bankes remembered (this must refer to something that actually happened), a hen interrupted it all, spreading her wings out to shield a brood of little chicks. Ramsay stopped, pointed his stick at them and said, “Pretty—pretty.” Bankes had taken it as a strange light thrown into his heart, a sign of his simplicity and his feeling for humble things. Yet it seemed to him that their friendship had stopped there, on that stretch of road. After that, Ramsay married. After that, what with one thing and another, the juice went out of their friendship. Whose fault that was he couldn’t say; it was only that, in time, repetition replaced newness. They met to repeat themselves. But in this wordless dialogue with the sand dunes he held that his affection for Ramsay was not the least bit smaller. There it lay, his friendship, as sharp and real as ever, laid up among the sandhills across the bay, like the body of a young man kept in peat for a hundred years with the red still fresh on his lips.

For the sake of this friendship he was anxious—and perhaps also to clear himself, in his own mind, of the charge of having dried up and shrunk, since Ramsay lived amid a crowd of children while Bankes was a childless widower—he was anxious that Lily Briscoe should not run Ramsay down (in his own way he was a great man), but should still understand how matters stood between them. The friendship had begun long years ago and had petered out on a road in Westmorland, where the hen spread her wings in front of her chicks. Ramsay had married after that, and because their paths went different ways there had been, through nobody’s fault certainly, a certain tendency to repeat themselves whenever they met.

Yes. That was it. He was done. He turned away from the view. And as he turned to walk back the other way, up the drive, Mr. Bankes noticed things that would never have struck him if those sandhills had not shown him the body of his friendship, laid up in peat with the red on its lips. There was Cam, for instance, the little girl, Ramsay’s youngest daughter, picking sweet alyssum on the bank. She was wild and fierce. The nursemaid told her to “give a flower to the gentleman,” and she would not. No! no! no! she would not! She clenched her fist. She stamped her foot. And about his friendship Mr. Bankes felt aged and saddened, and somehow put in the wrong by her. He must have dried up and shrunk.

The Ramsays weren’t rich, and how they managed it all was a wonder. Eight children! Eight children fed on philosophy! And here came another one, Jasper this time, wandering by to take a shot at a bird, as he put it casually, and pumping Lily’s hand like a pump handle on his way past, so that Mr. Bankes said bitterly how _she_ was a favorite. Now there was schooling to think about (though true, Mrs. Ramsay perhaps had a little money of her own), to say nothing of the everyday wear and tear on the shoes and stockings of those “great fellows,” well-grown, angular, ruthless young things every one of them. As for telling them apart, or knowing the order they came in, he couldn’t. In private he named them after the kings and queens of England: Cam the Wicked, James the Ruthless, Andrew the Just, Prue the Fair—because Prue would be beautiful, he thought, how could she not be?—and Andrew would have brains. Walking up the drive, while Lily Briscoe said yes and no and capped his remarks (she was in love with them all, in love with this world), he weighed up Ramsay’s case. He felt sorry for him; he envied him. It was as though he had watched Ramsay shed all the glories of isolation and austerity that crowned him as a young man, and load himself for good with fluttering wings and clucking domestic life. They gave him something—William Bankes granted that. It would have been nice if Cam had stuck a flower in his buttonhole, or climbed over his shoulder the way she climbed over her father’s, to look at a picture of Vesuvius erupting. But his old friends couldn’t help feeling that they had also destroyed something. What would a stranger make of him now? What did this Lily Briscoe make of him? Who could fail to notice that habits were growing on him—eccentricities, perhaps weaknesses? That a man with his intellect could sink so low—no, the phrase was too harsh—could lean so heavily on other people’s praise: that was astonishing.
“Oh, but,” said Lily, “think of his work!”

Whenever she “thought of his work,” she always saw a large kitchen table clearly in front of her. It was Andrew’s doing. She had asked him what his father’s books were about. “Subject and object and the nature of reality,” Andrew had said. And when she said Heavens, she had no idea what that meant, he told her, “Think of a kitchen table, then, when you’re not there.”

So whenever Mr. Ramsay’s work came to mind, what she saw was a scrubbed kitchen table. Just now it sat lodged in the fork of a pear tree, since they had come into the orchard. With a painful effort she concentrated her mind—not on the tree’s silver-studded bark, nor on its leaves shaped like fish, but on a phantom kitchen table stuck up there with its four legs in the air: one of those scrubbed plank tables, grained and knotted, whose virtue seems to have been laid bare by years of muscular honesty. Naturally, if you spent your days seeing angular essences like this, shrinking lovely evenings, with all their flamingo clouds and their blue and silver, down to a four-legged table of white pine (and the finest minds did exactly that), naturally you could not be judged like other people.

Mr. Bankes liked her for telling him to “think of his work.” He had thought about it, again and again. Countless times he had said, “Ramsay is one of those men who do their best work before they are forty.” At only twenty-five he had made a definite contribution to philosophy in one small book; everything afterward was more or less enlargement and repetition. But very few men, he said, stopping by the pear tree—well brushed, scrupulously precise, exquisitely judicial—ever make a definite contribution to anything at all. All at once, as if a movement of his hand had set it loose, the load of impressions of him that she had been storing up tipped over, and everything she felt about him came pouring down in a heavy avalanche. That was one sensation. Then the essence of the man rose up like a vapor. That was another. The sharpness of what she perceived held her fixed; it was his severity; his goodness. I respect you in every atom, she told him silently; you are not vain; you are wholly impersonal; you are finer than Mr. Ramsay; you are the finest human being I know; you have no wife and no child (she longed, with no sexual feeling at all, to cherish that loneliness); you live for science (sliced potatoes, seen in cross section, rose before her eyes without her willing it); to praise you would insult you; generous, pure-hearted, heroic man! Yet in the same breath she recalled that he had brought a valet all the way up here; that he disapproved of dogs on chairs; that he would lecture for hours (until Mr. Ramsay stormed out of the room) on salt in vegetables and the wickedness of English cooks.

How, then, did it all work out? How did you judge people, think of them? How did you add up this and that and conclude that what you felt was liking, or disliking? And what meaning did those words have, after all? Standing now by the pear tree, seemingly transfixed, she felt impressions of those two men pour in on her. Following her thought was like following a voice that speaks too fast for your pencil to take it down, and the voice was her own voice, saying unprompted things that were undeniable, everlasting, contradictory, so that even the cracks and bumps on the bark of the pear tree were fixed there irrevocably for eternity. You have greatness, she went on, but Mr. Ramsay has none of it. He is petty, selfish, vain, egotistical; he is spoiled; he is a tyrant; he wears Mrs. Ramsay to death; but he has what you (she addressed Mr. Bankes) do not have: a fiery unworldliness; he knows nothing about trifles; he loves dogs and his children. He has eight. You have none. Didn’t he come down in two coats the other night and let Mrs. Ramsay trim his hair into a pudding-bowl cut? All of this danced up and down like a swarm of gnats, each one separate but all marvelously held together in an invisible elastic net—danced up and down in Lily’s mind, in and around the branches of the pear tree, where the scrubbed kitchen table, symbol of her profound respect for Mr. Ramsay’s mind, still hung in effigy. Then her thought, which had spun faster and faster, exploded from its own intensity; she felt released; a shot went off close by, and out of its fragments there came flying, frightened, effusive, tumultuous, a flock of starlings.

“Jasper!” Mr. Bankes said. They turned in the direction the starlings had flown, over the terrace. Following the fast birds as they scattered across the sky, they went through the gap in the tall hedge and ran straight into Mr. Ramsay, who boomed at them tragically, “Someone had blundered!”

His eyes, glazed with emotion and defiant with tragic intensity, met theirs for a second and trembled on the edge of recognition. But then he raised his hand halfway to his face, as if to ward off, to brush away, in an agony of peevish shame, their ordinary gaze; as if he were begging them to hold back for a moment what he knew was inevitable; as if he were pressing on them his own childlike resentment at being interrupted, yet even in the moment of being found out would not be routed completely, but was determined to hold on to something of this delicious emotion, this impure rapture that he was ashamed of but reveled in. He turned abruptly and slammed his private door on them. And Lily Briscoe and Mr. Bankes, looking uneasily up into the sky, saw that the flock of starlings Jasper had scattered with his gun had settled on the tops of the elm trees.

chapters.title: The Window · 5
paragraphs: “And even if it isn’t fine tomorrow,” Mrs. Ramsay said, looking up at William Bankes and Lily Briscoe as they went by, “there’ll be another day. And now—” She was thinking that Lily’s charm lay in her Chinese eyes, set aslant in that small white puckered face, though only a clever man would see it. “And now stand up and let me measure your leg.” They might go to the Lighthouse after all, and she had to check whether the leg of the stocking should be an inch or two longer.

Smiling, because a wonderful idea had flashed on her that very second—William and Lily should marry—she took the heather-mixture stocking, with its crisscross of steel needles at the top, and measured it against James’s leg.

“My dear, stand still,” she said. For James, in his jealousy, did not like serving as a measuring block for the Lighthouse keeper’s little boy, and he fidgeted on purpose; and if he did that, how could she see whether it was too long or too short? she asked.

She glanced up—what demon had got into him, her youngest, her darling?—and her eye fell on the room and on the chairs, and she thought how dreadfully shabby they were. Their guts, as Andrew put it the other day, were spilling all over the floor. But then, she asked herself, why buy good chairs only to have them ruined up here all winter, when the house, with just one old woman to look after it, was absolutely dripping with damp? Never mind. The rent came to exactly twopence halfpenny; the children adored the place; it was good for her husband to be three thousand miles—or, to be accurate, three hundred—away from his library and his lectures and his disciples; and there was space for guests. Mats, camp beds, crazy ghosts of chairs and tables that had finished their years of service in London—up here they did well enough; and so did a photograph or two, and books. Books, she thought, seemed to grow on their own. She never had time to read them. Alas! Even the ones given to her and inscribed by the poet in his own hand—“For her whose wishes must be obeyed” … “The happier Helen of our days” …—it was a disgrace, but she had never read them. And neither Croom on the Mind nor Bates on the Savage Customs of Polynesia (“My dear, stand still,” she said) was something you could send to the Lighthouse. Sooner or later, she supposed, the house would be so shabby that something would have to be done about it. If only they could learn to wipe their feet and stop bringing the beach indoors—that would be something. As for crabs, she had to admit, if Andrew really wanted to dissect them, or if Jasper thought seaweed could be made into soup, there was no stopping it; nor Rose’s collections—shells, reeds, stones; for her children were gifted, though each in a quite different way. And so, she sighed, her eyes taking in the whole room from floor to ceiling while she held the stocking to James’s leg, the result was that things grew shabbier and shabbier, summer after summer. The mat was fading; the wallpaper was coming loose and flapping. Nobody could tell anymore that the pattern was roses. Still, things are bound to spoil if every door in a house stands open all the time and not one locksmith in all Scotland can fix a bolt. What good did it do to drape a green cashmere shawl over the corner of a picture frame? Within two weeks it would be the color of pea soup. But the doors were what annoyed her; every single door was left open. She listened. The drawing-room door stood open; so did the hall door; the bedroom doors sounded open too; and the landing window was certainly open, since she had opened it herself. Windows open, doors shut—simple as that was, could none of them remember it? At night she would go into the maids’ bedrooms and find them shut up tight as ovens—all except Marie’s, the Swiss girl, who would sooner do without a bath than without fresh air. But then at home, the girl had said, “the mountains are so beautiful.” She had said it last night, gazing out of the window with tears in her eyes. “The mountains are so beautiful.” Her father was dying there, as Mrs. Ramsay knew. He was going to leave them fatherless. When the girl spoke, all Mrs. Ramsay’s scolding and demonstrating (how to make a bed, how to open a window, her hands closing and spreading like a Frenchwoman’s) had quietly folded itself around her, just as a bird’s wings fold themselves quietly after a flight through the sunshine, and the blue of its feathers turns from bright steel to soft purple. She had stood there without a word, because there was nothing to say. He had cancer of the throat. Remembering it—how she had stood there, how the girl had said, “At home the mountains are so beautiful,” and how there was no hope, no hope of any kind—she felt a spasm of irritation, and spoke sharply to James:
“Stand still. Don’t be difficult,” so that he knew at once that her sternness was real, and he straightened his leg, and she measured it.
The stocking was too short by at least half an inch, even allowing for the fact that Sorley’s little boy would be smaller than James.
“It’s too short,” she said, “much too short.”

Nobody ever looked so sad. Bitter and black, halfway down, in the dark, in the shaft that ran from the sunlight into the depths, a tear perhaps formed; a tear dropped; the water swayed to and fro, received it, and grew still. Nobody ever looked so sad.

But was it nothing but looks? people said. What was there behind it—her beauty, her splendor? Had he blown his brains out, they asked; had he died the week before they were to be married—some other, earlier lover, rumors of whom reached you? Or was there nothing? Nothing but an incomparable beauty that she lived behind and could do nothing to disturb? For although she could easily have said, at some moment of intimacy, when stories of great passion, of love defeated, of ambition thwarted came her way, that she too had known it, or felt it, or been through it herself, she never spoke. She was always silent. So she knew—she knew without having learned. Her simplicity got to the bottom of what clever people falsified. Her singleness of mind made her drop straight down like a stone, land precisely like a bird; it gave her, naturally, this swoop and fall of the spirit onto the truth, which delighted, eased, sustained—falsely perhaps.

(Once, hearing her voice on the telephone, Mr. Bankes had said, “Nature has but little clay,” deeply moved by it, though all she was telling him was some fact about a train, “like that of which she moulded you.” He could see her at the far end of the line: Greek, blue-eyed, with a straight nose. How out of place it felt to be on the telephone to a woman like that. It was as if the Graces had come together and joined hands in fields of asphodel to make that face. Yes, he would take the 10:30 from Euston.

“But she’s no more aware of her beauty than a child is,” said Mr. Bankes, putting down the receiver and crossing the room to see how the workmen were getting on with a hotel they were building at the back of his house. And he thought of Mrs. Ramsay as he watched that bustle among the unfinished walls. For there was always, he thought, something incongruous to be worked into the harmony of her face. She would clap a deerstalker’s hat on her head; she would run across the lawn in galoshes to snatch a child out of mischief. So if it was merely her beauty you thought of, you had to remember the quivering thing, the living thing (they were carrying bricks up a little plank as he watched them), and work it into the picture. Or if you thought of her simply as a woman, you had to give her some freak of idiosyncrasy; or imagine some hidden wish to throw off her royalty of form, as if her beauty bored her, and everything men say about beauty, and she wanted only to be like other people, insignificant. He did not know. He did not know. He must get to his work.)

Mrs. Ramsay went on knitting her hairy, reddish-brown stocking, her head absurdly framed by the gilt picture frame, by the green shawl she had thrown over its edge, and by the authenticated masterpiece by Michelangelo. She smoothed away whatever had been harsh in her manner a moment ago, lifted his head, and kissed her little boy on the forehead. “Let’s find another picture to cut out,” she said.

chapters.title: The Window · 6
paragraphs: But what had happened?
Someone had blundered.

Starting out of her musing, she gave meaning to words she had been holding in her mind, meaningless, for a long stretch of time. “Someone had blundered”—the line from Tennyson’s “The Charge of the Light Brigade.” She fixed her shortsighted eyes on her husband, who was now bearing down on her, and gazed steadily until, as he came close, she could see (the jingle paired itself off in her head) that something had happened; someone had blundered. But she could not for the life of her think what.

He shivered; he quivered. It had all been shattered, destroyed: all his vanity, all his pleasure in his own splendor as he rode, fell as a thunderbolt, fierce as a hawk, at the head of his men through the valley of death. Stormed at by shot and shell, boldly we rode and well, flashed through the valley of death, volleyed and thundered—only to charge headlong into Lily Briscoe and William Bankes. He quivered; he shivered.

Not for the world would she have spoken to him. She knew the signs: his eyes turned away, and a curious gathering-in of his whole person, as if he were wrapping himself up and needed privacy in which to get his balance back. They told her he was outraged and in anguish. She stroked James’s head; she passed on to him what she felt for her husband. As she watched him color the white dress shirt of a gentleman in the Army and Navy Stores catalogue yellow with his chalk, she thought what a delight it would be to her if he turned out to be a great artist; and why shouldn’t he? He had a splendid forehead. Then, looking up as her husband passed her once more, she was relieved to find that the ruin was veiled. Domestic life had won; habit was crooning its soothing rhythm. So when he stopped deliberately at the window as his turn came round again, and bent down, teasing and whimsical, to tickle James’s bare calf with a sprig of something, she scolded him lightly for having sent off “that poor young man,” Charles Tansley. Tansley had had to go in and write his dissertation, he said.
“James will have to write _his_ dissertation one of these days,” he added ironically, flicking his sprig.
Hating his father, James brushed away the tickling spray with which his father was teasing his youngest son’s bare leg, in that way of his that was a mix of sternness and humor.
Mrs. Ramsay said she was trying to finish these wretched stockings so she could send them to Sorley’s little boy tomorrow.
There wasn’t the slightest chance in the world that they could go to the Lighthouse tomorrow, Mr. Ramsay snapped out irritably.
How did he know? she asked. The wind often changed.

It enraged him, the extraordinary irrationality of what she had just said, the folly of the female mind. He had ridden through the valley of death, had been shattered, had shivered; and now here she was defying the facts, letting his children hope for something utterly impossible—telling lies, in effect. He stamped on the stone step. “Damn you,” he said. Yet what had she actually said? Only that tomorrow might be fine. And so it might.
Not with the barometer falling and the wind due west.

To her it was a horrible outrage against human decency: to pursue the truth with so astonishing a disregard for other people’s feelings, to rip apart the thin veils of civilization so wantonly, so brutally. She gave no answer. Dazed and blinded, she bowed her head, as though letting the pelting of jagged hail, the soaking of dirty water, splash all over her without one word of reproach. There was nothing to be said.
He stood by her in silence. At last, very humbly, he said that he would walk over and ask the Coastguards, if she liked.
There was nobody she revered as she revered him.

She was perfectly willing to take his word for it, she said. It only meant they wouldn’t need to cut sandwiches—nothing more. Being a woman, she naturally had people coming to her all day long with one thing or another; this one wanted this, that one wanted that; the children were growing up; she often felt she was nothing but a sponge, soaked through with human emotions. And then he said, Damn you. He said, It must rain. He said, It won’t rain; and at once a Heaven of safety opened in front of her. There was no one she revered more. She wasn’t good enough to tie his shoelaces, she felt.

Already ashamed of that outburst, of the way he had waved his hands while charging at the head of his troops, Mr. Ramsay gave his son’s bare legs one more rather sheepish prod. Then, as though she had given him permission, he plunged off into the evening air. The movement struck his wife as oddly like the great sea lion at the Zoo, who tumbles over backward once he has swallowed his fish and flounders away, so that the water in the tank slops from one side to the other. The air was already thinning; it was drawing the substance out of the leaves and hedges, but, as if to make up for it, it gave the roses and pinks a luster they had lacked all day.
“Someone had blundered,” he said again, striding off, up and down the terrace.

How extraordinarily his tone had changed, though! It was like the cuckoo—“in June he gets out of tune”—as though he were trying out, groping toward, some phrase to suit a new mood, and, with nothing but this one to hand, made do with it, cracked as it was. Yet it sounded absurd, “Someone had blundered,” spoken that way, almost like a question, with no conviction at all, in a singsong voice. Mrs. Ramsay couldn’t help smiling, and before long, sure enough, pacing up and down, he hummed it, let it go, and went quiet.

He was safe; his privacy had been given back to him. He paused to light his pipe and glanced once at his wife and son in the window. You know how, on an express train, you lift your eyes from a page and see a farm, a tree, a huddle of cottages, as if they were a picture illustrating the printed words, a confirmation of them, and you go back to your book strengthened and content. Just so, without his really making out either his son or his wife, the sight of them gave him strength and contentment, and blessed his effort to reach a perfectly clear grasp of the problem that now absorbed the energies of his splendid mind.

It was a splendid mind. Suppose thought is like a piano keyboard, divided into so many notes, or like the alphabet, set out in twenty-six letters in order. Then his splendid mind could run through those letters one after another, firmly and accurately, with no trouble at all, until it arrived at, let us say, the letter Q. He reached Q. Hardly anyone in the whole of England ever gets to Q. Pausing a moment here by the stone urn with the geraniums in it, he caught sight of his wife and son together in the window, but far, far off now, like children gathering shells, divinely innocent, busy with small trifles at their feet, and somehow wholly unprotected against a doom that he could see coming. They needed his protection; he gave it to them. But what about after Q? What comes next? Beyond Q lie a number of letters, and the last of them can barely be seen by mortal eyes; it glimmers red, far away. Z is reached only once in a generation, by one man. Still, getting to R would be something. Here, at least, was Q. At Q he dug in his heels. Of Q he was certain. Q he could prove. If Q, then, is Q—R—At this point he knocked the ash out of his pipe with two or three ringing taps against the ram’s horn that formed the urn’s handle, and carried on. “Then R …” He steeled himself. He clenched himself.

Then came to his aid the qualities that would have saved a ship’s crew adrift on a scorching sea with a flask of water and six biscuits—endurance and fairness, foresight, devotion, skill. Well then, R is—what is R?

Like the leathery eyelid of a lizard, a shutter flickered down over his intense gaze and hid the letter R. In that flash of dark he could hear people saying it—that he was a failure, that R was beyond him. He would never get to R. Once more, on to R. R——

Once again the qualities came to his aid that, on some desolate expedition across the frozen solitudes of the Polar regions, would have made him the leader, the guide, the counselor—the one whose temper, neither hopeful nor gloomy, looks calmly at what lies ahead and meets it. R——

Again the lizard’s eye flickered. The veins stood out on his forehead. The geranium in the urn leapt startlingly into view, and there among its leaves, whether he wanted to or not, he could see that old, obvious division of men into two kinds. On one side were the steady ones, plodding and persevering with superhuman strength, who go through the whole alphabet in order, all twenty-six letters, beginning to end. On the other were the gifted, the inspired, who by some miracle take in all the letters at once, in a single flash—the way of genius. Genius he did not have; he made no claim to it. But he had, or might have had, the power to go through every letter from A to Z, accurately and in order. In the meantime, he was stuck on Q. Onward, then—on to R.

Over him crept feelings worthy of a leader who, with the snow now beginning to fall and mist closing over the mountaintop, knows he must lie down and die before morning. They faded the color of his eyes, and even in the two minutes it took him to walk the length of the terrace, they gave him the bleached look of shriveled old age. But he would not die lying down. He would find some crag of rock, and there, with his eyes on the storm, straining to the last to see through the darkness, he would die on his feet. R he would never reach.

He stood stock-still by the urn, the geranium spilling over its rim. After all, he asked himself, out of a thousand million men, how many ever get to Z? Surely the leader of a forlorn hope has the right to ask that, and to answer, without betraying the expedition following him, “One, perhaps.” One in a generation. Should he be blamed, then, for not being that one? so long as he has worked honestly, given everything in his power, until there is nothing left to give? And how long will his fame last? Even a dying hero may be forgiven for wondering, before he dies, how men will talk of him when he is gone. Perhaps his fame will last two thousand years. And what are two thousand years? (asked Mr. Ramsay ironically, staring at the hedge). What indeed, if you gaze down from a mountaintop across the long wastes of the ages? The very stone your boot kicks aside will outlast Shakespeare. His own small light would shine for a year or two, not very brightly, and would then be swallowed up in some larger light, and that in a larger one still. (He peered into the darkness, into the tangle of twigs.) So who could blame the leader of that forlorn party—which has, after all, climbed high enough to see the waste of the years and the stars perishing—if, before death stiffens his limbs so that he can no longer move, he lifts his numb fingers to his brow a little deliberately and squares his shoulders, so that the search party, when it comes, will find him dead at his post, a fine figure of a soldier? Mr. Ramsay squared his shoulders and stood very straight beside the urn.

If he stands like that for a moment, dwelling on fame, on search parties, on the cairns of stones that grateful followers will heap over his bones, who will blame him? And last of all, who will blame the leader of the doomed expedition if, after venturing to the very limit, spending his strength down to the final ounce, and falling asleep with little care whether he ever wakes, he now feels a pricking in his toes and realizes that he is alive—and that, on the whole, he doesn’t mind being alive, but wants sympathy, and whisky, and someone to hear the story of his sufferings right away? Who will blame him? Who will not be secretly glad when the hero lays his armor aside, and pauses by the window, and gazes at his wife and son? They are very far away at first, then little by little they draw nearer and nearer, until lips and book and head are plain before him, though still lovely and strange to him after the intensity of his isolation, and the waste of the ages, and the perishing of the stars. And when at last he slips his pipe into his pocket and bows his magnificent head before her—who will blame him for paying homage to the beauty of the world?

chapters.title: The Window · 7
paragraphs: But his son hated him. James hated him for coming up to them, for stopping and looking down at them; for interrupting them; for the lofty exaltation of his gestures; for his magnificent head; for his demands and his egotism (for there he stood, insisting that they attend to him). Most of all, though, he hated the twang and twitter of his father’s emotion, which quivered all around them and upset the perfect simplicity and good sense of the way things were between him and his mother. He stared hard at the page, hoping that would make his father move on; he pointed his finger at a word, hoping to win back his mother’s attention, which, he knew with anger, wavered the moment his father stopped. But no. Nothing would make Mr. Ramsay move on. There he stood, demanding sympathy.

Mrs. Ramsay had been sitting loosely, with her son folded in her arm. She braced herself, and, turning halfway round, seemed to raise herself with an effort, and then at once to send pouring straight up into the air a shower of energy, a column of spray. At the same time she looked vivid and alive, as though every energy she had were being fused into power, burning and lighting everything up (though she sat quietly, picking up her stocking again). And into this delicious fruitfulness, this fountain and spray of life, the fatal sterility of the male drove itself like a beak of brass, barren and bare. He wanted sympathy. He was a failure, he said. Mrs. Ramsay’s needles flashed. Never taking his eyes off her face, Mr. Ramsay said again that he was a failure. She blew the words back at him. “Charles Tansley …” she said. But he needed more than that. What he wanted was sympathy: to be reassured, first of all, that he was a genius, and then to be drawn inside the circle of life, warmed and comforted, to have his senses given back to him, his barrenness made fruitful, and every room in the house filled with life—the drawing room; the kitchen behind it; the bedrooms above the kitchen; and past those, the nurseries. They must be furnished; they must be full of life.

Charles Tansley considered him the greatest metaphysician of the day, she said. But he needed more than that. He needed sympathy. He needed to be told that he, too, lived at the heart of life; that he was needed; not just here, but everywhere in the world. Needles flashing, upright and sure of herself, she conjured up drawing room and kitchen and made them all glow; she invited him to be at ease there, to come and go, to enjoy himself. She laughed; she knitted. James stood very stiffly between her knees and felt all her strength blaze up only to be swallowed and put out by the beak of brass, the parched scimitar of the male, which struck without mercy, over and over, demanding sympathy.

He was a failure, he said again. Well, look, then; feel, then. Her needles flashing, glancing all around—out of the window, into the room, at James himself—she reassured him past any shadow of doubt, with her laugh, her poise, her capability (the way a nurse carrying a lamp through a dark room calms a fretful child), that it was real: the house was full; the garden was blossoming. If he trusted her completely, nothing would harm him; however deep he buried himself, or however high he climbed, never for a second would he be without her. And as she boasted like this of her power to enfold and protect, there was hardly a shell of her own self left for her to recognize herself by; it had all been poured out and spent. And James, standing stiffly between her knees, felt her rise up like a fruit tree full of rosy flowers, thick with leaves and dancing branches, and into it the beak of brass, the parched scimitar of his father, that egotistical man, plunged and struck, demanding sympathy.

At last, filled with her words like a child who falls asleep contented, he looked at her with humble gratitude, restored and renewed, and said he would go for a stroll; he would go and watch the children play cricket. Off he went.

All at once Mrs. Ramsay seemed to fold up on herself, one petal closing inside another, and the whole fabric collapsed on itself, worn out. She had just strength enough to move her finger across the page of Grimm’s fairy tale, in an exquisite giving-way to exhaustion. And through her there throbbed the rapture of successful creation, like the pulse in a spring that has stretched to its widest and now softly stops beating.

As he walked away, every beat of this pulse seemed to enclose her and her husband together, and to give each of them the comfort that two different notes, one high and one low, seem to give each other when they are struck at once and blend. But as the resonance faded, and she went back to the Fairy Tale, Mrs. Ramsay felt not just tired in body (she always felt this afterward, never at the time); her physical tiredness was also tinged with some faintly unpleasant feeling that had a different source. Not that she knew exactly what it came from as she read aloud the story of the Fisherman’s Wife. Nor would she let herself put her discontent into words when she saw—at the turn of the page, when she paused and heard, dully, ominously, a wave fall—what its source was. It was this. She disliked feeling, even for a second, that she was finer than her husband; and, beyond that, she could not stand being less than entirely sure, when she spoke to him, that what she said was true. The universities and the people who wanted him, the lectures and the books, and how supremely important they all were—none of that did she doubt for a moment. What unsettled her was the relationship between them, and the way he came to her like that, in the open, where anyone could see. Because then people said he depended on her, when they must surely know that he was by far the more important of the two, and that what she gave the world was nothing next to what he gave it. But then there was the other thing too: that she could not tell him the truth. She was afraid, say, about the greenhouse roof and how much it would cost to repair, fifty pounds perhaps; and about his books, afraid he might guess what she half suspected, that his latest book was not quite his best (she had picked that up from William Bankes); and then there were the small everyday things she hid, and the children noticing, and the weight it put on them. All this took away from the whole joy, the pure joy, of the two notes sounding together, and made the sound die in her ear now with a dreary flatness.

There was a shadow across the page; she looked up. It was Augustus Carmichael shuffling by—just now, of all moments, when it was painful to be reminded that human relationships fall short, that even the most perfect one had flaws and could not survive the scrutiny that she, loving her husband and having an instinct for truth, turned on it; when it was painful to feel herself found guilty of unworthiness, and held back from doing what she was meant to do by these lies, these exaggerations. It was at this moment, while she was fretting so ignobly in the wake of her exaltation, that Mr. Carmichael came shuffling by in his yellow slippers, and some demon in her made her call out to him as he passed,
“Going indoors, Mr. Carmichael?”

chapters.title: The Window · 8
paragraphs: He made no answer. He took opium. According to the children, it had stained his beard yellow. Perhaps it had. What was plain to her was that the poor man was unhappy, and that he came to them every year to escape; and still, every year, she felt the same thing: he did not trust her. She would say, “I’m going into town. Can I get you stamps, paper, tobacco?” and feel him flinch. He did not trust her. His wife was to blame. She remembered the wicked way his wife had treated him, which had turned her, Mrs. Ramsay, to steel and adamant right there in that horrid little room in St. John’s Wood, when she had watched with her own eyes as that hateful woman turned him out of the house. He was untidy; he spilled things on his coat; he had all the tedious habits of an old man with nothing in the world to do; and she turned him out of the room. In her hateful way she said, “Now, Mrs. Ramsay and I want to have a little talk together,” and Mrs. Ramsay could see, as clearly as if they were before her eyes, the endless miseries of his life. Had he enough money for tobacco? Did he have to ask his wife for it? Half a crown? Eighteen pence? Oh, she could not bear to think of the small humiliations that woman put him through. And always now (she could not guess why, unless it came from that woman somehow) he shrank away from her. He never confided in her. Yet what more could she have done? A sunny room had been set aside for him. The children were kind to him. Not once had she shown any sign that he was unwelcome. In fact she went out of her way to be friendly. Do you want stamps, do you want tobacco? Here’s a book you might enjoy, and so on. And after all—after all (at this point, without being aware of it, she drew herself up, and the sense of her own beauty, so seldom present to her, came to her now)—after all, she did not usually find it hard to make people like her. There was George Manning, for example; Mr. Wallace; famous men though they were, they would come to see her in the evening, quietly, and talk with her alone by her fire. She could not help knowing that she carried the torch of her beauty with her wherever she went; she carried it high into every room she walked into. And after all, however much she might veil it, and shrink from the monotonous bearing it forced on her, her beauty showed. She had been admired. She had been loved. She had walked into rooms where people sat mourning. Tears had been shed in front of her. Men, and women too, had set aside the multitude of things in their lives and allowed themselves, with her, the relief of simplicity. It wounded her that he should shrink from her. It hurt. And yet it was not a clean hurt, not a right one. That was what bothered her, coming as it did on top of her discontent with her husband: the feeling she had now—as Mr. Carmichael shuffled past, barely nodding in answer to her question, a book under his arm, in his yellow slippers—that she was under suspicion; that all this longing of hers to give, to help, was vanity. Was it for her own gratification that she wanted so instinctively to help, to give, so that people would say of her, “O Mrs. Ramsay! dear Mrs. Ramsay … Mrs. Ramsay, of course!” and need her, and send for her, and admire her? Wasn’t this what she secretly wanted? And so when Mr. Carmichael drew back from her, as he was doing at this very moment, slipping away to some corner where he did his acrostic puzzles endlessly, she felt not simply rebuffed in her instinct, but made aware of the pettiness of some part of herself, and of human relations—how flawed they are, how contemptible, how selfish, even at their best. Worn out and shabby, and presumably no longer (her cheeks were hollow, her hair was white) a sight to fill anyone’s eyes with joy, she had better give her mind to the story of the Fisherman and his Wife, and so calm that bundle of sensitiveness, her son James (none of her children was as sensitive as he was).

“The man’s heart grew heavy,” she read aloud, “and he did not want to go. ‘It is not right,’ he said to himself, but he went all the same. And when he reached the sea, the water was all purple and dark blue, and gray and thick, not green and yellow the way it had been, but it was still calm. And he stood there and said—”

Mrs. Ramsay could have wished her husband hadn’t picked that moment to stop. Why hadn’t he gone off to watch the children play cricket, as he’d said he would? But he said nothing; he looked; he nodded; he approved; he moved on. Before him he saw the hedge that had so many times rounded off a pause, signaled a conclusion; he saw his wife and child; he saw once more the urns with their trailing red geraniums, which had so often decorated his processes of thought and which bore them written up among their leaves, like scraps of paper you scribble notes on in the rush of reading. Seeing all this, he slid smoothly into speculation prompted by an article in _The Times_ on how many Americans visit Shakespeare’s house each year. Had Shakespeare never existed, he asked, would the world be much different from the way it is now? Does civilization advance because of great men? Is the ordinary person better off now than under the Pharaohs? And yet, he asked himself, is the ordinary person’s lot the right yardstick for measuring civilization? Possibly not. Possibly the greatest good depends on there being a slave class. The man who operates the lift in the Underground will always be necessary. He found the thought distasteful. He tossed his head. To escape it, he would find a way to take the arts down a peg. He would argue that the world exists for the ordinary person; that the arts are just ornament laid on top of human life; they do not express it. Nor does life need Shakespeare. Without knowing quite why he wanted to run Shakespeare down and to rescue the man who stands forever in the door of the lift, he snapped a leaf off the hedge. All this would have to be served up for the young men at Cardiff next month, he thought; out here on his terrace he was only foraging and picnicking (he tossed away the leaf he had picked so peevishly), like a man leaning down from his horse to gather a bunch of roses, or filling his pockets with nuts as he ambles comfortably through the lanes and fields of the countryside he has known since he was a boy. All of it was familiar: this bend, that stile, that path across the fields. He would spend hours this way in the evenings, with his pipe, thinking his way up and down and in and out of the old familiar lanes and commons, which were all dotted with the history of that campaign over there, the life of this statesman here, with poems and anecdotes, and with figures too, this thinker, that soldier; everything brisk and clear. But eventually the lane, the field, the common, the fruitful nut tree and the flowering hedge brought him to that further bend in the road where he always dismounted, tied his horse to a tree, and went on alone, on foot. He came to the edge of the lawn and gazed out over the bay below.

It was his fate, his particular nature, whether he liked it or not, to come out like this onto a spit of land that the sea is slowly eating away, and to stand there by himself like some desolate seabird. It was his power, his gift, to throw off everything superfluous all at once, shrinking and dwindling until he looked barer and felt leaner, even in his body, yet without losing any of the intensity of his mind; and in that state to stand on his little ledge, facing the darkness of human ignorance—how we know nothing, and the sea eats away the ground we stand on. That was his fate, his gift. But when he dismounted he had cast off every gesture and frill, all his trophies of nuts and roses, and had shrunk until he had forgotten not only his fame but his very name; and even in that desolation he stayed alert, sparing no phantom, indulging in no vision.
