And it was in this guise that he inspired a deep reverence, and pity, and gratitude as well, in William Bankes (now and then), in Charles Tansley (fawningly), and in his wife now, as she looked up and saw him standing at the edge of the lawn. It was the kind of gratitude that a stake, driven into the bed of a channel, with gulls perching on it and waves beating against it, inspires in boatloads of merrymakers, for the duty it has taken on of marking the channel out there in the floods, alone.

“But the father of eight children has no choice. …” He broke off his half-audible muttering, turned, sighed, lifted his eyes, looked for the figure of his wife reading stories to the little boy, and filled his pipe. He turned his back on the sight of human ignorance and human fate and the sea eating the ground we stand on—a sight which, had he been able to hold his gaze on it, might have led somewhere. And he took comfort in trifles so slight, next to the grand theme he had just been facing, that he was inclined to skip over that comfort, to disown it, as though for an honest man to be caught being happy in a world of misery were the most shameful crime of all. It was true: most of the time he was happy; he had his wife; he had his children; in six weeks he had promised to talk “some nonsense” to the young men of Cardiff about Locke, Hume, Berkeley, and the causes of the French Revolution. But all this, and the pleasure he took in it—in the phrases he turned, in the ardor of the young, in his wife’s beauty, in the tributes that came to him from Swansea, Cardiff, Exeter, Southampton, Kidderminster, Oxford, Cambridge—all of it had to be made light of and hidden under the words “talking nonsense,” because, in effect, he had not done the thing he might have done. It was a disguise. It was where a man took refuge who was afraid to own his own feelings, who could not say, This is what I like—this is what I am. And William Bankes and Lily Briscoe found it rather pitiful and distasteful; they wondered why such concealments were needed; why he always needed praise; why a man so brave in his thinking should be so timid in his living; how oddly he was both venerable and laughable at once.

Lily suspected that teaching and preaching are more than any human being can manage. (She was packing up her things.) If you are lifted up high, you are bound to come down with a crash somehow. Mrs. Ramsay gave him what he wanted too easily. And then the change must be so jarring, Lily said. He comes in from his books and finds us all playing games and chattering nonsense. Just think what a change that is from the things he thinks about, she said.
He was bearing down on them. Now he had stopped dead and was standing, silent, looking out at the sea. Now he had turned away again.

chapters.title: The Window · 9
paragraphs: Yes, Mr. Bankes agreed, his eyes following Mr. Ramsay as he went. It was a real shame. (Lily had said something about how he frightened her—how suddenly he swung from one mood to another.) Yes, said Mr. Bankes, it was a real shame that Ramsay couldn’t manage to behave a little more like other people. (He liked Lily Briscoe; with her he could talk about Ramsay perfectly openly.) That, he said, was exactly why young people no longer read Carlyle. Here was a crusty old grumbler who flew into a temper if his porridge was cold—so why should he lecture us? That, as far as Mr. Bankes could tell, was how the young talked these days. And it was a real shame, if you happened to believe, as he did, that Carlyle was among the great teachers of humanity. Lily was embarrassed to confess she hadn’t read a line of Carlyle since her schooldays. But to her mind, Mr. Ramsay was all the more likable for believing that if his little finger hurt, the entire world must be ending. _That_ wasn’t what bothered her. After all, who could be taken in by him? He openly begged you to flatter him and admire him; nobody was fooled by his little maneuvers. What she objected to, she said, gazing after him, was how narrow he was, how blind.

“Something of a hypocrite?” offered Mr. Bankes, who was also watching Mr. Ramsay’s retreating back. Wasn’t he thinking about their friendship, and about Cam refusing to give him a flower, and about all those boys and girls—and about his own house, so comfortable, but rather quiet since his wife died? He had his work, of course. … Still, he rather hoped Lily would agree that Ramsay was, in his phrase, “something of a hypocrite.”

Lily Briscoe kept on packing her brushes away, glancing up, glancing down. When she glanced up, there he was—Mr. Ramsay—striding toward them, swinging, careless, oblivious, far away. Something of a hypocrite? she echoed. Oh no. He was the most sincere of men, the truest (here he came), the best. Yet when she looked down, she thought: he’s wrapped up in himself, he’s a tyrant, he’s unfair. And she deliberately kept her eyes lowered, because that was the only way she could keep her balance while she was staying with the Ramsays. As soon as you raised your eyes and saw them, they were flooded with what she called “being in love.” They turned into part of that unreal yet piercing and thrilling universe, the world as the eyes of love see it. The sky clung to them; the birds sang right through them. And—more thrilling still—as she watched Mr. Ramsay bearing down and then retreating, and Mrs. Ramsay sitting in the window with James, and the cloud drifting and the tree bending, she felt too how life stopped being a string of small separate incidents, lived one at a time. It curled up and became whole, like a wave that carried you up with it and flung you down with it, there, crashing on the beach.

Mr. Bankes was waiting for her reply. She was on the point of saying something against Mrs. Ramsay—that she was frightening too, in her own way, overbearing, or something of the kind—when Mr. Bankes’s rapture made it quite unnecessary for her to say anything at all. And rapture was the word, given that he was over sixty, and so clean and so impersonal, and seemed to go about clothed in a white scientist’s coat. The way Lily saw him gazing at Mrs. Ramsay was a rapture that matched, she felt, the passions of dozens of young men (and perhaps Mrs. Ramsay had never inspired the passions of dozens of young men). This was love, she thought, as she made a show of shifting her canvas—love distilled and filtered, love that never tried to grasp what it loved. Like the love mathematicians have for their symbols, or poets for their phrases, it was meant to spread across the world and add to what humanity had gained. And so, indeed, it was. The world ought by all means to have shared in it, if only Mr. Bankes could have explained why that woman gave him such pleasure. Why did watching her read a fairy tale to her little boy affect him in precisely the way a solved scientific problem did? He rested, contemplating it, and felt what he felt when he had proved something absolute about how plants digest: that barbarism had been tamed, and the reign of chaos brought under control.

A rapture like this—what else could you possibly call it?—drove what she had been about to say clean out of Lily Briscoe’s head. It hadn’t mattered much; something about Mrs. Ramsay. Next to this “rapture,” this silent gaze, it faded to nothing, and she felt deeply grateful for it. Nothing consoled her like this; nothing so relieved her of life’s bewilderment, or so miraculously lifted its weight, as this sublime power, this gift from heaven. While it lasted, you would no more interrupt it than you would break up the beam of sunlight lying flat across the floor.

It helped her, it lifted her up, that people could love like this, that Mr. Bankes could feel this way about Mrs. Ramsay (she glanced over at him, lost in his thoughts). Deliberately, like a servant, she wiped her brushes one after another on a scrap of old rag. She was sheltering under the reverence that covered all women; she felt praised herself. Let him go on gazing; she would sneak a look at her painting.

She could have cried. It was bad, bad, infinitely bad! Of course, she could have done it another way. She could have thinned and faded the color and made the shapes airy and ethereal; that was how Paunceforte would have seen it. But that wasn’t how she saw it. What she saw was color burning on a steel framework; the light of a butterfly’s wing resting on a cathedral’s arches. All that was left of it was a few random marks scrawled across the canvas. And no one would ever see it; it would never even be hung. And there was Mr. Tansley, whispering in her ear, “Women can’t paint, women can’t write …”

Now it came back to her, what she had meant to say about Mrs. Ramsay. She couldn’t tell how she would have phrased it, but it would have been a criticism. The other night some bit of high-handedness had irritated her. Following the line of Mr. Bankes’s gaze toward Mrs. Ramsay, she thought that no woman could worship another woman as he worshipped her; women could only shelter together in the shade he cast over them both. Following his beam, she added her own, different ray. Mrs. Ramsay, she thought, was without question the loveliest of people (bent over her book there); perhaps the best; but also unlike the perfect form you saw before you. Yet why unlike, and unlike in what way? she wondered, scraping off her palette all those heaps of blue and green, which looked to her now like lifeless lumps of earth—though she swore that tomorrow she would breathe life into them, make them move and flow and obey her. In what way was Mrs. Ramsay different? What was the spirit in her, the essence, so that if you came across a glove tucked into the corner of a sofa you would know from its twisted finger that it was hers, beyond any doubt? For speed she was like a bird; for directness, an arrow. She was headstrong; she was commanding (naturally, Lily reminded herself, I’m thinking of how she is with women, and I’m much younger, a nobody, living off the Brompton Road). She threw open bedroom windows. She shut doors. (In this way Lily tried to get the tune of Mrs. Ramsay started in her head.) She would turn up late at night, tapping lightly on your bedroom door, wrapped in an old fur coat (that was always the setting for her beauty—hurried, but just right), and act out once again whatever it happened to be: Charles Tansley losing his umbrella; Mr. Carmichael snuffling and sniffing; Mr. Bankes announcing, “the vegetable salts are lost.” She would shape it all skillfully, even give it a malicious twist. Then she would move across to the window, pretending she had to go—it was dawn, she could see the sun coming up—and half turn back, more intimate now, yet still always laughing, to insist that she must, Minta must, all of them must marry. Because in the whole world, whatever laurels might be thrown her way (but Mrs. Ramsay didn’t care a fig about her painting), or whatever triumphs she might win (Mrs. Ramsay had probably had her share of those)—and here she grew sad and dark and returned to her chair—one thing was beyond dispute: an unmarried woman (she took Lily’s hand lightly for a moment), an unmarried woman has missed the best of life. The house seemed full of sleeping children and of Mrs. Ramsay listening; of lamps turned low and steady breathing.

Oh, but, Lily would answer, she had her father; her home; even, if she had dared say so, her painting. Yet set against the other thing, all of it seemed so slight, so virginal. Still, as the night went on and white light slipped between the curtains, and now and then some bird even chirped in the garden, she would summon up a desperate courage and argue that the universal law did not apply to her; beg to be excused from it. She liked being alone; she liked being herself; she wasn’t made for that. And then she would have to face a solemn look from eyes of matchless depth, and meet Mrs. Ramsay’s simple conviction (she was like a child now) that her dear Lily, her little Brisk, was a fool. Then, she remembered, she had put her head in Mrs. Ramsay’s lap and laughed and laughed and laughed—laughed almost hysterically at the idea of Mrs. Ramsay ruling, with unshakable calm, over destinies she didn’t understand in the least. There she sat, simple and serious. Lily had her sense of her back now—this was the glove’s twisted finger. But what sanctuary had she broken into? At last Lily Briscoe had raised her eyes, and there was Mrs. Ramsay, with no idea at all what had made her laugh, still presiding, but with every trace of willfulness gone now. In its place was something clear, like the space the clouds finally uncover—that little patch of sky asleep beside the moon.

Was it wisdom? Was it knowledge? Or was it, yet again, beauty deceiving you, so that everything you perceived got caught halfway to the truth in a golden net? Or did she keep some secret locked inside her—the kind of secret Lily Briscoe was sure people must have, if the world was to keep going at all? Not everyone could be as haphazard, as hand-to-mouth, as she was. But if they did know, could they tell you what it was they knew? She had sat on the floor with her arms wrapped around Mrs. Ramsay’s knees, as close as she could get, smiling at the thought that Mrs. Ramsay would never know why she was pressing so hard. And she had imagined that in the chambers of this woman’s mind and heart—this woman whose body was actually touching hers—there stood, like treasures in royal tombs, tablets carved with sacred inscriptions. If you could only spell them out they would teach you everything, but they would never be offered openly, never made public. What art was there, known to love or to cunning, that would let you press on into those secret chambers? What device was there for becoming one with the thing you adored, inseparably the same, like waters poured into a single jar? Could the body do it? Or the mind, blending subtly in the brain’s intricate passages? Or the heart? Could loving, as people called it, make her and Mrs. Ramsay one? Because what she longed for was not knowledge but unity—not inscriptions on tablets, not anything that could be written in any human language, but intimacy itself, which is knowledge, she had thought, resting her head on Mrs. Ramsay’s knee.

Nothing happened. Nothing! Nothing! as she leaned her head against Mrs. Ramsay’s knee. And yet she knew that Mrs. Ramsay’s heart held stores of knowledge and wisdom. How, then, she had wondered, could you know anything at all about people, sealed up as they were? Only the way a bee does, drawn by some sweetness or sharpness in the air that can’t be touched or tasted: you hovered around the dome-shaped hive, roamed alone across the empty reaches of the air over all the countries of the world, and then hovered again around the hives with their murmurings and stirrings—the hives that were people. Mrs. Ramsay stood up. Lily stood up. Mrs. Ramsay left. For days afterward, more vividly than anything she had said, a sound of murmuring clung about her, the way after a dream you sense some subtle change in the person you dreamed about. And as she sat in the wicker armchair in the drawing-room window, she took on, in Lily’s eyes, an august shape: the shape of a dome.

Lily’s ray ran level with Mr. Bankes’s, straight to Mrs. Ramsay, sitting there reading with James at her knee. But now, while Lily was still looking, Mr. Bankes had finished. He had put his spectacles on. He had taken a step back. He had lifted his hand. He had narrowed his clear blue eyes a little—and Lily, coming to herself, saw what he was about to do and cringed, like a dog seeing a hand raised to hit it. She would have snatched her painting off the easel, but she told herself, One must. She steeled herself for the dreadful ordeal of having someone look at her picture. One must, she said, one must. And if it had to be seen, Mr. Bankes was less frightening than anyone else would be. But it was agony that any other eyes should see what her thirty-three years had left behind, the sediment of every day she had lived, mixed with something more secret than anything she had ever said or shown in all those days. And at the same time, it was enormously exciting.

Nothing could have been calmer or quieter. Mr. Bankes took out a penknife and tapped the canvas with its bone handle. What was she trying to show with that triangular purple shape, “just there?” he asked.

It was Mrs. Ramsay reading to James, she told him. She knew what he would object—that nobody could tell it was a human figure. But she hadn’t tried for a likeness, she said. So why had she put them in at all? he asked. Why indeed?—except that, since it was bright over there in that corner, she felt she needed something dark here in this one. It was simple, obvious, ordinary, but Mr. Bankes was interested. So a mother and child, he reflected—objects of universal reverence, and this mother famous for her beauty besides—could be reduced to a purple shadow without any disrespect.

But it wasn’t a picture of them, she said. Or not in the sense he meant. There were other ways, too, of honoring them. With a shadow here and a light there, for instance. That was the form her tribute took, if, as she vaguely assumed, a picture had to be a tribute. You could reduce a mother and child to a shadow without disrespect. A light here called for a shadow there. He thought it over. He was interested. He approached it scientifically, and in complete good faith. The fact was, he explained, all his prejudices ran the other way. The biggest picture in his drawing-room, which painters had admired and priced higher than what he had paid for it, showed the cherry trees in blossom along the banks of the Kennet. He had spent his honeymoon on the Kennet, he said. Lily must come and see that picture, he said. But now—he turned, spectacles raised, to examine her canvas scientifically. The question was one of how masses relate, how lights relate to shadows, and he had honestly never thought about that before; so he would like it explained to him. What, then, did she mean to make of it? And he pointed at the scene before them. She looked. She couldn’t show him what she meant to make of it; without a brush in her hand she couldn’t even see it herself. Once again she took up her old painting stance, eyes dimmed, manner absent, subduing all her impressions as a woman to something far more general. Once again she fell under the power of that vision she had once seen clearly and now had to grope for among hedges and houses and mothers and children—her picture. The question, she remembered, was how to join this mass on the right to that one on the left. She might do it by carrying the line of the branch across, like so; or she might break the empty foreground with some object (James, perhaps), like so. But the danger was that doing so might break the unity of the whole. She stopped; she didn’t want to bore him; she lifted the canvas gently off the easel.

But it had been seen; it had been taken from her. This man had shared something deeply intimate with her. She thanked Mr. Ramsay for it, and Mrs. Ramsay, and the hour and the place; she gave the world credit for a power she had never suspected it had—that you could walk away down that long gallery no longer alone, but arm in arm with someone. It was the strangest feeling in the world, and the most exhilarating. She snapped the catch of her paintbox shut, harder than she needed to, and the snap seemed to draw a circle that closed forever around the paintbox, the lawn, Mr. Bankes, and that wild villain Cam, racing past.

chapters.title: The Window · 10
paragraphs: Cam had missed the easel by an inch. She wouldn’t stop for Mr. Bankes and Lily Briscoe, even though Mr. Bankes, who would have liked a daughter of his own, reached out his hand to her. She wouldn’t stop for her father, whom she also missed by an inch; nor for her mother, who called out “Cam! I want you a moment!” as she tore by. She was off like a bird, a bullet, an arrow—but driven by what longing, fired by whom, aimed at what, who could tell? What was it, what? Mrs. Ramsay wondered, watching her. Perhaps a vision—of a shell, a wheelbarrow, a fairyland on the other side of the hedge; or perhaps just the glory of speed; nobody knew. But when Mrs. Ramsay called “Cam!” again, the missile fell to earth in mid-flight, and Cam came dragging her feet back to her mother, plucking a leaf as she went.

What was the child dreaming about? Mrs. Ramsay wondered. She stood there so absorbed in some private thought that the message had to be given twice: go and ask Mildred whether Andrew, Miss Doyle, and Mr. Rayley are back yet. The words seemed to drop into a well whose water, clear as it was, bent things so strangely that you could watch them twisting as they sank, making heaven knows what pattern on the floor of the child’s mind. What message would Cam actually deliver to the cook? Mrs. Ramsay wondered. And in fact it was only by waiting patiently, and hearing all about an old woman in the kitchen with very red cheeks who was drinking soup out of a bowl, that Mrs. Ramsay finally set off that parrot-like instinct in her. It had caught Mildred’s words quite exactly, and could now repeat them, if you were patient, in a flat singsong. Shifting from one foot to the other, Cam recited: “No, they haven’t, and I’ve told Ellen to clear away tea.”

So Minta Doyle and Paul Rayley weren’t back yet. That could mean only one thing, Mrs. Ramsay thought. Minta must accept him, or she must refuse him. Going off for a walk after lunch like this, even with Andrew along—what else could it mean? Only that she had made up her mind, and rightly, thought Mrs. Ramsay (who was very, very fond of Minta), to accept that good fellow. He might not be brilliant. But then, Mrs. Ramsay thought—aware that James was pulling at her to make her keep reading the Fisherman and his Wife aloud—deep down she infinitely preferred dunces to clever men who wrote dissertations; men like Charles Tansley. At any rate, by now it must have happened, one way or the other.
But what she read was: “The next morning the wife woke up first. It was just dawn, and from her bed she could see the lovely countryside spread out before her. Her husband was still stretching. …”

But how could Minta turn him down now? Not if she had agreed to spend entire afternoons tramping around the countryside alone with him—for Andrew would go off after his crabs—though Nancy might have been with them. Mrs. Ramsay tried to call up the picture of them standing at the front door after lunch. There they had stood, looking up at the sky and wondering what the weather would do. And she had said, partly to cover up their shyness, partly to urge them to get going (for she was on Paul’s side),

“Not a cloud for miles in any direction,” and at that she had sensed little Charles Tansley, who had trailed out after them, snickering. But she had said it deliberately. As for whether Nancy had been there, she couldn’t be sure, going from face to face in her mind’s eye.

She read on: “ ‘Oh, wife,’ said the man, ‘why should we be King? I have no wish to be King.’ ‘Well,’ the wife answered, ‘if you won’t be King, then I will. Go to the Flounder, because I will be King.’ ”

“Either come in or go out, Cam,” she said. She knew it was only the word “Flounder” that had drawn Cam, and that any minute she would start fidgeting and fighting with James the way she always did. Off Cam shot. Relieved, Mrs. Ramsay kept reading, for she and James liked the same things and were at ease with each other.
“And when he reached the sea it was a very dark gray, and the water was heaving up from underneath and had a rotten smell. Then he went and stood beside it and said,

‘Flounder, flounder, in the sea.
Come, I pray thee, here to me;
For my wife, good Ilsabil,
Wills not as I’d have her will.’

‘Well, what does she want, then?’ said the Flounder.” And where had they got to by now? Mrs. Ramsay wondered. She could read and think at once with no trouble at all, for the story of the Fisherman and his Wife was like a bass line quietly accompanying a tune, now and then running up without warning into the melody. And when was she going to be told? If nothing had happened, she would have to have a serious talk with Minta. Minta simply couldn’t go tramping all over the countryside, even with Nancy along (once more she tried, and failed, to picture their backs going down the path, and to count them). She was answerable to Minta’s parents—the Owl and the Poker. Her nicknames for them flashed into her mind as she read. The Owl and the Poker—yes, they would be displeased if they heard (and they were sure to hear) that Minta, while staying with the Ramsays, had been seen et cetera, et cetera, et cetera. “He wore a wig in the House of Commons and she ably assisted him at the head of the stairs,” she said over to herself, hauling them up out of her memory with a phrase she had invented, on the way home from some party, to amuse her husband. Dear me, Mrs. Ramsay said to herself, how had those two ever produced such an unlikely daughter? This tomboy Minta, with a hole in her stocking? How did she survive in that ponderous atmosphere, where the maid was forever sweeping into a dustpan the sand the parrot had scattered, and conversation had shrunk almost entirely to that bird’s exploits—interesting, perhaps, but limited, when all was said and done? Naturally she had invited Minta to lunch, then tea, then dinner, and in the end to come and stay with them up at Finlay. That had caused some friction with the Owl, her mother, and led to more calls, and more conversation, and more sand, until, by the end of it, she had told enough lies about parrots to last a lifetime (as she had put it to her husband that night, on the way home from the party). Still, Minta came. … Yes, she had come, Mrs. Ramsay thought, feeling some thorn caught in the tangle of this thought; and when she worked it loose, she found that it was this. A woman had once accused her of “robbing her of her daughter’s affections”; and something Mrs. Doyle had said brought that accusation back to her. That she wanted to dominate, wanted to interfere, made people do what she wanted—that was the charge against her, and she thought it deeply unfair. How could she help looking “like that”? Nobody could say she went to any trouble to impress. She was often ashamed of how shabby she was. Nor was she domineering, nor tyrannical. It was truer where hospitals and drains and the dairy were concerned. About things like that she did feel passionately, and, given the chance, she would have liked to grab people by the scruff of the neck and make them see. Not one hospital on the whole island. It was a disgrace. Milk left on your doorstep in London that was actually brown with dirt. There ought to be a law against it. A model dairy and a hospital here—those were the two things she would have liked to do, with her own hands. But how? With all these children? Later, when they were older, maybe she would have time; once they were all at school.

Oh, but she never wanted James to get one day older, nor Cam either. These two she would have liked to keep just as they were, forever—demons of wickedness, angels of delight—and never watch them turn into long-legged monsters. Nothing could make up for that loss. Just now, when she had read James the line “and there were numbers of soldiers with kettledrums and trumpets,” and his eyes had darkened, she had thought: why should they grow up and lose all that? Of all her children he was the most gifted, the most sensitive. But every one of them, she thought, was full of promise. Prue was an absolute angel with the others, and these days, especially in the evenings, her beauty could take your breath away. Andrew—even her husband granted that he had an extraordinary gift for mathematics. And Nancy and Roger had both turned into wild creatures, running all over the countryside from morning till night. As for Rose, her mouth was too big, but she was wonderful with her hands. When they put on charades, it was Rose who made the costumes; she made everything; what she liked best was arranging things—tables, flowers, anything at all. Mrs. Ramsay didn’t like Jasper shooting birds; but that was only a phase; they all went through phases. Why, she asked, resting her chin on the top of James’s head, must they grow up so quickly? Why must they go off to school? She would have liked always to have a baby. She was never happier than with one in her arms. Then people could call her tyrannical, domineering, overbearing, whatever they pleased; she didn’t care. And as she touched his hair with her lips she thought, he will never be this happy again—but she stopped herself, remembering how angry her husband got when she said that. Still, it was true. They were happier now than they would ever be again. A tenpenny tea set could keep Cam happy for days. The moment they woke, she heard them stamping and crowing on the floor over her head. They came clattering along the passage. Then the door burst open and in they came, fresh as roses, wide-eyed, wide awake, as if coming into the dining room after breakfast—which they did every single day of their lives—were a real occasion for them. And so it went, one thing after another, all day long, until she went up to say good night and found them caught in their cots like birds netted among the cherries and raspberries, still inventing stories about some scrap of rubbish—something they had overheard, something they had found in the garden. They each had their little treasures. … And so she went downstairs and said to her husband, Why must they grow up and lose it all? They’ll never be so happy again. And he was angry. Why take such a gloomy view of life? he said. It isn’t sensible. For it was strange—and she believed it to be true—that for all his gloom and despair he was happier than she was, more hopeful on the whole. Perhaps it was that he was less exposed to human troubles. He always had his work to fall back on. Not that she was “pessimistic” herself, as he accused her of being. It was only that she thought life—and a small strip of time appeared before her eyes, her fifty years. There it lay in front of her—life. Life, she thought, but she didn’t finish the thought. She took a look at life, because she had a distinct sense of it there, something real, something private, which she shared with neither her children nor her husband. A kind of transaction went on between the two of them, with her on one side and life on the other. She was always trying to get the upper hand of it, as it was of her; and sometimes they held talks (when she sat by herself); there had been, she remembered, great scenes of reconciliation. But mostly, oddly enough, she had to admit that she felt this thing she called life to be terrible, hostile, ready to spring on you the moment you gave it the chance. There were the eternal problems: suffering; death; the poor. Even here there was always some woman dying of cancer. And yet she had told all these children, You shall go through with it. To eight people she had said it, relentlessly (and the greenhouse bill would come to fifty pounds). And for that reason, knowing what lay in store for them—love and ambition and being miserable and alone in dreary places—she often felt: Why must they grow up and lose it all? And then, brandishing her sword at life, she told herself, Nonsense. They’ll be perfectly happy. And here she was, she thought, feeling again that life was rather sinister, making Minta marry Paul Rayley. Because whatever she might feel about her own transaction—and she had been through things that needn’t happen to everyone (she didn’t name them, even to herself)—she was driven on, too fast, she knew, almost as if it were an escape for her as well, to declare that people must marry; people must have children.

Was she wrong about this? she asked herself, going over how she had behaved in the last week or two, and wondering whether she really had pushed Minta, who was only twenty-four, to make up her mind. It made her uneasy. Hadn’t she laughed about it? Wasn’t she forgetting, once again, how powerfully she influenced people? Marriage called for—oh, all kinds of qualities (the greenhouse bill would come to fifty pounds); and one—she didn’t need to name it—_that_ was essential; the thing she and her husband had. Did they have it?

“Then he pulled on his trousers and ran off like a madman,” she read. “But outside a great storm was raging, and the wind blew so hard he could barely keep his feet. Houses and trees were toppling, the mountains shook, rocks went rolling into the sea, the sky was pitch-black, there was thunder and lightning, and the sea rolled in with black waves as tall as church towers and mountains, every one of them crested with white foam.”

She turned the page. Only a few lines were left, so she would finish the story, even though bedtime had passed. It was getting late. She could tell from the light in the garden; and the flowers turning white and something gray in the leaves combined to wake a feeling of anxiety in her. At first she couldn’t think what it was about. Then it came to her: Paul and Minta and Andrew weren’t back. Once more she summoned up the little group on the terrace outside the hall door, standing there looking up at the sky. Andrew had taken his net and basket. That meant he meant to catch crabs and so on. That meant he would clamber out onto some rock and be cut off by the tide. Or, coming home in single file along one of those narrow paths above the cliff, one of them might slip. He would roll, and then crash. It was getting quite dark.

But she didn’t let her voice alter in the slightest as she read the story to its end. Then, closing the book, she looked into James’s eyes and added the last words as if she had invented them herself: “And there they are, living still at this very time.”

“And that’s the end,” she said. As the interest of the story faded from his eyes, she saw something else take its place: something wondering, pale, like a reflected light, that at once made him gaze and marvel. She turned and looked out across the bay, and there, sure enough, coming steadily over the waves—first two quick strokes, then one long steady stroke—was the light of the Lighthouse. It had been lit.

Any moment now he would ask her, “Are we going to the Lighthouse?” And she would have to tell him, “No, not tomorrow; your father says not.” Fortunately Mildred came in just then to fetch them, and the bustle took their minds off it. But as Mildred carried him out, he kept looking back over his shoulder, and she was sure he was thinking, we are not going to the Lighthouse tomorrow. And she thought, he will remember that for the rest of his life.

chapters.title: The Window · 11
paragraphs: No, she thought, gathering up a few of the pictures he had cut out—a refrigerator, a lawn mower, a gentleman in evening dress—children never forget. That was why it mattered so much what you said and what you did, and why it came as a relief when they were in bed. Now she didn’t need to think about anyone. She could be herself, by herself. And lately that was what she often felt the need of—to think; well, not even to think. To be silent; to be alone. All the being and doing, expansive, glittering, talkative, evaporated; and with a sense of solemnity you shrank to being yourself, a wedge-shaped core of darkness, something invisible to others. Though she kept on knitting and sat upright, this was how she felt herself to be; and this self, having shed its attachments, was free for the strangest adventures. When life sank down for a moment, the range of experience seemed to have no limit. And everyone, she supposed, always had this sense of unlimited resources; one after another, she, Lily, Augustus Carmichael, must feel that our apparitions, the things you recognize us by, are simply childish. Underneath, it is all dark, it is all spreading, it is unfathomably deep; but every now and then we rise to the surface, and that is what you see us by. Her horizon seemed to her boundless. There were all the places she had never seen; the plains of India; she felt herself pushing aside the heavy leather curtain at the door of a church in Rome. This core of darkness could go anywhere, because nobody saw it. They couldn’t stop it, she thought, exulting. Here was freedom, here was peace, here was—most welcome of all—a gathering together, a resting on a platform of stability. You never found rest as yourself, in her experience (at this point her needles did something deft), but as a wedge of darkness. Once you lost your personality, you lost the fret, the hurry, the stir. And whenever things came together in this peace, this rest, this eternity, some cry of triumph over life rose to her lips. Pausing there, she looked out to meet that stroke of the Lighthouse, the long steady stroke, the last of the three, which was her stroke. For watching them in this mood, always at this hour, you couldn’t help attaching yourself to one thing above all among the things you saw; and this thing, the long steady stroke, was her stroke. Often she caught herself sitting and looking, sitting and looking, her work in her hands, until she became the thing she was looking at—that light, say. And it would lift up some little phrase or other that had been lying in her mind like that—“Children don’t forget, children don’t forget”—and she would repeat it and start adding to it. It will end, It will end, she said. It will come, it will come, when all at once she added, We are in the hands of the Lord.

But at once she was annoyed with herself for saying that. Who had said it? Not she; she had been tricked into saying something she didn’t mean. Glancing up over her knitting, she met the third stroke, and it was to her like her own eyes meeting her own eyes, searching her mind and her heart as only she could search them, and purifying that lie, any lie, out of existence. Praising the light, she praised herself, without vanity, because she was stern, she was searching, she was beautiful, like that light. How odd it was, she thought, that when you were alone you leaned toward things, lifeless things—trees, streams, flowers; you felt they expressed you; felt they became you; felt they knew you, in a sense were you; and so you felt an irrational tenderness for them (she looked at that long steady light) as if for yourself. There rose—and she looked and looked, her needles held in midair—there curled up off the floor of the mind, rose from the lake of one’s being, a mist, a bride to meet her lover.

What made her say that: “We are in the hands of the Lord”? she wondered. That insincerity, slipping in among the truths, stirred and annoyed her. She took up her knitting once more. How could any Lord have made this world? she asked. Her mind had always grasped the fact that there is no reason, no order, no justice—only suffering, death, the poor. The world would stoop to any betrayal, however low; she knew that. Happiness never lasted; she knew that. Firm and composed, she knitted, lips slightly pursed, and without realizing it she had set the lines of her face into such a habit of sternness that her husband, walking past, couldn’t help noticing it: the sternness at the heart of her beauty. He was chuckling as he passed, at the thought of Hume, the philosopher, grown enormously fat and stuck in a bog. But her look saddened him; her remoteness hurt him; going by, he felt he couldn’t protect her, and by the time he got to the hedge, he was sad. There was nothing he could do for her. He had to stand by and watch her. The damnable truth, in fact, was that he made things worse for her. He was irritable—he was touchy. He had lost his temper over the Lighthouse. He stared into the hedge, into its tangle, its darkness.

Always, Mrs. Ramsay felt, you pulled yourself out of solitude unwillingly, grabbing hold of some small odd or end, some sound, some sight. She listened, but all was very quiet; the cricket was finished; the children were in their baths; there was only the sound of the sea. She stopped knitting; for a moment the long reddish-brown stocking hung from her hands. Again she saw the light. Her questioning had some irony in it, since once you woke up at all, your relations changed. She looked at the steady light, the pitiless, the remorseless, which was so much her, yet so little her; which had her at its beck and call (waking in the night, she would see it bent across their bed, stroking the floor). And yet, she thought—watching it with fascination, hypnotized, as though with its silver fingers it were stroking some sealed vessel in her brain that would flood her with delight if it burst—she had known happiness, exquisite happiness, intense happiness. And as the daylight faded, it silvered the rough waves a little more brightly, and the blue drained out of the sea, and the sea rolled in waves of pure lemon that curved and swelled and broke on the beach, and the ecstasy burst in her eyes, and waves of pure delight raced across the floor of her mind, and she felt, It is enough! It is enough!

He turned and saw her. Ah! She was lovely—lovelier now than ever, he thought. Yet he couldn’t speak to her. He couldn’t interrupt her. Now that James had gone and she was at last alone, he badly wanted to talk to her. But no, he decided; he wouldn’t interrupt. In her beauty, in her sadness, she stood apart from him now. He would leave her alone; and he went by without a word, though it hurt him that she looked so far away, that he couldn’t reach her, that there was nothing he could do for her. And once more he would have gone by without speaking, if she hadn’t, at that very moment, freely given him what she knew he would never ask for: she called to him, lifted the green shawl off the picture frame, and went to him. For he wanted, she knew, to protect her.

chapters.title: The Window · 12
paragraphs: She drew the green shawl around her shoulders and took his arm. He was so beautiful, she said, launching straight into the subject of Kennedy the gardener; so terribly good-looking that she couldn’t bring herself to fire him. A ladder leaned against the greenhouse, and little lumps of putty were stuck about, since they were starting on repairs to the greenhouse roof. Yes, but strolling along with her husband, she felt that this particular worry had been dealt with. “It’ll cost fifty pounds” was on the tip of her tongue as they walked; instead, because her nerve failed her where money was concerned, she brought up Jasper shooting birds. At once he soothed her: it was natural in a boy, he said, and he trusted the boy would find better amusements before long. Her husband was so sensible, so fair. So she said, “Yes; all children go through phases,” and turned her attention to the dahlias in the big bed, and wondered about next year’s flowers—and had he heard what the children called Charles Tansley? she asked. The atheist, they called him; the little atheist. “He’s hardly a polished specimen,” Mr. Ramsay said. “Far from it,” said Mrs. Ramsay.

She supposed it was fine to leave him to amuse himself, said Mrs. Ramsay, wondering whether there was any point in sending bulbs down; would anyone plant them? “Oh, he’s got his dissertation to write,” Mr. Ramsay said. She knew all about _that_, said Mrs. Ramsay. It was all he ever talked about. It concerned the influence of somebody on something. “Well, it’s the only thing he has to count on,” Mr. Ramsay said. “God forbid he should fall in love with Prue,” said Mrs. Ramsay. If she married him, he’d cut her out of his will, said Mr. Ramsay. His eyes weren’t on the flowers his wife was looking over but on a spot a foot or so above them. The young man meant no harm, he went on, and he was about to add that at any rate he was the only young man in England who admired his—when he swallowed the words. He wouldn’t trouble her about his books again. The flowers looked very creditable, Mr. Ramsay said, dropping his eyes and noticing something red, something brown. Yes, but these were ones she had planted herself, said Mrs. Ramsay. The question was what happened when she sent bulbs down; did Kennedy plant them? It was his hopeless laziness, she added, walking on. If she stood over him all day with a spade in her hand, now and then he would do a stroke of work. So they wandered on toward the red-hot pokers. “You’re teaching your daughters to exaggerate,” Mr. Ramsay said reprovingly. Her Aunt Camilla was much worse than she was, Mrs. Ramsay pointed out. “Nobody ever held up your Aunt Camilla as a model of virtue, so far as I know,” said Mr. Ramsay. “She was the most beautiful woman I ever saw,” said Mrs. Ramsay. “Somebody else was that,” Mr. Ramsay said. Prue would be far more beautiful than she was, said Mrs. Ramsay. He couldn’t see any sign of it, Mr. Ramsay said. “Well then, look tonight,” said Mrs. Ramsay. They stopped. He wished Andrew could be got to work harder. If he didn’t, he’d throw away every chance of a scholarship. “Oh, scholarships!” she said. Mr. Ramsay thought it foolish of her to say that about something as serious as a scholarship. He’d be very proud of Andrew if he won one, he said. She would be every bit as proud of him if he didn’t, she replied. They always disagreed on this, but it didn’t matter. She liked him to believe in scholarships, and he liked her to be proud of Andrew no matter what he did. All at once she remembered those little paths along the edge of the cliffs.

Wasn’t it getting late? she asked. They still weren’t home. Carelessly he flicked open his watch. But it was only just after seven. For a moment he held the watch open, making up his mind to tell her what he had felt on the terrace. First of all, it was unreasonable to be so nervous. Andrew could take care of himself. Then he wanted to tell her that just now, as he was walking on the terrace—and here he grew uneasy, as though he were intruding on that solitude, that aloofness, that remoteness of hers. … But she urged him on. What was it he’d wanted to say? she asked, supposing it was about the trip to the Lighthouse, and that he was sorry for having said “Damn you.” But no. He didn’t like to see her looking so sad, he said. She was only daydreaming, she protested, coloring slightly. Both of them felt awkward, unsure whether to go forward or turn back. She’d been reading fairy tales to James, she said. No, that they couldn’t share; that they couldn’t say.

They had come to the gap between the two clumps of red-hot pokers, and there was the Lighthouse again, but she wouldn’t allow herself to look at it. Had she known he was watching her, she thought, she would never have let herself sit there thinking. She disliked anything that reminded her she had been seen sitting and thinking. So she glanced back over her shoulder at the town. Its lights rippled and ran like drops of silver water held steady in a wind. And all the poverty, all the suffering, had turned into that, thought Mrs. Ramsay. The lights of the town, the harbor, and the boats looked like a phantom net floating there to mark the place where something had sunk. Well, if he couldn’t share her thoughts, Mr. Ramsay told himself, then he’d go off on his own. He wanted to keep thinking, to keep telling himself the story of Hume stuck in a bog; he wanted to laugh. But first, it was nonsense to worry about Andrew. At Andrew’s age he used to tramp about the countryside all day with nothing but a biscuit in his pocket, and nobody fretted about him or imagined he had fallen off a cliff. Aloud he said he thought he might go off for a day’s walk, if the weather held. He’d had just about enough of Bankes and Carmichael. He’d like a little solitude. Yes, she said. Her not protesting annoyed him. She knew he would never do it. He was too old now to walk all day with a biscuit in his pocket. The boys she worried about, but not him. Years ago, before his marriage, he thought, gazing across the bay as they stood between the clumps of red-hot pokers, he had walked all day. He had eaten bread and cheese for his meal in a pub. He had worked ten hours at a stretch, with an old woman looking in every so often to see to the fire. That was the country he loved best, over there; those sandhills fading away into the dark. You could walk all day and never meet a soul. There was hardly a house, not one village, for miles and miles. You could work things out alone. There were little sandy beaches where nobody had been since the beginning of time. The seals sat up and stared at you. Sometimes it seemed to him that in a little house out there, by himself—he broke off with a sigh. He had no right. The father of eight children—he reminded himself of that. And he’d have been a brute and a cur to wish one thing different. Andrew would turn out a better man than he had. Prue would be a beauty, her mother said. They would hold back the flood a little. On the whole, that was a good piece of work—his eight children. They proved he didn’t utterly damn the poor little universe; for on an evening like this, he thought, watching the land fade away, the little island looked pitifully small, half swallowed by the sea.
“Poor little place,” he murmured, and sighed.

She heard him. He said the gloomiest things, yet she noticed that the moment he’d said them he always seemed more cheerful than usual. All this making of phrases was a game, she thought; if she’d said half of what he said, she would have blown her brains out long ago.

This phrase-making irritated her, and in a matter-of-fact voice she told him what a perfectly lovely evening it was. And what was he groaning about? she asked, half laughing and half complaining, because she guessed what was in his mind—he would have written better books if he hadn’t married.

He wasn’t complaining, he said. She knew he never complained. She knew he had absolutely nothing to complain about. And he grabbed her hand, lifted it to his lips, and kissed it so intensely that tears came into her eyes; then he quickly let it drop.

Turning from the view, they began to walk arm in arm up the path where the silver-green, spear-shaped plants grew. His arm was almost like a young man’s, Mrs. Ramsay thought, thin and hard; and she thought with delight of how strong he still was, though over sixty, how untamed and hopeful; and how strange it was that being convinced, as he was, of every kind of horror seemed not to depress him but to cheer him. Wasn’t that odd? she reflected. At times, really, he seemed to her made differently from other people: blind, deaf, and dumb from birth to ordinary things, but to extraordinary things, eagle-eyed. How much he understood often astonished her. But did he notice the flowers? No. Did he notice the view? No. Did he even notice how beautiful his own daughter was, or whether his plate held pudding or roast beef? He would sit at the table with them like someone in a dream. And she was afraid his habit of talking aloud, or reciting poetry aloud, was getting worse; for sometimes it was embarrassing—
Best and brightest, come away!

poor Miss Giddings, when he bellowed that at her, nearly leaped out of her skin. But then—and Mrs. Ramsay sided with him instantly against all the silly Giddingses in the world—then, she thought, pressing his arm lightly to tell him he was going uphill too fast for her, and that she needed to stop a moment to see whether those molehills on the bank were fresh—then, she thought, bending down to look, a great mind like his must be unlike ours in every way. Every great man she had ever known, she thought, concluding that a rabbit must have got in, had been like that; and it was good for young men (though she found the air of lecture halls stuffy and depressing almost past bearing) simply to listen to him, simply to look at him. But unless you shot rabbits, how were you to keep their numbers down? she wondered. Maybe a rabbit; maybe a mole. Anyway, some creature was wrecking her evening primroses. And glancing up, she saw above the thin trees the first pulse of the full-throbbing star, and wanted her husband to look at it, for the sight gave her such sharp pleasure. But she held back. He never looked at things. And if he did, he would only say, Poor little world, and give one of his sighs.

Just then he said “Very fine,” to please her, and made a show of admiring the flowers. But she knew perfectly well he didn’t admire them, or even realize they were there. He was only trying to please her. … Oh, but wasn’t that Lily Briscoe strolling with William Bankes? She fixed her shortsighted eyes on the backs of a couple moving away. Yes, it certainly was. Didn’t that mean they’d marry? Yes, it had to! What a splendid idea! They must marry!

chapters.title: The Window · 13
paragraphs: He had been to Amsterdam, Mr. Bankes was telling Lily Briscoe as they walked across the lawn. He’d seen the Rembrandts. He’d been to Madrid. Unluckily it was Good Friday, and the Prado was closed. He’d been to Rome. Had Miss Briscoe never been to Rome? Oh, she ought to— It would be a marvelous experience for her—the Sistine Chapel; Michelangelo; and Padua, with its Giottos. For years his wife’s health had been poor, so their sightseeing had been done on a modest scale.

She had been to Brussels; she had been to Paris, though only on a quick trip to visit a sick aunt. She had been to Dresden; there were masses of pictures she’d never seen; but perhaps, Lily Briscoe reflected, it was better not to see pictures: all they did was make you hopelessly dissatisfied with your own work. Mr. Bankes felt you could take that view too far. We can’t all be Titians and we can’t all be Darwins, he said; yet he doubted whether there could be any Darwin or Titian without humble people like ourselves. Lily wanted to pay him a compliment; you’re not humble, Mr. Bankes, she would have liked to say. But he didn’t want compliments (most men do, she thought), and a little ashamed of the impulse, she kept quiet while he remarked that perhaps what he’d said didn’t apply to pictures. At any rate, said Lily, dashing off her small insincerity, she would always keep on painting, because it interested her. Yes, Mr. Bankes said, he was sure of that. As they came to the end of the lawn he was asking whether she found it hard to find subjects in London, when they turned and saw the Ramsays. So that is marriage, Lily thought: a man and a woman watching a girl throw a ball. That is what Mrs. Ramsay was trying to tell me the other night, she thought. For Mrs. Ramsay had on a green shawl, and the two stood close together, watching Prue and Jasper throw catches. And suddenly the meaning that comes down on people for no reason at all—as they’re stepping out of the Underground, perhaps, or ringing a doorbell—and makes them symbolic, makes them representative, came down on these two, and turned them, standing and gazing in the dusk, into the symbols of marriage, husband and wife. Then, after an instant, the symbolic outline that rose above the real figures sank again, and as Lily and Mr. Bankes came up to them they were simply Mr. and Mrs. Ramsay watching the children throw catches. Yet for a moment still—though Mrs. Ramsay greeted them with her usual smile (oh, she thinks we’re going to get married, Lily thought) and said, “I’ve triumphed tonight,” meaning that for once Mr. Bankes had agreed to have dinner with them rather than hurrying back to his lodgings, where his manservant cooked vegetables the proper way—still, for a single moment, there was a feeling of things blown apart, of space, of irresponsibility, as the ball soared up, and their eyes followed it and lost it and found the one star and the draped branches. In the fading light they all looked sharp-edged and unearthly and set apart by great distances. Then, dashing backward across the huge space (for solidity seemed to have vanished completely), Prue ran full tilt into them and brilliantly caught the ball high up in her left hand; and her mother said, “Aren’t they back yet?” and at that the spell broke. Now Mr. Ramsay felt free to laugh out loud at Hume, who had got stuck in a bog and was rescued by an old woman on condition that he said the Lord’s Prayer; and chuckling to himself, he wandered off to his study. Mrs. Ramsay, drawing Prue back into the alliance of family life, which she had escaped while she was throwing catches, asked,
“Did Nancy go with them?”

chapters.title: The Window · 14
paragraphs: (Of course Nancy had gone with them, because Minta Doyle had asked her to, with that mute look of hers, holding out her hand just as Nancy was escaping after lunch to her attic, away from the horror of family life. Then she supposed she had to go. She didn’t want to. She didn’t want to be dragged into it all. For all along the road to the cliff Minta kept taking her hand. Then she would drop it. Then she would take it again. What did she want? Nancy asked herself. People did want something, of course; because when Minta took her hand and held it, Nancy, against her will, saw the whole world spread out below her, like Constantinople seen through a mist, and then, however heavy your eyes, you had to ask, “Is that Santa Sofia?” “Is that the Golden Horn?” So when Minta took her hand, Nancy asked, “What is it she wants? Is it that?” And what was that? Here and there (as Nancy gazed down at life spread out below) something rose out of the mist—a pinnacle, a dome; prominent things with no names. But whenever Minta let go of her hand, as she did when they raced down the hillside, all of it—the dome, the pinnacle, whatever had been poking up through the mist—sank back into it and was gone.

Minta, Andrew noticed, walked rather well. Her clothes were more sensible than most women’s. She wore very short skirts and black knickerbockers. She’d jump right into a stream and flounder across. He liked how reckless she was, but he could see it wouldn’t do—one of these days she’d kill herself in some idiotic way. Nothing seemed to frighten her—except bulls. The mere sight of a bull in a field and up went her arms and off she ran, screaming, which was of course just what would enrage a bull. But she didn’t mind confessing it in the slightest; you had to give her that. She was a dreadful coward about bulls, she said, she knew. She thought she must have been tossed in her baby carriage when she was tiny. She didn’t seem to care what she said or did. Now all of a sudden she flung herself down at the edge of the cliff and started singing some song about
Damn your eyes, damn your eyes.
Everyone had to join in the chorus and shout it out together:
Damn your eyes, damn your eyes.
but letting the tide come in and cover all the good hunting grounds before they reached the beach would be a disaster.

“A disaster,” agreed Paul, leaping to his feet; and as they slid and scrambled down, he kept quoting the guidebook about “these islands being justly celebrated for their park-like prospects and the extent and variety of their marine curiosities.” But it wasn’t quite right, Andrew felt, picking his way down the cliff—all this shouting and damning your eyes, this slapping him on the back and calling him “old fellow” and the rest of it; it wasn’t quite right. That was the trouble with taking women on walks. On the beach they split up. Andrew went out onto the Pope’s Nose, took off his shoes, rolled his socks up inside them, and left that couple to look after themselves; Nancy waded out to rocks of her own and searched pools of her own and left that couple to look after themselves. Crouching low, she touched the smooth, rubbery sea anemones that clung like lumps of jelly to the side of the rock. Brooding, she made the pool into the sea, and the minnows into sharks and whales; she held her hand up against the sun and threw vast clouds over this tiny world, bringing darkness and desolation, like God himself, to millions of ignorant, innocent creatures; then all at once she pulled her hand away and let the sunlight pour down. Across the pale crisscrossed sand stalked some fantastic leviathan, high-stepping, fringed, gauntleted (she was still making the pool bigger), and slid into the vast cracks of the mountainside. And then, as her eyes slid imperceptibly up above the pool and came to rest on the wavering line where sea met sky, on the tree trunks that steamer smoke set wavering on the horizon, all that power sweeping savagely in and inevitably pulling back held her hypnotized. And the two sensations, of that hugeness and of this tininess (the pool had shrunk again), flowering inside it, made her feel tied hand and foot, unable to move, under the intensity of feelings that shrank her own body, her own life, and the lives of everyone in the world, forever, to nothing. So she brooded, crouched over the pool, listening to the waves.

Then Andrew shouted that the sea was coming in, so she went leaping and splashing through the shallows to the shore and ran up the beach, and her own impulsiveness and her wish to move fast carried her right around behind a rock, and there—oh heavens!—were Paul and Minta, in each other’s arms! Kissing, probably. She was outraged, indignant. In dead silence she and Andrew put their shoes and stockings on, and neither said a word about it. They were actually rather snappish with each other. She could have called him when she saw the crayfish, or whatever it was, Andrew grumbled. Still, both of them felt, it isn’t our fault. They hadn’t wanted this horrid nuisance to happen. All the same, Andrew was irritated that Nancy should be a woman, and Nancy that Andrew should be a man; and they tied their laces very neatly and pulled the bows rather tight.

Only when they had climbed all the way back to the top of the cliff did Minta cry out that she had lost her grandmother’s brooch—her grandmother’s brooch, the one ornament she owned—a weeping willow (they must remember it) set in pearls. Surely they’d seen it, she said, tears running down her cheeks: the brooch her grandmother had pinned her cap with until the last day of her life. And now it was lost. She would rather have lost anything else! She was going back to look for it. They all went back. They poked about and peered and searched. They kept their heads down low and spoke in short, gruff bursts. Paul Rayley hunted like a madman all around the rock where they’d been sitting. All this fuss over a brooch really wasn’t right at all, Andrew thought, while Paul told him to make a “thorough search between this point and that.” The tide was rising fast. In a minute the sea would be over the spot where they’d sat. There wasn’t a ghost of a chance they’d find it now. “We’ll be cut off!” Minta shrieked, suddenly terrified. As if there were the least danger of that! It was the bulls all over again—she couldn’t control her feelings, Andrew thought. Women couldn’t. Poor Paul had to calm her. The men (Andrew and Paul at once turned manly and unlike their usual selves) held a brief council and decided to stick Rayley’s cane in the ground where they’d been sitting and return at low tide. For now, nothing more could be done. If the brooch was there, it would still be there in the morning, they promised her; yet Minta went on sobbing all the way to the top of the cliff. It was her grandmother’s brooch; she’d rather have lost anything but that. And yet Nancy felt that, though she might really mind losing her brooch, that wasn’t all she was crying for. She was crying about something else. We could all sit down and cry, Nancy felt. But what for, she didn’t know.

Paul and Minta went on ahead together, and he comforted her, telling her how famous he was for finding things. When he was a small boy he had once found a gold watch. He’d get up at daybreak, and he was certain he’d find it. It seemed to him it would still be nearly dark, and he’d be alone on the beach, and somehow there would be a bit of danger in it. Still, he began assuring her he would definitely find it, and she said she wouldn’t hear of him getting up at dawn: it was gone: she knew it was: she’d had a feeling when she put it on that afternoon. And privately he made up his mind not to tell her, but to slip out of the house at dawn while everyone slept; and if he couldn’t find it he’d go to Edinburgh and buy her another, exactly like it but lovelier. He’d show what he could do. And as they came out on the hill and saw the town’s lights below, the lights springing out one by one seemed like the things that were going to happen to him—his marriage, his children, his house. And once more, as they came out onto the main road, shaded by tall bushes, he thought of how they would withdraw into solitude together and walk on and on, he always leading, she pressed close at his side (as she was now). As they turned at the crossroads he thought what a terrifying ordeal he had been through, and that he had to tell someone—Mrs. Ramsay, naturally, for it took his breath away to think what he had been and what he had done. Asking Minta to marry him had been far and away the worst moment of his life. He’d go straight to Mrs. Ramsay, because somehow he felt she was the one who had made him do it. She’d made him think he could do anything. No one else took him seriously. But she made him believe he could do whatever he liked. All day today he had felt her eyes on him, following him everywhere (though she never said a word), as if she were saying, “Yes, you can do it. I believe in you. I expect it of you.” She had made him feel all that, and the moment they were back (he searched for the lights of the house above the bay) he would go to her and say, “I’ve done it, Mrs. Ramsay; thanks to you.” And so, turning into the lane that led to the house, he could see lights moving about in the upstairs windows. So they must be terribly late. People were dressing for dinner. The whole house was lit, and after the dark, the lights made his eyes feel full, and walking up the drive he said to himself, childishly, Lights, lights, lights, and said it over again in a daze, Lights, lights, lights, as they came into the house, staring around him, his face quite stiff. But good heavens, he told himself, reaching for his tie, I mustn’t make a fool of myself.)

chapters.title: The Window · 15
paragraphs: “Yes,” Prue said thoughtfully, in answer to her mother’s question, “I think Nancy did go with them.”

chapters.title: The Window · 16
paragraphs: Well then, Nancy had gone with them, Mrs. Ramsay supposed. Putting down a brush, picking up a comb, and calling “Come in” at a tap on the door (Jasper and Rose came in), she wondered whether Nancy’s being with them made anything happening less likely or more likely. Less likely, somehow, Mrs. Ramsay felt—quite irrationally—though after all, disaster on such a scale wasn’t probable. They couldn’t all be drowned. And once again she felt herself alone, facing her old enemy, life.
Mildred wanted to know, said Jasper and Rose, whether she should hold dinner back.
“Not for the Queen of England,” Mrs. Ramsay said firmly.
“Not for the Empress of Mexico,” she added, laughing at Jasper; for he shared his mother’s vice: he, too, exaggerated.

And while Jasper took the message, she told Rose that, if she liked, she could pick out the jewels her mother would wear. With fifteen people sitting down to dinner, you can’t keep things waiting forever. Now she was starting to feel annoyed with them for being so late. It was thoughtless of them; and on top of her worry about them, it annoyed her that they should pick this very night to stay out late, when she particularly wanted the dinner to go well, since William Bankes had at last agreed to eat with them; and they were having Mildred’s masterpiece—Bœuf en Daube, a French beef stew slow-cooked in wine. Everything depended on dishes going to the table at the exact moment they were ready. The beef, the bay leaf, the wine—every bit had to be cooked to perfection. Keeping it waiting was unthinkable. And yet, naturally, tonight of all nights, out they went, and back they came late, and dishes had to be sent out again, dishes had to be kept warm; the Bœuf en Daube would be utterly ruined.

Jasper held out an opal necklace; Rose a gold one. Which looked better against her black dress? Yes, which? said Mrs. Ramsay vaguely, studying her neck and shoulders in the mirror (but keeping away from her face). Then, while the children rummaged through her things, she gazed out of the window at a sight that never failed to amuse her—the rooks trying to make up their minds which tree to settle in. Each time, they seemed to change their minds and rise into the air again, because, she thought, the old rook, the father rook—old Joseph, she called him—had a very trying and difficult temperament. He was a disreputable old bird, missing half his wing feathers. He reminded her of some shabby old gentleman in a top hat she had once seen playing the horn outside a pub.

“Look!” she said, laughing. They really were fighting. Joseph and Mary were fighting. In any case, up they all went again, and their black wings shoved the air aside and cut it into exquisite scimitar shapes. That movement of wings beating out, out, out—she never could describe it precisely enough to satisfy herself—was among the loveliest things of all to her. Look at that, she said to Rose, hoping Rose would see it more clearly than she could. Because so often your children gave your own perceptions a little push forward.

But which one was it to be? They had opened every tray of her jewel box. The gold necklace, which was Italian, or the opal one Uncle James had brought her from India; or should she wear her amethysts?
“Choose, dearests, choose,” she said, hoping they would be quick.

But she let them take their time over it. Rose especially she let pick up first this and then that, and hold the jewels against the black dress; for this little ceremony of choosing jewels, gone through every night, was what Rose loved best, she knew. Rose had some secret reason of her own for thinking it tremendously important to choose what her mother wore. What could the reason be? Mrs. Ramsay wondered, standing still while Rose did up the clasp of the necklace she had picked. Through her own past she could guess at some deep, buried, wholly wordless feeling that you had for your mother at Rose’s age. Like every feeling felt for yourself, Mrs. Ramsay thought, it made you sad. What you could give back was so inadequate; and what Rose felt was out of all proportion to anything she really was. And Rose would grow up; and Rose would suffer, she supposed, with such deep feelings. Now she said she was ready, and they would go down, and Jasper, being the gentleman, should give her his arm, and Rose, being the lady, should carry her handkerchief (she handed her the handkerchief), and what else? Oh yes, it might be cold: a shawl. Choose me a shawl, she said, because that would please Rose, who was bound to suffer so. “There,” she said, pausing at the window on the landing, “there they are again.” Joseph had landed on a different treetop. “Don’t you think they mind,” she asked Jasper, “having their wings broken?” Why did he want to shoot poor old Joseph and Mary? He shuffled a bit on the stairs and felt told off, though not seriously, for she didn’t understand the fun of shooting birds; that birds didn’t feel; and being his mother, she lived far away in another part of the world. Still, he rather liked her stories about Mary and Joseph. She made him laugh. But how did she know those were Mary and Joseph? Did she think the same birds came to the same trees every night? he asked. But at this point, all of a sudden, she stopped paying him the slightest attention, the way grown-ups always did. She was listening to a clatter in the hall.

“They’re back!” she exclaimed, and immediately she felt far more annoyed with them than relieved. Then she wondered: had it happened? She would go down, and they would tell her—but no. With all these people around, they couldn’t tell her anything. So she had to go down, start dinner, and wait. And like some queen who finds her people gathered in the hall, gazes down at them, descends among them, silently acknowledges their tributes, and accepts their devotion and their bowing down before her (Paul kept perfectly still and looked straight ahead as she went by), she came downstairs and crossed the hall, bowing her head ever so slightly, as though accepting what they couldn’t say: their tribute to her beauty.

But she stopped. Something was burning. Could they have let the Bœuf en Daube boil too long? she wondered. Please heaven, no! And then the great clanging of the gong announced, solemnly and with authority, that everyone scattered through the house—in attics, in bedrooms, on little perches of their own, reading, writing, giving their hair a final smoothing, or doing up their dresses—must leave all that, and the little odds and ends on their washstands and dressing tables, and the novels on their bedside tables, and the diaries that were so private, and gather in the dining room for dinner.

chapters.title: The Window · 17
paragraphs: But what have I done with my life? Mrs. Ramsay thought, as she took her seat at the head of the table and looked down at all the plates making white circles on it. “William, sit by me,” she said. Then, wearily: “Lily—over there.” Paul Rayley and Minta Doyle had that; she had only this—a table stretching on forever, plates, knives. Down at the far end sat her husband, slumped all in a heap, frowning. Frowning at what? She had no idea, and she didn’t care. She couldn’t understand how she had ever felt any emotion, any affection at all, for him. Serving out the soup, she felt she was past everything, through everything, out of everything. It was as though there were an eddy—there—and you could be in it or you could be out of it, and she was out. It’s all over, she thought, as they came in one by one—Charles Tansley (“Sit there, please,” she told him), Augustus Carmichael—and took their seats. And all the while she waited, passively, for someone to answer her, for something to happen. But this, she thought as she ladled the soup, is not a thing you say.

She lifted her eyebrows at the mismatch—that this was what she was thinking, and that this was what she was doing, ladling soup—and felt herself, more and more strongly, outside that eddy. Or it was as though a shadow had come down, and, with the color drained away, she was seeing things as they really were. The room (she glanced around it) was very shabby. Nowhere was there any beauty. She would not let herself look at Mr. Tansley. Nothing seemed to have blended. Each of them sat apart. And the entire effort of blending and flowing and creating was left to her. Once more she felt the sterility of men—not with any hostility, simply as a fact: if she didn’t do it, nobody would. So she gave herself the small shake you give a stopped watch, and the old familiar pulse started up again, as the watch starts ticking—one, two, three, one, two, three. And so on and so on, she repeated, listening to it, protecting and coaxing the still faint pulse the way you might shelter a feeble flame behind a newspaper. And so, she decided, bending silently toward William Bankes—poor man! no wife, no children, eating alone in his lodgings every night but this one—out of pity for him, now that life was strong enough to carry her again, she started up the whole business. She was like a sailor who, a little wearily, watches the wind fill his sail and hardly wants to set out again, and thinks that if the ship had gone down he would have spun round and round and come to rest on the sea floor.
“Did you find your letters? I told them to leave them in the hall for you,” she said to William Bankes.

Lily Briscoe watched her drift off into that strange no-man’s-land where no one can follow. Yet when people go there, it chills those watching so much that they always try, at least, to keep them in sight—the way you watch a ship fading until its sails have dropped below the horizon.

How old she looks, Lily thought, how worn out, and how distant. Then Mrs. Ramsay turned to William Bankes with a smile, and it was as though the ship had come about and the sun had caught its sails again. Lily, a little amused because she was relieved, wondered: Why does she feel sorry for him? For that was the impression she gave as she told him his letters were in the hall—Poor William Bankes, she seemed to be saying—as if her tiredness had come in part from pitying people, and pity had stirred up the life in her, her determination to live again. And that wasn’t true, Lily thought. It was one of her misjudgments, the kind that seemed instinctive and seemed to spring from some need of her own rather than anyone else’s. There’s nothing pitiable about him at all. He has his work, Lily told herself. And suddenly, as though she had stumbled on treasure, it came back to her that she had her work too. In a flash she saw her picture. Yes, she thought, I’ll move the tree more toward the middle; that way I’ll get rid of that awkward gap. That’s what I’ll do. That’s what has been bothering me. She picked up the saltcellar and set it down on a flower in the tablecloth’s pattern, as a reminder to move the tree.
“It’s odd that you hardly ever get anything worth having in the mail, and yet you always want your letters,” said Mr. Bankes.

What utter damned nonsense they talk, Charles Tansley thought, and set his spoon down exactly in the center of his plate, which he had scraped clean—as though, it struck Lily (he sat across from her, his back to the window, squarely in the middle of the view), he meant to make quite certain of his meals. Everything about him had that same thin rigidity, that same bare lack of grace. And yet the fact remained that it was nearly impossible to dislike anybody once you looked at them. She liked his eyes. They were blue, set deep, and frightening.

“Do you write a lot of letters, Mr. Tansley?” asked Mrs. Ramsay. She was sorry for him too, Lily supposed—that was true of Mrs. Ramsay: she always pitied men, as if something were missing in them, and never women, as if women had something. Mr. Tansley answered curtly that he wrote to his mother; beyond that, he doubted he wrote a single letter a month.

He had no intention of talking the kind of nonsense these people wanted from him. He wasn’t going to let these silly women patronize him. He had been up in his room reading, and now that he had come down it all struck him as silly, shallow, flimsy. What did they dress up for? He had come down in his everyday clothes; he had no evening clothes to put on. “You never get anything worth having in the mail”—that was just the kind of thing they always said. They got men to say things like that. Well, yes, it was more or less true, he thought. From one year’s end to the next they never got anything worth having. All they did was talk, talk, talk, eat, eat, eat. The women were to blame. With all their “charm,” all their silliness, women made civilization impossible.

“No trip to the Lighthouse tomorrow, Mrs. Ramsay,” he said, to assert himself. He liked her. He admired her. He still thought about the man in the drainpipe gazing up at her. But he felt he needed to assert himself.

In spite of his eyes—but then, look at his nose, look at his hands—he really was, Lily Briscoe thought, the most charmless human being she had ever come across. So why did she care what he said?
