Women can’t write, women can’t paint—what did it matter, coming from him? Obviously he didn’t believe it; for some reason it was useful to him, and that was why he said it. Then why did her whole being bend down, like wheat in the wind, and only lift itself back up out of that humiliation by a huge and rather painful effort? She had to make that effort again. There’s the sprig on the tablecloth. There’s my painting. I have to move the tree to the middle. That’s what matters—nothing else. Couldn’t she just keep a firm grip on that, she asked herself, and not lose her temper, not argue—and if she wanted a bit of revenge, get it by laughing at him?
“Oh, Mr. Tansley,” she said, “please take me to the Lighthouse with you. I’d love that so much.”

She was lying; he could tell. For some reason she was saying things she didn’t mean, just to annoy him. She was making fun of him. He had on his old flannel trousers—the only ones he had. He felt coarse and shut out and very lonely. He knew she was teasing him for some reason of her own. She had no wish to go to the Lighthouse with him. She despised him, and so did Prue Ramsay, and so did the whole lot of them. But no woman was going to make a fool of him. So he deliberately turned in his chair, stared out the window, and told her, abruptly and very rudely, that the sea would be too rough for her tomorrow. She’d be sick.

He was annoyed that she had made him talk like that, and with Mrs. Ramsay listening. If only he could be up in his room, alone, working, he thought—among his books. That was where he was comfortable. And he had never owed anyone a penny; since the age of fifteen he had never cost his father a penny; he had helped out at home from his savings; he was paying for his sister’s schooling. All the same, he wished he had known how to give Miss Briscoe a proper answer, and that it hadn’t come out so abruptly. “You’d be sick.” If only he could think of something to say to Mrs. Ramsay, something to show her he wasn’t just a dry prig—which was what they all took him for. He turned toward her. But she was talking to William Bankes about people he had never heard of.

“Yes, you can take it away,” she told the maid shortly, breaking off her conversation with Mr. Bankes. “It must be fifteen—no, twenty years since I last saw her,” she was saying, turning straight back to him, as if she couldn’t spare a moment from their talk, it absorbed her so. So he had actually had a letter from her this evening! Was Carrie still living at Marlow, and was everything just the same? Oh, she remembered it as clearly as yesterday—going out on the river, and being very cold. But when the Mannings made a plan, they stuck to it. She would never forget Herbert on the riverbank, killing a wasp with a teaspoon! And it was all still going on, Mrs. Ramsay thought dreamily, drifting like a ghost among the chairs and tables of that drawing room beside the Thames, where she had been so very, very cold twenty years before. Now she moved among them like a ghost, and it fascinated her—as though she had changed, but that particular day, grown very still and lovely now, had stayed right there all these years. Had Carrie written to him herself? she asked.
“Yes. She says they’re putting in a new billiard room,” he said. No! No! That couldn’t be! A billiard room! To her it seemed impossible.
Mr. Bankes couldn’t see what was so strange about it. They were quite well off these days. Should he send Carrie her love?

“Oh,” Mrs. Ramsay said, slightly startled. “No,” she added, thinking that she didn’t know this Carrie with her new billiard room. But how strange it was, she said again—which amused Mr. Bankes—that they should still be carrying on there. It was extraordinary to think that they had managed to keep on living all these years while she had thought of them barely once in all that time. And what a lot had happened in her own life over those same years. Then again, maybe Carrie Manning hadn’t thought about her either. It was a strange thought, and not a pleasant one.

“People soon drift apart,” said Mr. Bankes. Still, he felt a certain satisfaction at the thought that, after all, he knew both the Mannings and the Ramsays. He himself had not drifted apart, he thought, putting down his spoon and wiping his clean-shaven lips with scrupulous care. Though perhaps he was rather unusual that way, he thought; he never let himself fall into a rut. He had friends in every circle. … At this point Mrs. Ramsay had to stop and tell the maid something about keeping the food hot. That was why he liked to eat alone. All these interruptions irritated him. Well, William Bankes thought, keeping up a manner of perfect politeness and simply spreading the fingers of his left hand on the tablecloth—the way a mechanic, in a spare moment, inspects a tool that is beautifully polished and ready for use—these are the sacrifices your friends demand of you. She would have been hurt if he had said no. But for his part it wasn’t worth it. Looking at his hand, he thought that if he had been on his own, dinner would nearly be over by now and he would be free to work. Yes, he thought, it is a dreadful waste of time. Children were still trickling in. “I wish one of you would run up to Roger’s room,” Mrs. Ramsay was saying. How petty it all is, how dull, he thought, next to the other thing—work. Here he was drumming his fingers on the tablecloth when he could have been—and he took a swift bird’s-eye view of his work. What a waste of time it all was, really! And yet, he thought, she’s one of my oldest friends. I’m more or less devoted to her. Yet just now, at this moment, her presence meant nothing whatever to him. Her beauty meant nothing to him. Her sitting at the window with her little boy—nothing, nothing. All he wanted was to be alone and pick up that book. He felt uneasy; he felt like a traitor, sitting beside her and feeling nothing for her. The truth was, he didn’t enjoy family life. It was in a mood like this that you asked yourself, What are we living for? Why, you wondered, go to all this trouble to keep the human race going? Is it really so desirable? Are we an attractive species? Not especially, he thought, glancing at those rather scruffy boys. His favorite, Cam, must be in bed, he supposed. Silly questions, useless questions, questions you never asked when you had something to do. Is human life this? Is human life that? There was never time to think about it. Yet here he was asking himself exactly that kind of thing, because Mrs. Ramsay was busy giving the servants orders—and also because, when he saw how surprised Mrs. Ramsay was that Carrie Manning still existed, it had struck him that friendships, even the best ones, are fragile. People drift apart. Again he reproached himself. Here he sat next to Mrs. Ramsay, and he had nothing in the world to say to her.

“I’m so sorry,” Mrs. Ramsay said, finally turning to him. He felt stiff and barren, like a pair of boots that has been drenched and then dried out, so you can hardly squeeze your feet into them. But squeeze his feet in he must. He must force himself to talk. If he wasn’t very careful, she would see through this betrayal of his—see that he didn’t care two straws about her—and that would be anything but pleasant, he thought. So he inclined his head politely toward her.

“You must hate eating in this madhouse,” she said, slipping, as she always did when her mind was elsewhere, into her social manner. It is the same as when a meeting breaks into a clash of voices, and the chairman, to restore unity, proposes that everyone speak French. The French may be bad; it may lack the words for what the speaker actually thinks; all the same, speaking French imposes a certain order, a certain sameness. Mr. Bankes answered her in the same language—“No, not at all”—and Mr. Tansley, who knew nothing of that language, even in words of one syllable like these, immediately suspected it of being insincere. The Ramsays really did talk nonsense, he thought, and he seized on this new example gleefully, making a note that some day he would read aloud to a friend or two. There, among people who could speak their minds, he would give a sarcastic account of “staying with the Ramsays” and the nonsense they talked. Worth doing once, he would say, but never again. The women were so boring, he would say. Ramsay, of course, had done for himself by marrying a beautiful woman and having eight children. It would come out roughly like that. But right now, stuck in his chair with an empty seat next to him, none of it had come out at all. It was nothing but scraps and fragments. He felt terribly uncomfortable, physically uncomfortable, even. He wanted someone to give him a chance to make his mark. He wanted it so badly that he squirmed in his chair, looked at one person and then another, tried to cut into their talk, opened his mouth and closed it again. They were discussing the fishing industry. Why didn’t anybody ask what he thought? What did they know about the fishing industry?

Lily Briscoe knew all that. Sitting across from him, couldn’t she see it, as if in an X-ray, the ribs and thighbones of the young man’s craving to impress, lying dark inside the mist of his flesh—that thin mist convention had spread over his burning urge to break into the conversation? But why, she thought, narrowing her Chinese eyes and remembering how he sneered at women—“can’t paint, can’t write”—why should I help him find relief?

There is a code of manners, she knew, and its seventh article (possibly) states that on occasions like this one it falls to the woman, whatever her own work may be, to come to the aid of the young man across from her, so that he can bring out and ease the thighbones and ribs of his vanity, his pressing need to assert himself. Just as it is their duty, she thought, with her old-maidish sense of fair play, to help us if, for instance, the Underground caught fire. In that case, she thought, I’d certainly expect Mr. Tansley to get me out. But what if, she wondered, neither of us did either? So she sat there, smiling.

“You aren’t thinking of going to the Lighthouse, are you, Lily?” Mrs. Ramsay said. “Remember poor Mr. Langley. He’d sailed around the world dozens of times, but he told me he’d never suffered anything like it until my husband took him out there. Mr. Tansley, are you a good sailor?”

Mr. Tansley lifted a hammer and swung it high overhead; but as it came down he saw that he could not crush that butterfly with a tool like that, and all he said was that he had never been seasick in his life. Yet packed tight into that one sentence, like gunpowder, lay everything: that his grandfather had been a fisherman and his father a pharmacist; that he had worked his own way up, entirely; that he was proud of it; that he was Charles Tansley—which nobody here seemed to grasp, though one of these days every last one of them would know it. He scowled straight in front of him. He could almost feel sorry for these gentle, cultured people, who one of these days would be blown sky-high, like bales of wool and barrels of apples, by the gunpowder inside him.

“Will you take me, Mr. Tansley?” Lily said, quickly and kindly. Because of course, if Mrs. Ramsay told her—and in effect that is what she did—“My dear, I’m drowning in seas of fire. Unless you soothe the agony of this hour with some balm, and say something nice to that young man, life will run aground on the rocks—in fact I can hear the grinding and growling right now. My nerves are stretched tight as violin strings. One more touch and they’ll snap”—when Mrs. Ramsay said all that, as the look in her eyes did say it, then naturally, for the hundred and fiftieth time, Lily Briscoe had to abandon the experiment—what happens if you are not nice to that young man?—and be nice.

He read the shift in her mood correctly—she was friendly to him now—and, released from his egotism, he told her how as a baby he had been tossed out of a boat, and how his father used to hook him back out of the water with a boathook; that was how he learned to swim. One of his uncles, he said, kept the light on some rock or other off the coast of Scotland, and he had been out there with him during a storm. He said this loudly, into a pause. They had no choice but to listen when he announced that he had been in a lighthouse in a storm with his uncle. Ah, Lily Briscoe thought, as the talk took this hopeful turn and she sensed Mrs. Ramsay’s gratitude (Mrs. Ramsay was now free to talk a little herself)—ah, she thought, but what haven’t I paid to get this for you? She hadn’t been sincere.

She had played the usual trick: she had been nice. She would never know him, and he would never know her. All human relationships were like that, she thought, and the worst of all (if it weren’t for Mr. Bankes) were the ones between men and women. Those were bound to be deeply insincere. Then her glance fell on the saltcellar she had set there as a reminder, and she remembered that in the morning she was going to move the tree further toward the middle. The thought of painting tomorrow lifted her spirits so high that she burst out laughing at something Mr. Tansley said. Let him go on all night, if he enjoyed it.

“But how long do they keep men on a Lighthouse?” she asked. He told her; he was amazingly well informed. And because he was grateful, and he liked her, and he was starting to have a good time, Mrs. Ramsay thought that now she could slip back into that dreamland, that unreal but fascinating place—the Mannings’ drawing room at Marlow twenty years ago—where you moved about unhurried and untroubled, because there was no future to fret about. She knew what had become of them, and of herself. It was like rereading a good book, because she knew how that story ended—it had all happened twenty years ago—and life, which came spilling in cascades even off this dining table, heaven knows where to, was sealed up there, lying calm between its banks like a lake. He had said they’d built a billiard room—could it be true? Would William keep talking about the Mannings? She wanted him to. But no—for some reason the mood had left him. She tried, and he didn’t respond. She couldn’t make him. She felt let down.
“The children are a disgrace,” she said with a sigh. He remarked that punctuality was one of the minor virtues, one we only pick up later in life.

“If ever,” said Mrs. Ramsay, only to fill the silence, and thought what an old maid William was getting to be. Knowing he had been disloyal, knowing she wanted to talk about something more personal, and yet not in the mood for it at the moment, he felt the dreariness of life settle on him as he sat there, waiting. Maybe the others were saying something interesting? What were they talking about?

That it had been a bad fishing season, and the men were emigrating. They were discussing wages and unemployment. The young man was laying into the government. William Bankes, thinking how good it was to have something like this to grab hold of when your private life was disagreeable, heard him mention “one of the most scandalous acts of this present government.” Lily was listening, Mrs. Ramsay was listening; everyone was listening. But Lily, bored already, felt that something was lacking. Mr. Bankes felt that something was lacking. Drawing her shawl around her, Mrs. Ramsay felt that something was lacking. As they all leaned in to listen, every one of them was thinking, “Please God, don’t let the inside of my mind show.” For each of them thought, “The others feel all this. They’re furious and indignant at the government on the fishermen’s behalf. And I feel nothing whatsoever.” But then again, Mr. Bankes thought, looking at Mr. Tansley, perhaps this is the man. You were always waiting for the man; there was always the chance. At any moment the leader might come along—the man of genius, in politics or in anything else. He’ll most likely be extremely disagreeable to us old fogies, Mr. Bankes thought, trying hard to be tolerant. He could tell, from an odd physical sensation, as though the nerves along his spine were bristling, that he was jealous—partly on his own account, but more likely on account of his work, his point of view, his science. And so he wasn’t entirely open-minded or entirely fair. For Mr. Tansley seemed to be saying, You’ve wasted your lives. You’ve got it all wrong, every one of you. Poor old fogies, you’re hopelessly out of date. He did seem rather full of himself, this young man, and his manners were poor. But Mr. Bankes made himself notice that he had nerve, and talent, and a remarkable grasp of the facts. Very likely, Mr. Bankes thought, while Tansley laid into the government, there’s a good deal of truth in what he says.

“Tell me now …” he said. And so they argued about politics. Lily looked at the leaf on the tablecloth; Mrs. Ramsay left the argument wholly to the two men and wondered why the talk bored her so much, and she looked down the table at her husband and wished he would say something. Just one word, she told herself. If he said anything at all, it would change everything. He got to the heart of things. He cared about the fishermen and their pay. Thinking about them kept him awake at night. When he spoke, everything was different; you didn’t feel, then, please God don’t let them see how little I care—because you did care. Then she realized that she was waiting for him to speak because she admired him so much, and she felt as though someone had been praising her husband and their marriage to her face, and she glowed all over, never noticing that the praise had been her own. She looked at him, expecting to see all this in his face; surely he would be looking magnificent. … Not in the slightest! His face was screwed up; he was scowling and frowning and going red with rage. What on earth was the matter? she wondered. What could it possibly be? Only that poor old Augustus had asked for a second plate of soup—nothing more. It was unthinkable, it was loathsome (he signaled this to her across the table) that Augustus should be starting on his soup all over again. He hated people eating after he had finished. She watched his anger leap into his eyes, into his forehead, like a pack of hounds, and she knew that any moment something violent would burst out, and then—but thank goodness! she saw him take hold of himself and jam a brake on the wheel, and his whole body seemed to throw off sparks, but no words. He sat there scowling. He had said nothing, he wanted her to note. She should give him credit for that! But after all, why shouldn’t poor Augustus ask for more soup? All he had done was touch Ellen’s arm and say:
“Ellen, please, another plate of soup”—and at that Mr. Ramsay had scowled like that.

Well, why not? Mrs. Ramsay demanded. Surely they could let Augustus have soup if he wanted soup. He couldn’t stand people wallowing in their food, Mr. Ramsay frowned back. He couldn’t stand everything dragging on for hours this way. But he had kept himself under control, Mr. Ramsay wanted her to note, revolting as it was to watch. But why make it so obvious? Mrs. Ramsay demanded. (They were looking at each other down the length of the table, sending these questions and answers back and forth, each knowing precisely what the other felt.) Everyone could see it, Mrs. Ramsay thought. There was Rose, staring at her father; there was Roger, staring at his father; another second and they would both be doubled up with laughter, she knew—and so she said quickly (and it was high time):
“Light the candles,” and at once they sprang up and went fumbling at the sideboard.

Why could he never keep his feelings to himself? Mrs. Ramsay wondered—and had Augustus Carmichael noticed? Maybe he had, maybe he hadn’t. She couldn’t help respecting the calm way he sat there, drinking his soup. When he wanted soup, he asked for it. Laugh at him or be angry with him, he stayed exactly the same. He didn’t like her; she knew that; but that was partly the very reason she respected him. And watching him drink his soup, huge and calm in the dimming light, monumental, lost in thought, she wondered what he actually did feel at such times, and why he was always so contented and dignified. She thought, too, of how devoted he was to Andrew—how he would call him into his room and, in Andrew’s words, “show him things.” And then he would lie out on the lawn all day, presumably brooding over his poetry, until he put you in mind of a cat watching birds; and when he had found the word, he clapped his paws together, and her husband would say, “Poor old Augustus—he’s a true poet,” which from her husband was high praise.

Now eight candles stood in a row down the table. After their first dip the flames straightened, and they drew the whole long table into view, and in its center a yellow and purple dish of fruit. What had she done with it? Mrs. Ramsay wondered. For Rose’s arrangement—the grapes and pears, the horny shell lined with pink, the bananas—made her think of a trophy hauled up from the seabed, of a banquet of Neptune, of the cluster of grapes that hangs with its vine leaves over Bacchus’s shoulder (in some painting or other), among leopard skins and torches flaring and drooping, red and gold. … Lifted suddenly into the light like that, it seemed enormous and deep, like a world where you could pick up your walking stick and climb its hills, she thought, and walk down into its valleys. And to her delight (because for a moment it made them feel in tune) she saw that Augustus, too, was feasting his eyes on the same dish of fruit: diving in, snapping off a bloom here, a tassel there, and then, having feasted, going back to his hive. That was how he looked at things, not the way she did. But looking together brought them together.

Now all the candles were burning, and the candlelight drew the faces on either side of the table closer and gathered them, as the twilight had not, into a party sitting around a table. For now the night was shut out by panes of glass, and the glass, far from showing any true picture of the world outside, rippled it so oddly that in here, inside the room, there seemed to be order and solid ground, while out there was only a reflection in which things wavered and melted away, as if in water.

At once a change passed through all of them, as though this had actually happened. Each of them was aware that together they made a party in a hollow, on an island, with a shared cause against the fluid world out there. Mrs. Ramsay had been restless while she waited for Paul and Minta to come in, unable, as she felt it, to settle to anything. Now that unease turned into expectation. They must come now. Lily Briscoe, meanwhile, tried to work out where this sudden lift of spirits came from, and she compared it with that moment on the tennis lawn when solid things all at once dissolved and such vast distances opened between people. Here the same effect came from the crowd of candles in the barely furnished room, from the windows with no curtains, and from the bright, masklike look that candlelight gives to faces. A weight had been lifted from them; anything could happen, she felt. They must come now, thought Mrs. Ramsay, her eyes on the door, and in that instant Minta Doyle and Paul Rayley came in, together with a maid holding a great dish in both hands. They were terribly late, Minta said; horribly late. And the two of them made their way to opposite ends of the table.

“I lost my brooch—my grandmother’s brooch,” Minta said, and there was a note of mourning in her voice; her large brown eyes were swimming, and she looked down, then up, as she took her seat beside Mr. Ramsay. All this stirred his chivalry, and he began to tease her,
How could she be such a goose, he asked her, as to go climbing over rocks with jewelry on?

In a way she was terrified of him—he was so dreadfully clever. On that first night, when she had been placed beside him and he talked about George Eliot, she had been truly frightened, because she had left the third volume of _Middlemarch_ behind on the train and never learned how it ended. Later, though, the two of them got along perfectly, and she pretended to be even more ignorant than she was, since he enjoyed telling her she was a fool. So tonight, as soon as he laughed at her, her fear was gone. Besides, she had known the moment she walked into the room that the miracle had happened: she was wearing her golden haze. Some days she had it; some days she didn’t. Why it came and why it went she never knew, and she could not even tell whether she had it until she entered a room; then she knew at once, from the way some man looked at her. Yes, tonight she had it, enormously; she could tell from the way Mr. Ramsay ordered her not to be a fool. She sat next to him and smiled.

So it must have happened, Mrs. Ramsay thought; they are engaged. For a moment she felt something she had never expected to feel again: jealousy. Because her husband felt it as well—the glow coming off Minta. He was fond of these girls, these girls with golden-red hair who had something flying loose about them, something a bit wild and harum-scarum; girls who didn’t “scrape their hair off,” who were not, in his phrase for poor Lily Briscoe, “skimpy.” They had some quality she lacked herself, a luster, a richness, and it drew him, amused him, and made him pick out girls like Minta as his favorites. They were allowed to cut his hair, or braid watch-chains for him, or break in on his work, shouting to him (she could hear them), “Come along, Mr. Ramsay; it’s our turn to beat them now,” and out he would come to play tennis.

Yet she was not really jealous. It was only that now and then, when she forced herself to look in the mirror, she resented a little having grown old—through her own fault, perhaps. (The greenhouse bill, and all the rest of it.) She was grateful to these girls for laughing at him (“How many pipes have you smoked today, Mr. Ramsay?” and so on), because then he seemed a young man again, a man women found very attractive. He was no longer loaded down, no longer crushed by the greatness of his work and the sorrows of the world and his fame or his failure; he was once more the man she had first known, gaunt but gallant, handing her out of a boat, she remembered, with charming ways like that (she glanced at him, and teasing Minta he looked astonishingly young). As for herself—“Put it down there,” she said, and helped the Swiss girl lower the huge brown pot with the Bœuf en Daube gently onto the table in front of her—as for herself, she liked her dunces. Paul must sit by her; she had saved a place for him. Honestly, she sometimes thought the dunces were the ones she liked best. They didn’t weary you with their dissertations. These very clever men, how much they missed, after all! How dried-up they became, there was no denying it. As Paul sat down, she thought there was something very charming about him. She loved his manners, and his sharp, clean-cut nose, and his bright blue eyes. He was so thoughtful. Now that everyone was talking again, would he tell her what had happened?

“We went back to look for Minta’s brooch,” he said, as he sat down beside her. “We”—she needed no more. From the effort, from the way his voice climbed to get over a hard word, she knew it was the first time he had said “we.” “We” did this, “we” did that. They will be saying it for the rest of their lives, she thought. Marthe lifted off the lid with a little flourish, and a wonderful smell of olives and oil and juices rose from the big brown dish. The cook had worked three days on it. And she must be very careful, Mrs. Ramsay thought as she dug into the soft mass, to pick out an especially tender piece for William Bankes. She looked down into the dish, at its glossy sides and its muddle of savory brown and yellow meats, its bay leaves and its wine, and she thought, This will celebrate the occasion. A strange feeling rose in her, whimsical and tender at once, of keeping a festival, as though two emotions had been summoned in her. One was deep—for what could be more serious than the love of a man for a woman, what more powerful or more impressive, when it carries inside it the seeds of death? And at the same time these lovers, these people walking with shining eyes into illusion, had to be danced around mockingly and decked with garlands.

“It’s a triumph,” Mr. Bankes said, and he put his knife down for a moment. He had been eating with great attention. It was rich; it was tender; it was cooked to perfection. How did she manage such things so far out in the country? he asked. What a wonderful woman she was. All his love and all his reverence had come back to him; and she knew it.

“My grandmother’s recipe—it’s French,” said Mrs. Ramsay, and her voice rang with pleasure. French, naturally. What they call cooking in England is an abomination, the two of them agreed. It means dropping cabbages into water. It means roasting meat till it turns to leather. It means peeling away the lovely skins of vegetables. “And the skin,” Mr. Bankes put in, “is where all the virtue of the vegetable lies.” And then the waste, said Mrs. Ramsay. What an English cook throws out would feed an entire French family. She felt that William’s affection had returned to her, that all was well again, that the suspense was over and she was free now to triumph and to mock; and, spurred on by this, she laughed and waved her hands about, until Lily thought, How childlike she is, how absurd, sitting up there with all her beauty unfolded in her once more, talking about vegetable skins. There was something frightening in her. Nobody could resist her. In the end, Lily thought, she always had her way. Now she had managed this—Paul and Minta, it seemed, were engaged. Mr. Bankes was having dinner here. She cast a spell over all of them just by wanting things, so simply and so directly. Lily measured that abundance against her own poverty of spirit. Part of it, she supposed, was Mrs. Ramsay’s belief (her face was all lit up—she did not look young, but she looked radiant) in this strange and terrifying thing that had set Paul Rayley, at the center of it, trembling all over, and yet left him remote, absorbed and silent. As she talked about vegetable skins, Mrs. Ramsay, Lily felt, was exalting that thing, worshipping it, holding her hands over it both to warm them and to shelter it; and yet, having brought it all about, she was somehow laughing, leading her victims, Lily felt, to the altar. Now it came over Lily as well—the emotion, the vibration of love. Next to Paul, how unnoticeable she felt! He was glowing, burning; she was aloof and satirical. He was setting out on an adventure; she was moored to the shore. He was launched and heedless; she was alone, left out. And, ready to plead for a share in his disaster, if disaster it was, she asked shyly:
“When did Minta lose her brooch?”
His smile was the most exquisite smile, clouded with memory, tinted with dreams. He shook his head. “On the beach,” he said.
“I’m going to find it,” he said. “I’ll get up early.” Because Minta was not to know, he dropped his voice, and his eyes went to where she sat laughing next to Mr. Ramsay.

Lily wanted to declare, violently, outrageously, how much she longed to help him. She imagined herself on the beach at dawn, the one who swooped on the brooch lying half-hidden by a stone, and so found herself counted among the sailors and adventurers. But what was his answer to her offer? With a feeling she rarely allowed to show, she actually said, “Let me come with you”; and he laughed. He might have meant yes, or no—perhaps either. It was not his meaning that mattered, though; it was that odd chuckle, as if he had said, Go and throw yourself off the cliff if you want, it’s nothing to me. He turned the heat of love on her cheek—its horror, its cruelty, its lack of all scruple. She was scorched by it. Then, looking down the table at Minta being charming to Mr. Ramsay, Lily flinched on Minta’s behalf, exposed as she was to those fangs, and felt thankful. At any rate, she told herself, her eye falling on the saltcellar in the pattern, she did not have to marry, thank Heaven; that humiliation was not for her. She had been spared that watering-down. She would move the tree a little more toward the middle.

That was how complicated things were. Because what happened to her, particularly when she stayed with the Ramsays, was that she was made to feel two contrary things, violently, both at once. One said, that’s what you feel; the other said, that’s what I feel; and then the two fought it out in her mind, as they were doing now. Love is so lovely, so thrilling, that I tremble on its brink and, quite unlike myself, volunteer to hunt for a brooch on a beach; and love is also the stupidest, most savage of human passions, and it takes a nice young man with a profile like a cameo (Paul’s profile was exquisite) and turns him into a bully with a crowbar (he was swaggering, he was insolent) in the Mile End Road, in the East End of London. And yet, she told herself, odes have been sung to love since the dawn of time, wreaths and roses have been piled up for it, and nine people out of ten, if you asked them, would say this was the one thing they wanted; while all along the women, to judge by her own experience, would be feeling, This isn’t what we want; nothing is more boring, more childish, more inhuman than love; and yet it is beautiful as well, and necessary. Well then? Well then? she asked, somehow expecting the others to take up the argument, as though in an argument of this kind you fired off your own small bolt, which obviously fell short, and left the rest to the others. So she listened once more to their talk, in case they shed some light on the question of love.
“And then,” said Mr. Bankes, “there’s that liquid the English call coffee.”

“Oh, coffee!” said Mrs. Ramsay. But the real question, much more, was one of real butter and clean milk (she was thoroughly roused, Lily could see, and was speaking very forcefully). With warmth and eloquence she laid out the wickedness of the English dairy system and the condition milk was in when it reached your door, and she was just about to prove her charges, having gone into the matter, when laughter broke out all around the table. It started with Andrew in the middle and leaped like fire from one tuft of gorse to the next: her children laughed; her husband laughed; she was laughed at, surrounded by fire, and forced to lower her crest and take down her guns. All she could do in return was point out the table’s mockery and teasing to Mr. Bankes, as an example of what you had to put up with if you attacked the prejudices of the British Public.

She made a deliberate exception of Lily, though, and did not count her with the rest, because it weighed on her that Lily, who had helped her with Mr. Tansley, was out of things. “Lily agrees with me, anyway,” she said, and in this way drew her in, a little flustered, a little startled. (Lily had been thinking about love.) Both of them were out of things, Mrs. Ramsay had been thinking, Lily and Charles Tansley alike. The glow of the other two made both of them suffer. He plainly felt himself completely out in the cold; with Paul Rayley in the room, no woman would look at him. Poor man! Still, he had his dissertation, on the influence of somebody on something: he could take care of himself. Lily was another matter. Under Minta’s glow she faded, and became even less noticeable than usual, in her little gray dress, with her little puckered face and her little Chinese eyes. Everything about her was so small. And yet, Mrs. Ramsay thought, setting her beside Minta as she appealed to her for support (Lily should bear her out that she went on about her dairies no more than her husband went on about his boots—he could talk about his boots for hours), of the two girls, Lily at forty will be the finer. Lily had a thread of something in her, a flare of something, something all her own, which Mrs. Ramsay liked very much indeed, but which no man would like, she was afraid. Clearly not, unless he were a much older man, like William Bankes. But then he cared—well, since his wife died, Mrs. Ramsay sometimes thought, he perhaps cared for her. Not that he was “in love,” of course; it was one of those unclassified affections, of which there are so many. Oh, but that’s nonsense, she thought; William must marry Lily. They have so much in common. Lily loves flowers. Both of them are cold and aloof and rather self-sufficient. She must arrange a long walk for the two of them.

It had been foolish to seat them across from each other. That could be fixed tomorrow. If it was fine, they would go for a picnic. Anything seemed possible. Everything seemed right. Just now (though this can’t last, she thought, standing apart from the moment while the rest of them talked about boots), just now she had arrived at safety. She hovered like a hawk held still in the air; she floated like a flag in an element of joy that filled every nerve of her body, fully and sweetly—not loudly, but rather solemnly, because it came, she thought, as she watched them all eating, from her husband and children and friends. All this, rising in the deep stillness (she was giving William Bankes one very small piece more, and peering into the depths of the earthenware pot), now seemed, for no particular reason, to linger there like smoke, like a vapor drifting upward, keeping them safe together. Nothing needed saying; nothing could be said. There it was, all around them. It had something of eternity in it, she felt, as she carefully served Mr. Bankes an especially tender piece—just as she had felt once already that afternoon about something else. There is a coherence in things, a steadiness; something, she meant, that change cannot touch, and that shines out (she glanced at the window, rippling with reflected lights) against the flowing, the fleeting, the ghostly, like a ruby. So tonight, once more, she had the feeling she had had earlier today, of peace, of rest. It is from moments like these, she thought, that the thing is made that remains forever after. This would remain.
“Yes,” she told William Bankes reassuringly, “there’s plenty for everyone.”

“Andrew,” she said, “hold your plate lower, or I’ll spill it.” (The Bœuf en Daube was a complete triumph.) Here, she felt, laying down the spoon, was the still space around the heart of things, where you could move about or rest. She could wait now (everyone had been served), and listen; and then, like a hawk that suddenly drops from its height, she could flaunt and sink easily into laughter, leaning her whole weight on what her husband, at the far end of the table, was saying about the square root of one thousand two hundred and fifty-three, which happened to be the number on his train ticket.

What did any of it mean? Even now she had no idea. A square root—what was that? Her sons knew. She leaned on them, on cubes and square roots, which was the subject now; on Voltaire and Madame de Staël; on Napoleon’s character; on how land was held in France; on Lord Rosebery; on Creevey’s Memoirs. She let this admirable structure of the masculine mind hold her up and carry her. It ran up and down and crisscrossed like iron girders across the swaying fabric, supporting the world, so that she could give herself up to it entirely, could even close her eyes, or let them flicker for a moment, the way a child lying on its pillow blinks up at the countless layers of leaves on a tree. Then she came to. The building was still going on. William Bankes was praising the Waverley novels.

Every six months he read one of them, he said. And why should that make Charles Tansley angry? In he rushed (all because Prue won’t be nice to him, Mrs. Ramsay thought) and attacked the Waverley novels without knowing a thing about them, not a single thing, Mrs. Ramsay thought, watching him rather than attending to his words. His manner told her how it was: he wanted to assert himself, and he would always be like this until he had his professorship or had married his wife, and then he would not need to keep on saying, “I—I—I.” Because that was all his criticism of poor Sir Walter Scott—or maybe it was Jane Austen—came to. “I—I—I.” She could hear from his voice, from his emphasis and his uneasiness, that he was thinking of himself and of the impression he made. Success would do him good. Anyway, they were off again, and she did not have to listen now. It would not last, she knew, but for the moment her eyes were so clear that they seemed to travel around the table, effortlessly uncovering each of these people, their thoughts and feelings, like a light slipping under water, so that the ripples and the reeds and the minnows balancing there and the sudden silent trout are all lit up, hanging, trembling. That was how she saw them and heard them. But whatever they said had this quality too, as though their words were like a trout moving while you can see, at the same time, the ripple and the gravel, something on the right, something on the left, and all of it held together. For in active life she would be netting things, sorting one from another; she would be saying that she liked the Waverley novels, or that she hadn’t read them; she would be pushing herself forward. Now she said nothing. For the moment she hung there, suspended.

“Ah, but how long do you think it will last?” somebody said. It was as if trembling antennae reached out from her, catching certain sentences and pressing them on her notice. This was one. She scented danger to her husband. A question like that was almost sure to lead to some remark that would remind him of his own failure. How long will I be read?—that would be his immediate thought. William Bankes, who was quite free of any such vanity, laughed and said that changes in fashion meant nothing to him. Who could say what would last, in literature or in anything else, for that matter?

“Let’s enjoy what we enjoy,” he said. To Mrs. Ramsay his integrity seemed altogether admirable. Not for a moment did he seem to think, But what does this mean for me? But if your temperament was the other kind, the kind that needs praise and needs encouragement, then of course you started (and she knew Mr. Ramsay was starting) to grow uneasy, to want someone to say, Oh, but your work will last, Mr. Ramsay, or something of the sort. He made his uneasiness plain enough now, remarking with some irritation that Scott (or was it Shakespeare?) would see him through his lifetime, anyway. He said it irritably. Everyone, she thought, felt slightly uncomfortable, without knowing why. Then Minta Doyle, who had good instincts, declared bluntly and absurdly that she didn’t believe anybody truly enjoyed reading Shakespeare. Very few people, Mr. Ramsay said grimly (though his mind had turned away again), liked it as much as they claimed. Still, he added, some of the plays have considerable merit, and Mrs. Ramsay saw that for now, at least, all would be well. He would laugh at Minta; and Minta, Mrs. Ramsay saw, sensing how intensely anxious he was about himself, would make sure in her own way that he was looked after, and would praise him somehow. But she wished it weren’t necessary; perhaps it was her own fault that it was. In any case, she was free now to listen to Paul Rayley, who was trying to say something about the books you read as a boy. Those lasted, he said. At school he had read some Tolstoy. There was one he never forgot, though he couldn’t remember what it was called. Russian names were impossible, said Mrs. Ramsay. “Vronsky,” said Paul. He remembered that one because he had always thought it made such a good name for a villain. “Vronsky,” Mrs. Ramsay said. “Oh, _Anna Karenina_.” But that did not get them much further; books were not really their line. No—Charles Tansley could correct them both about books in a moment, but with him it was all so tangled up with Am I saying the right thing? Am I making a good impression? that in the end you found out more about him than about Tolstoy. What Paul said, on the other hand, was simply about the thing itself, not about him. Like all stupid people he had a sort of modesty as well, a thought for what you were feeling, and every so often, at least, she found that attractive. At this moment he was thinking neither about himself nor about Tolstoy, but whether she was cold, whether there was a draft on her, whether she would like a pear.

No, she said, she didn’t want a pear. The truth was she had been jealously guarding the dish of fruit (without knowing it), hoping no one would touch it. Her eyes had been wandering in and out of the curves and shadows of the fruit, among the deep purples of the lowland grapes, then over the horny ridge of the shell, laying a yellow beside a purple, a curved shape beside a round one, not knowing why she did it, or why each time she felt calmer and calmer; until—oh, what a shame that they should do it—a hand stretched out, took a pear, and ruined everything. She looked at Rose in sympathy. She looked at Rose, sitting between Jasper and Prue. How strange that your own child should do such a thing!

How strange it was to see them sitting there in a row, her children, Jasper, Rose, Prue and Andrew, hardly speaking, but sharing some joke of their own, she guessed, from the way their lips twitched. It was something quite separate from everything else, something they were storing up to laugh at later in their own room. She hoped it was not about their father. No, she thought not. What could it be? she wondered, a little sadly, because it seemed to her that they would laugh when she wasn’t there. All of that was kept hidden behind those rather fixed, still, masklike faces, for they did not easily join in; they were like watchers, like surveyors, raised a little above the grown-ups or set a little apart from them. But looking at Prue tonight, she saw that this was no longer entirely true of her. Prue was just starting, just stirring, just coming down. There was the faintest light on her face, as though the glow of Minta across from her, some excitement, some expectation of happiness, were mirrored in her—as though the sun of the love between men and women were coming up over the edge of the tablecloth, and she, not knowing what it was, leaned toward it and greeted it. Again and again she looked at Minta, shy but curious, so that Mrs. Ramsay looked from one girl to the other and said to Prue inside her own mind, One of these days you will be as happy as she is. You will be far happier, she added—because you are my daughter, she meant; her own daughters had to be happier than other people’s. But dinner was finished. It was time to leave. They were only fiddling with things on their plates. She would wait till they had stopped laughing at some story her husband was telling. He was joking with Minta about a bet. Then she would get up.

All of a sudden she thought that she liked Charles Tansley; she liked the way he laughed. She liked him for being so angry with Paul and Minta. She liked his clumsiness. There was a good deal in that young man, after all. And Lily, she thought, laying her napkin beside her plate—Lily always has a private joke of her own. You never need to worry about Lily. She waited. She tucked her napkin under the rim of her plate. Well, had they finished now? No. One story had led to another. Her husband was in high spirits tonight; wanting, she supposed, to make up to old Augustus after that business over the soup, he had pulled him in, and the two of them were telling stories about someone they had both known at college. She looked at the window, where the candle flames burned brighter now that the panes had gone black, and as she gazed out there the voices reached her very strangely, like voices at a service in a cathedral, since she was not following the words. The sudden gusts of laughter, and then one voice (Minta’s) speaking by itself, reminded her of men and boys calling out the Latin of a service in some Roman Catholic cathedral. She waited. Her husband was speaking. He was repeating something, and she could tell it was poetry from the rhythm and from the note of exaltation and sadness in his voice:

Come out and climb the garden path,
Luriana Lurilee.
The China rose is all abloom and buzzing with the yellow bee.

The words (she was looking at the window) seemed to be floating out there like flowers on water, cut off from all of them, as though nobody had spoken them and they had simply come into being on their own.

And all the lives we ever lived and all the lives to be
Are full of trees and changing leaves.

What they meant, she did not know; but the words, like music, seemed to be spoken in her own voice, somewhere outside her, saying quite easily and naturally what had been in her mind all evening while she was saying other things. Without looking around she knew that everyone at the table was listening to the voice as it said:

I wonder if it seems to you
Luriana, Lurilee
and listening with the same relief and pleasure she felt, as if at last this were the natural thing to say, as if it were their own voice that was speaking.
Then the voice broke off. She looked around, and made herself stand up. Augustus Carmichael was on his feet, holding his napkin so that it hung like a long white robe, and he stood there chanting:

To see the Kings go riding by
Over lawn and daisy lea
With their palm leaves and cedar sheaves,
Luriana, Lurilee,
and when she went past him he turned a little toward her and said the last words again:
Luriana, Lurilee,

and he bowed to her as though paying her homage. She did not know why, but she felt that he liked her better now than he ever had; and, relieved and grateful, she bowed back to him and went out through the door he was holding open for her.

Now everything had to be carried one step further. She stood with her foot on the threshold, lingering a moment more in a scene that was fading even as she watched it; then, as she moved and took Minta’s arm and left the room, it changed and took on a different shape. Glancing back at it one last time over her shoulder, she knew it had already become the past.

chapters.title: The Window · 18
paragraphs: As usual, Lily thought. At that exact moment there was always something that had to be done — something Mrs. Ramsay, for private reasons, had decided to do at once, even if, as now, everyone was standing around making jokes, unable to make up their minds whether to go to the smoking-room, the drawing-room or up to the attics. And then, in the middle of all the noise, you would see Mrs. Ramsay standing there with Minta’s arm in hers, suddenly recollect, “Yes, it’s time for that now,” and slip off at once, secretive, to do something by herself. The minute she left, things began to fall apart. People drifted, hesitated, went their separate ways. Mr. Bankes took Charles Tansley by the arm and headed for the terrace to finish the political argument they had started over dinner, and that shifted the whole balance of the evening, tipped its weight another way. Watching them go, and catching a word or two about Labour Party policy, Lily felt as though the two men had climbed up to the ship’s bridge to take their bearings; that was how the switch from poetry to politics struck her. So off they went, Mr. Bankes and Charles Tansley, while the rest stood and watched Mrs. Ramsay climbing the stairs alone in the lamplight. Where, Lily wondered, was she off to in such a hurry?

In fact she was not running or hurrying at all; if anything she went rather slowly. After all that talk, she felt like standing still for a moment and picking out one particular thing — the thing that mattered — detaching it, setting it apart, cleaning off all the emotions and odds and ends that clung to it, so that she could hold it up in front of her and bring it before the court where the judges she had appointed to decide such matters sat assembled in council. Is it good, is it bad, is it right or wrong? Where are we all heading? and so on. In this way she recovered her balance after the shock of what had happened, and without knowing it, and rather absurdly, she used the elm branches outside to help steady herself. Her world was changing; the trees were still. The event had given her a feeling of motion. Everything had to be put in order. That must be set right, and that, she thought, silently admiring how dignified the trees were in their stillness, and then again the magnificent upward sweep of the elm branches (like a ship’s prow riding up a wave) when the wind lifted them. For there was a wind (she paused to look out). There was a wind, so that every so often the leaves brushed aside to uncover a star, and the stars themselves seemed to tremble and dart light, straining to flash out between the leaves’ edges. Yes, then, that was done, finished; and like everything finished, it had turned solemn. Thought of now, stripped of chatter and emotion, it seemed to have been there forever and only now revealed; and in being revealed it fixed everything firmly in place. No matter how long they lived, she thought, walking on, they would return to this night, this moon, this wind, this house — and to her as well. It flattered her, in the place where she was most open to flattery, to think that however long they lived she would be woven into their hearts, wound among them; and this, and this, and this, she thought as she climbed, laughing — but lovingly — at the sofa on the landing (her mother’s), at the rocking-chair (her father’s), at the map of the Hebrides. All of it would be brought back to life in Paul’s and Minta’s lives. “The Rayleys” — she tried out the new name. And with her hand on the nursery door she felt that sense of shared feeling with others that emotion brings, as though the dividing walls had worn so thin that practically (it was a feeling of relief and happiness) everything flowed in one stream; the chairs, the tables, the maps were hers, were theirs, whose did not matter; and Paul and Minta would carry it on after she was dead.

Firmly, so it wouldn’t squeak, she turned the handle and went in, her lips pressed together a little as though reminding herself not to talk out loud. But the instant she was inside she saw, irritated, that there had been no need for care. The children were awake. It was really too annoying. Mildred ought to be more careful. James was wide awake, Cam was sitting bolt upright, Mildred was out of bed in her bare feet, it was nearly eleven, and every one of them was talking. What was wrong? That horrid skull again. She had asked Mildred to move it, but of course Mildred had forgotten, and now here were Cam and James, both wide awake and squabbling, when they should have been asleep hours ago. Whatever had made Edward send them this horrid skull? It had been silly of her to let them nail it up there. It was nailed on tight, Mildred said, and Cam couldn’t get to sleep with it in the room, and James screamed if she touched it.

Then Cam must go to sleep (it had great big horns, Cam said) — must go to sleep and dream about lovely palaces, said Mrs. Ramsay, sitting down beside her on the bed. Cam said she could see the horns all over the room. And so she could. Wherever they set the light (and James couldn’t sleep without one), a shadow fell somewhere.

“But think, Cam, it’s just an old pig,” Mrs. Ramsay said, “a nice black pig, like the ones at the farm.” Cam, though, thought it was a horrid thing, sending its branches at her from every corner of the room.

“All right, then,” said Mrs. Ramsay, “we’ll cover it up.” They all watched as she went to the chest of drawers and pulled open the little drawers one after another, fast; and when nothing in them would do, she whipped off her own shawl and wrapped it around the skull, round and round and round. Then she went back to Cam, laid her head almost flat on the pillow next to Cam’s, and told her how lovely it looked now; how the fairies would love it; it was like a bird’s nest; it was like a beautiful mountain of the kind she had seen abroad, with valleys and flowers and bells ringing and birds singing and little goats and antelopes. … As she said the words, rhythmically, she could see them echoing in Cam’s mind; Cam was saying after her that it was like a mountain, a bird’s nest, a garden, and there were little antelopes, and her eyes kept opening and closing. And Mrs. Ramsay kept on, ever more monotonous, ever more rhythmic and nonsensical, telling her to shut her eyes and sleep and dream of mountains and valleys and stars falling and parrots and antelopes and gardens and everything lovely, she said — lifting her head very slowly and speaking more and more mechanically — until she was sitting upright and could see that Cam had fallen asleep.

Now, she whispered, going across to his bed, James had to go to sleep too, because look, she said, the boar’s skull was still there; nobody had touched it; they’d done exactly what he wanted; there it was, not hurt at all. He checked that the skull really was still under the shawl. But there was something else he wanted to ask her. Would they be going to the Lighthouse tomorrow?

No, she said, not tomorrow, but soon, she promised — the next fine day. He was very good about it. He lay down, and she pulled the covers over him. But he would never forget, she knew; and she felt angry with Charles Tansley, with her husband and with herself, because she had raised his hopes. Then, reaching for her shawl and remembering that it was wrapped around the boar’s skull, she stood up and lowered the window another inch or two. She heard the wind and breathed in the chill night air, which did not care at all; she murmured good night to Mildred, left the room, let the latch-tongue slide slowly out into the lock, and was gone.

She hoped he wouldn’t go banging his books on the floor above their heads, she thought, still dwelling on how irritating Charles Tansley was. Neither child was a good sleeper; they were excitable, and a man who could say such things about the Lighthouse seemed to her quite likely to knock over a pile of books just as they were dropping off, clumsily sweeping them off the table with his elbow. She assumed, that is, that he had gone up to work. And yet he looked so forlorn; and yet it would be a relief when he left; and yet she would see to it that he was treated better tomorrow; and yet he was wonderful with her husband; and yet his manners really did need improving; and yet she liked the way he laughed — and as she thought this, coming down the stairs, she noticed that the moon itself was now visible through the staircase window, the yellow harvest moon, and she turned; and they looked up and saw her standing above them on the stairs.

“That’s my mother,” Prue thought. Yes; Minta ought to look at her; Paul Rayley ought to look at her. There is the thing itself, she felt, as if there were only one such person in the whole world — her mother. A moment ago, chatting with the others, she had been completely grown-up; now she turned into a child again, and what they had been up to was a game, and she wondered whether her mother would allow their game or forbid it. And thinking what a chance this was for Minta and Paul and Lily to see her, and feeling what an amazing piece of luck it was that she herself had her, and that she would never grow up and never go away from home, she said, like a child, “We thought we’d go down to the beach and watch the waves.”

All at once, for no reason whatever, Mrs. Ramsay was like a girl of twenty, brimming with fun. A holiday mood seized her out of nowhere. Of course they must go; of course they must go, she cried, laughing; and running quickly down the last three or four stairs, she turned from one of them to the next, laughing, pulling Minta’s wrap around her, saying how she only wished she could come too — and would they be very late, and did any of them have a watch?

“Yes, Paul does,” Minta said. Out of a small chamois-leather case Paul slid a beautiful gold watch to show her. And holding it out on his palm in front of her, he felt, “She knows everything. I don’t need to say a word.” What he was saying to her, as he showed her the watch, was, “I’ve done it, Mrs. Ramsay. I owe it all to you.” And looking at the gold watch lying in his hand, Mrs. Ramsay felt: What extraordinary luck Minta has! She’s marrying a man who keeps his gold watch in a chamois-leather bag!

“Oh, how I wish I could come with you!” she cried. But something held her back, something so strong that it never even crossed her mind to ask what it was. Naturally, going with them was out of the question. Still, she would have liked to go, if it weren’t for the other thing; and amused by the absurdity of what she had been thinking (what luck to marry a man with a chamois-leather bag for his watch), she went, smiling, into the other room, where her husband was sitting reading.

chapters.title: The Window · 19
paragraphs: Naturally, she told herself as she came in, she had had to come in here to fetch something she wanted. The first thing she wanted was to sit in one particular chair under one particular lamp. But she wanted something more besides, though what it was she did not know, could not think. Picking up her stocking and starting to knit, she glanced at her husband and saw that he did not want to be disturbed; that much was obvious. Whatever he was reading moved him deeply. He was half smiling, and then she could tell he was keeping his feelings under control. He was flipping the pages over. He was playing it out — maybe he fancied himself the man in the book. What book was it, she wondered. Oh, one of old Sir Walter Scott’s, she saw, tilting her lampshade so the light fell on her knitting. Because Charles Tansley had been saying (she looked up, half expecting to hear books crash to the floor overhead) — had been saying that nobody reads Scott any more. So her husband had thought, “That’s what they’ll say about me,” and had gone and fetched one of those books. And if he decided that Charles Tansley was right, he would accept it where Scott was concerned. (As he read she could see him weighing it up, considering, setting this against that.) But he would not accept it about himself. About himself he was always uneasy. That worried her. He would forever be fretting over his own books — will they be read, are they any good, why aren’t they better, what do people think of me? She didn’t like thinking of him that way; and wondering whether they had guessed at dinner why he turned so irritable all of a sudden when the talk was of fame and books that last, and whether the children were laughing about it, she gave the stocking a twitch; and around her lips and forehead all the fine lines appeared, as though cut with steel tools, and she grew still, like a tree that has been tossing and trembling and now, when the wind dies down, settles into quiet, one leaf after another.

None of it mattered, she thought. A great man, a great book, fame — who could say? She knew nothing about such things. But it was just his way, his honesty — at dinner, for example, she had caught herself thinking, quite by instinct, If only he would speak! She trusted him entirely. And letting all this go by, the way a diver slips past first a weed, then a straw, then a bubble, she felt again, sinking lower, what she had felt in the hall while the others talked: There is something I want — something I came here for. And, eyes shut, she sank further and further down, not quite knowing what it was. For a while she waited, knitting, wondering; and gradually the words they had said at dinner, “the China rose is all abloom and buzzing with the honey bee,” started washing to and fro across her mind in rhythm. And as they washed back and forth, words like small shaded lamps — a red one, a blue one, a yellow one — lit up in her mind’s darkness and seemed to leave their high perches and fly across and back again, or to call out and be answered by echoes. So she turned and felt around on the table next to her for a book.

And all the lives we ever lived
And all the lives to be,
Are full of trees and changing leaves,

she murmured, pushing her needles into the stocking. Then she opened the book and started reading, dipping in here and there at random; and as she read, it felt to her like climbing backwards and upwards, shouldering her way up through petals that arched over her head, so that all she knew was that this one is white, or this one is red. To begin with, the words meant nothing to her at all.
Steer, hither steer your winged pines, all beaten Mariners

she read, and turned the page, and swung herself, zigzagging here and there, from line to line as if from branch to branch, from one red and white flower to the next, until she was roused by a small sound — her husband slapping his thighs. For a second their eyes met; but neither wanted to talk. There was nothing to say, and still something seemed to pass between them, from him to her. It was the life of the book, its power, its enormous humor, she knew, that made him slap his thighs. Don’t interrupt, he seemed to be telling her; don’t speak; just sit. And he read on. His lips twitched. It filled him up. It gave him strength. All the petty irritations and jabs of the evening went clean out of his head — how unbearably dull he found it to sit still while people went on eating and drinking forever, how snappish he had been with his wife, how thin-skinned, how he had minded when they skipped over his books as if they did not exist. But now, he felt, it didn’t matter a damn who got to Z (if thought ran like an alphabet from A to Z). Someone would get there — if not he, then another man. The strength and sanity of this writer, his feeling for plain and simple things, these fishermen, the poor crazed old creature in Mucklebackit’s cottage (all in Scott’s The Antiquary), made him feel so full of vigor, so freed of something, that he was stirred and triumphant and could not choke back his tears. Lifting the book slightly to hide his face, he let the tears fall, and shook his head from side to side, and lost himself entirely (apart from one or two thoughts about morality, and French novels versus English ones, and how Scott’s hands were tied, though his view was perhaps as true as the other one) — lost all his own worries and failures in poor Steenie’s drowning and Mucklebackit’s grief (that was Scott at his finest) and in the astonishing pleasure and energy it gave him.

Well, let them do better than that, he thought, finishing the chapter. He had the feeling of having argued with someone and won. Whatever they said, they could not do better than that; and his own standing felt more secure. The lovers were rubbish, he thought, gathering the whole thing together in his mind once more. That part’s rubbish, this part’s first-rate, he thought, setting one piece against another. But he would have to read it again. The overall shape of it escaped him. He must keep his verdict open. So he went back to his other thought — if the young men didn’t care for this, then of course they didn’t care for him either. You mustn’t complain, Mr. Ramsay told himself, trying to smother his wish to complain to his wife that the young men didn’t admire him. But he had made up his mind: he would not bother her again. At this point he looked over at her, reading. She looked very peaceful as she read. He liked to think that the others had all gone off and left the two of them alone. Going to bed with a woman was not the whole of life, he thought, turning back to Scott and Balzac, to the English novel and the French.

Mrs. Ramsay lifted her head, and, like someone lightly asleep, seemed to be saying that if he wanted her to wake she would — she really would; but if not, could she please go on sleeping, just a little longer, only a little longer? She was climbing up those branches, this way and that, putting her hand now on one flower, now on another.
Nor praise the deep vermilion in the rose,

she read; and reading, she felt she was rising higher, up to the top, up onto the peak. How satisfying it was! How restful! Every scrap and odd end of the day clung to this magnet; her mind felt swept out, clean. And then, suddenly, there it was, whole, taking shape in her hands, beautiful and reasonable, clear and complete — life’s essence drawn out of it and held here, rounded: the sonnet.

But she was growing aware that her husband was watching her. He was smiling at her, quizzical, as though teasing her gently for dozing in broad daylight; yet at the same time he was thinking, Keep reading. You don’t look sad now, he thought. He wondered what she was reading, and made her out to be more ignorant, more simple, than she was, because he liked to think of her as not clever, not bookish at all. Did she understand what she was reading, he wondered. Probably not. She was astonishingly beautiful. To him her beauty seemed, if such a thing could be, to be increasing.

Yet seem’d it winter still, and, you away,
As with your shadow I with these did play,
she finished reading.
“Well?” she said, looking up from her book and dreamily echoing his smile.
As with your shadow I with these did play,
she murmured, laying the book down on the table.

As she took up her knitting she wondered: what had happened since the last time she had seen him alone? She remembered getting dressed, and seeing the moon; Andrew holding his plate up too high at dinner; feeling low because of something William had said; the birds in the trees; the sofa on the landing; the children awake; Charles Tansley waking them with his books falling — oh no, she’d invented that; and Paul keeping his watch in a chamois-leather case. Which one should she tell him?
“They’re engaged,” she said as she began to knit. “Paul and Minta.”

“So I guessed,” he said. There was not much more to say about it. Her mind still went up and down, up and down, with the poetry; he still felt full of vigor, very plain-spoken, after reading about Steenie’s funeral. So they sat and said nothing. Then it dawned on her that she wanted him to speak.
Anything, anything, she thought, knitting on. Anything at all will do.
“How lovely it would be to marry a man who keeps his watch in a chamois-leather bag,” she said, because that was the kind of joke the two of them shared.

He snorted. He felt about this engagement what he always felt about every engagement: the girl is far too good for the young man. And slowly a question rose in her mind: why, then, do we want people to marry? What was the value, the meaning, of things? (Anything they said now would be true.) Please say something, she thought, longing only to hear his voice. Because the shadow, the thing that wrapped the two of them round, was starting, she felt, to close in on her again. Say anything, she begged, looking at him as if for help.

He said nothing, but swung the compass on his watch-chain to and fro, thinking about Scott’s novels and Balzac’s. Yet through the dusky walls of their closeness — for they were drawing together without meaning to, coming side by side, very near — she could feel his mind like a hand lifted over hers, throwing it into shade. And now that her thoughts were turning in a direction he disliked, toward what he called her “pessimism,” he began to fidget, though he still did not speak — putting a hand to his forehead, twisting a strand of hair, letting it drop.

“You won’t get that stocking finished tonight,” he said, pointing at it. That was just what she wanted — the edge in his voice as he scolded her. If he says being pessimistic is wrong, then it’s probably wrong, she thought; the marriage will turn out fine.
“No,” she said, smoothing the stocking flat on her knee, “I won’t get it finished.”

And then what? She could feel that he was still looking at her, but that the look was different now. He wanted something — the thing she always found so hard to give him: he wanted her to say that she loved him. And that, no, she could not do. Talking came so much more easily to him than to her. He was able to say things — she never was. So of course it was always he who said them; and then, for some reason, he would suddenly resent it and reproach her. A heartless woman, he called her; she never once told him she loved him. But that wasn’t true — it wasn’t true. It was only that she never could put what she felt into words. Wasn’t there a crumb on his coat? Nothing she could do for him? She got up and stood at the window holding the reddish-brown stocking, partly to turn away from him and partly because now, with him watching, she did not mind looking at the Lighthouse. For she knew he had turned his head when she turned; he was watching her. She knew what he was thinking: You are more beautiful than ever. And she felt very beautiful. Won’t you tell me just this once that you love me? That was what he was thinking, because he was stirred — what with Minta, and his book, and the day coming to an end, and their quarrel about going to the Lighthouse. But she couldn’t; she couldn’t say it. Then, knowing he was watching her, instead of speaking she turned around, the stocking in her hands, and looked at him. And as she looked at him she began to smile, for although she had not said a word, he knew — of course he knew — that she loved him. He could not deny it. And smiling, she looked out of the window and said (thinking to herself, Nothing on earth can equal this happiness) —
“Yes, you were right. It’s going to be wet tomorrow.” She hadn’t said it, but he knew. And she looked at him, smiling. For she had triumphed yet again.

chapters.title: Time Passes · 1
paragraphs: “Well, only the future can tell us that,” Mr. Bankes said as he came in from the terrace.
“It’s nearly too dark to see anything,” said Andrew, coming up from the beach.
“One can scarcely tell which is sea and which is land,” said Prue.
“Are we leaving that light burning?” Lily asked as they took off their coats inside.
“No,” Prue said, “not if everybody’s in.”
“Andrew,” she called over her shoulder, “just go and put out the hall light.”
One after another the lamps were all put out — except that Mr. Carmichael, who liked lying awake a while reading Virgil, kept his candle alight somewhat longer than everyone else.

chapters.title: Time Passes · 2
paragraphs: So, with the lamps all put out, the moon gone down, and a thin rain drumming on the roof, a great downpour of darkness began. Nothing, it seemed, could survive the flood, the sheer abundance of darkness, which crept in at keyholes and cracks, stole around window blinds, came into bedrooms, and swallowed up here a jug and basin, there a bowl of red and yellow dahlias, there the sharp edges and solid bulk of a chest of drawers. It was not only the furniture that was blurred together; there was hardly anything left of body or mind by which you could say, “This is he,” or “This is she.” Sometimes a hand was raised as if to grasp something or fend something off, or somebody groaned, or somebody laughed aloud as if sharing a joke with nothingness.

Nothing stirred in the drawing-room or the dining-room or on the staircase. Only, through the rusty hinges and the swollen, sea-damp woodwork, certain breaths of air, broken off from the body of the wind (the house was ramshackle, after all), crept around corners and ventured indoors. You could almost imagine them, as they came into the drawing-room, questioning and wondering, playing with the loose flap of hanging wallpaper, asking: would it hang much longer, when would it fall? Then, smoothly brushing the walls, they passed on thoughtfully, as if asking the red and yellow roses on the wallpaper whether they would fade, and questioning (gently, for they had time to spare) the torn letters in the wastepaper basket, the flowers, the books, all of which were now open to them — asking, Were they allies? Were they enemies? How long would they last?

So, guided by some stray light from an uncovered star, or a wandering ship, or even the Lighthouse, with its pale footfall on stair and mat, the little breaths of air climbed the staircase and nosed around the bedroom doors. But here, surely, they must stop. Whatever else may perish and disappear, what lies here is steadfast. Here you might say to those sliding lights, those fumbling airs that breathe and bend over the bed itself: here you can neither touch nor destroy. At which, wearily, ghostlike, as if they had feather-light fingers and the light persistence of feathers, they would look once at the shut eyes and the loosely clasped fingers, and wearily fold their garments and disappear. And so, nosing, rubbing, they went to the window on the staircase, to the servants’ bedrooms, to the boxes in the attics; coming down again, they whitened the apples on the dining-room table, fumbled at the petals of the roses, tried the picture on the easel, brushed the mat and blew a little sand along the floor. At last, giving up, they all stopped together, gathered together, sighed together; all together they let out an aimless gust of lament, to which some door in the kitchen answered: it swung wide, let nothing in, and slammed shut.
[At this point Mr. Carmichael, who was reading Virgil, blew out his candle. It was after midnight.]

chapters.title: Time Passes · 3
paragraphs: But what, after all, is one night? A short space of time, especially when the darkness fades so soon, and so soon a bird sings, a cock crows, or a faint green stirs, like a turning leaf, in the hollow of the wave. Night, however, follows night. Winter holds a whole pack of them in reserve and deals them out equally, evenly, with tireless fingers. They lengthen; they darken. Some of them hold up clear planets, plates of brightness. The autumn trees, ravaged as they are, take on the gleam of tattered flags glowing in the gloom of cool cathedral vaults, where gold letters on marble pages describe death in battle, and bones bleaching and burning far away in Indian sands. The autumn trees shine in the yellow moonlight, in the light of harvest moons — the light that softens the energy of labor, and smooths the stubble, and brings the wave lapping blue to the shore.

It seemed now as if, moved by human repentance and all its toil, divine goodness had drawn back the curtain and shown, behind it, single and distinct, the hare standing upright; the wave falling; the boat rocking — things which, if we deserved them, would be ours always. But alas, divine goodness twitches the cord and draws the curtain shut; it does not please him; he covers his treasures in a drenching of hail, and so breaks them, so scatters them, that it seems impossible their calm should ever return, or that we should ever put together a perfect whole from their fragments, or read the clear words of truth in the littered pieces. For our repentance earns only a glimpse; our toil, only a rest.

The nights now are full of wind and destruction. The trees plunge and bend, and their leaves fly helter-skelter until the lawn is plastered with them and they lie packed in gutters, choke the rain-pipes and litter the damp paths. The sea, too, tosses itself and breaks itself; and if some sleeper, imagining that he might find on the beach an answer to his doubts, someone to share his solitude, should throw off his bedclothes and go down alone to walk on the sand, no image that seems to serve him with divine readiness comes easily to hand, bringing the night to order and making the world reflect the range of the soul. The hand dwindles in his hand; the voice bellows in his ear.
