It would almost seem useless, in such confusion, to ask the night those questions — what, and why, and for what purpose — that tempt the sleeper from his bed to look for an answer.
[Stumbling along a passage one dark morning, Mr. Ramsay stretched out his arms; but—Mrs. Ramsay had died rather suddenly the night before—he stretched his arms out. They stayed empty.]

chapters.title: Time Passes · 4
paragraphs: So, with the house empty and the doors locked and the mattresses rolled up, those stray breaths of air, the advance guard of great armies, blustered in, brushed the bare boards, nibbled and fanned, and met nothing in bedroom or drawing-room that fully resisted them — only hangings that flapped, wood that creaked, the bare legs of tables, saucepans and china already furred, tarnished, cracked. What people had shed and left behind — a pair of shoes, a shooting cap, some faded skirts and coats in the wardrobes — these alone kept the human shape, and in the emptiness showed how once they had been filled and brought to life; how once hands had been busy with hooks and buttons; how once the looking-glass had held a face, had held a hollowed-out world in which a figure turned, a hand flashed, the door opened, and in came children rushing and tumbling, and went out again. Now, day after day, the light turned its clear image on the opposite wall, like a flower reflected in water. Only the shadows of the trees, tossing in the wind, bowed low on the wall and for a moment darkened the pool in which the light reflected itself; or birds, flying past, made a soft spot flutter slowly across the bedroom floor.

So loveliness reigned, and stillness, and together they made the shape of loveliness itself, a form that life had left; solitary, like a pool at evening, far off, seen from a train window, vanishing so quickly that the pool, pale in the evening, is hardly robbed of its solitude, though it has once been seen. Loveliness and stillness clasped hands in the bedroom; and among the shrouded jugs and sheeted chairs, even the prying of the wind, and the soft noses of the clammy sea airs, rubbing, snuffling, repeating and repeating their questions — “Will you fade? Will you perish?” — hardly disturbed the peace, the indifference, the air of pure integrity, as if the question they asked scarcely needed an answer: we remain.

Nothing, it seemed, could break that image, spoil that innocence, or disturb the swaying cloak of silence which, week after week, in the empty room, wove into itself the falling cries of birds, ships hooting, the drone and hum of the fields, a dog’s bark, a man’s shout, and folded them around the house in silence. Only once did a board spring loose on the landing; once, in the middle of the night, with a roar, with a rupture, as when after centuries of stillness a rock tears itself from the mountain and hurtles crashing into the valley, one fold of the shawl came loose and swung back and forth. Then peace came down again; and the shadow wavered; the light bowed to its own image in adoration on the bedroom wall — when Mrs. McNab, tearing the veil of silence with hands that had stood in the washtub, grinding it under boots that had crunched the shingle, came as she had been told to open all the windows and dust the bedrooms.

chapters.title: Time Passes · 5
paragraphs: As she lurched (for she rolled like a ship at sea) and leered (for her eyes never fell on anything directly, but only with a sidelong glance that asked to be spared the scorn and anger of the world — she was witless, she knew it), as she clutched the banisters and hauled herself upstairs and rolled from room to room, she sang. Rubbing the glass of the long mirror and leering sideways at her swaying figure, she let a sound come from her lips — something that had perhaps been cheerful on the stage twenty years before, had been hummed and danced to, but now, coming from this toothless, bonneted caretaker, was robbed of meaning. It was like the voice of witlessness, of humor, of persistence itself, trodden down but springing up again; so that as she lurched along, dusting, wiping, she seemed to be saying how it was all one long sorrow and trouble, how it was getting up and going to bed again, and getting things out and putting them away again. It had not been easy or cozy, this world she had known for close on seventy years. She was bowed down with weariness. How long, she asked, creaking and groaning on her knees under the bed, dusting the boards, how long is it to go on? But she hobbled to her feet again, pulled herself up, and again, with her sidelong leer that slipped and turned aside even from her own face and her own sorrows, stood and gaped in the glass, smiling at nothing, and began again the old amble and hobble, taking up mats, putting down china, looking sideways in the glass — as if, after all, she had her consolations; as if some incorrigible hope really did twine itself around her dirge. There must have been visions of joy at the washtub, say, with her children (though two had been born out of wedlock and one had deserted her), or at the pub, drinking, or turning over odds and ends in her drawers. There must have been some break in the dark, some channel in the depths of obscurity through which enough light came to twist her face into a grin in the glass, and make her, turning to her work again, mumble out the old music-hall song. Meanwhile the mystics, the visionaries, walked the beach, stirred a puddle, looked at a stone, and asked themselves, “What am I?” “What is this?” — and suddenly an answer was granted them (what it was they could not say), so that they were warm in the frost and had comfort in the desert. But Mrs. McNab went on drinking and gossiping as before.

chapters.title: Time Passes · 6
paragraphs: Spring came without a single leaf to toss about. Bare and bright, like a virgin fierce in her chastity and scornful in her purity, she lay spread over the fields, wide-eyed and watchful, and not in the least concerned with what anyone looking at her might do or think.
[That May, Prue Ramsay, leaning on her father’s arm, was given away in marriage. Could anything have been more fitting? people asked. And how beautiful she looked, they added!]

As summer drew near and the evenings lengthened, the wakeful and the hopeful who walked the beach and stirred the pools began to have the strangest imaginings: of flesh turned into atoms that drove before the wind, of stars flashing in their hearts, of cliff, sea, cloud and sky gathered together on purpose so that, out there, they might assemble the scattered pieces of the vision within. In those mirrors, the minds of men—in those pools of uneasy water, where clouds are always turning and shadows forming—dreams persisted. Every gull, flower, tree, man and woman, even the white earth itself, seemed to declare (though, if you questioned it, it would at once take the words back) that good triumphs, that happiness prevails, that order rules; and it was impossible to resist this strange hint. It was just as impossible to resist the extraordinary urge to roam this way and that in search of some absolute good, some crystal of intensity, far removed from familiar pleasures and known virtues—something alien to the business of domestic life, single, hard, bright, like a diamond in the sand, that would make its owner safe. Spring, meanwhile, had grown gentler and more yielding. With her bees humming and her gnats dancing, she drew her cloak around her, veiled her eyes and turned her head aside, and among the passing shadows and small gusts of rain she seemed to have taken on some knowledge of human sorrow.
[That summer Prue Ramsay died of an illness connected with childbirth. It was a real tragedy, people said. Nobody, they said, had deserved happiness more.]

And now, in the summer heat, the wind once more sent its spies around the house. In the sunny rooms flies spun a web; weeds that had sprung up against the glass overnight tapped at the windowpane in a steady rhythm. When darkness came, the stroke of the Lighthouse—which in the dark had once laid itself across the carpet with such authority, tracing out its pattern—now arrived in the softer spring light, mixed with moonlight. It glided in gently, as if laying a caress, lingering in secret, looking, and coming lovingly back again. Yet in the very hush of that loving caress, as the long stroke leaned across the bed, the rock split apart; another fold of the shawl worked loose, and hung there, swaying. All through the short summer nights and long summer days, while the empty rooms seemed to murmur with echoes from the fields and the buzzing of flies, the long streamer stirred gently and swung without purpose. The sun, meanwhile, laid such stripes and bars across the rooms and filled them with so yellow a haze that when Mrs. McNab broke in and lurched about with her duster and broom, she looked like a tropical fish paddling its way through water pierced with sunbeams.

Yet however deeply the house might slumber and sleep, later that summer ominous sounds reached it, like hammer blows falling in a slow rhythm, muffled on felt. Their repeated shocks loosened the shawl further still and cracked the teacups. Every so often a glass tinkled in the cupboard, as though some giant voice had screamed so loud in its agony that even the tumblers standing inside a cupboard shook too. Then silence fell once more. And then, night after night—and sometimes in the full light of noon, when the roses were bright and the light printed its shape plainly on the wall—there seemed to drop into this silence, this indifference, this wholeness, the thud of something falling.
[A shell burst. In France twenty or thirty young men were blown up, and Andrew Ramsay was one of them. His death, mercifully, was instant.]

That season, people who had gone down to walk the beach and ask the sea and sky what message they carried, or what vision they confirmed, found something new to consider. Among the familiar signs of heaven’s generosity—sunset on the sea, the pale dawn, the rising moon, fishing boats against the moon, children throwing handfuls of grass at one another—there was something that did not fit with all this gaiety and calm. There was, for instance, a gray ship, the color of ash, that silently appeared and was gone; there was a purple stain on the smooth sea, as though something underneath had boiled and bled out of sight. These things broke into a scene built to call up the loftiest thoughts and lead to the most reassuring conclusions, and they stopped the walkers in their tracks. It was hard to pass over them calmly, to cancel out what they meant in the landscape; hard to keep walking by the sea and marveling that the beauty outside mirrored the beauty within.

Did Nature add her part to what man offered? Did she finish what he started? She looked on his misery with the same complacency, excused his meanness, and consented to his torture. So was that dream—of sharing, of completing, of finding an answer alone on the beach—nothing but a reflection in a mirror? And was the mirror nothing but the glassy film that forms on the surface in stillness, while the nobler powers lie sleeping below? Impatient and despairing, yet unwilling to leave (for beauty has her lures to offer, and her consolations), they could no longer pace the beach; contemplation had become unbearable; the mirror was broken.
[That spring Mr. Carmichael published a book of poems, and it turned out to be an unexpected success. People said the war had brought back their interest in poetry.]

chapters.title: Time Passes · 7
paragraphs: Night after night, summer and winter, the torment of storms and the arrow-straight stillness of fair weather held court undisturbed. Had anyone been listening from the upper rooms of the empty house, all they could have heard was a gigantic chaos, streaked with lightning, rolling and heaving. The winds and the waves played together like the shapeless bulks of leviathans, their foreheads pierced by no light of reason. They piled one on top of another, lunged and plunged in darkness or daylight (for night and day, months and years, ran together without shape) in idiot games, until it seemed the universe itself was fighting and tumbling, alone, in brute confusion and wanton lust, and to no end.

In spring the garden urns, planted by chance with whatever the wind had blown into them, were as bright as ever. Violets came, and then daffodils. Yet the calm and brightness of the day were just as strange as the chaos and uproar of the night. There the trees stood, and there the flowers stood, gazing in front of them, gazing upward, yet seeing nothing at all; they had no eyes, and that made them terrible.

chapters.title: Time Passes · 8
paragraphs: She meant no harm by it. The family wouldn’t come, never again, some said, and maybe the house would be sold at Michaelmas, the autumn quarter day. So Mrs. McNab bent down and picked a bunch of flowers to carry home. While she dusted, she set them on the table. She liked flowers. It seemed a shame to let them go to waste. Say the house was sold (and she stood, hands on hips, before the looking glass)—well, it would need seeing to, that it would. All these years it had stood there with nobody in it. The books and all were gone moldy, what with the war and help being so hard to come by; the place hadn’t been cleaned the way she’d have wanted. It would take more than one pair of hands to set it right now. She was too old for it. Her legs hurt. Every one of those books ought to be laid out on the grass in the sun; plaster had come down in the hall; the drainpipe over the study window had got blocked and let the rain in; the carpet was ruined, clean ruined. But folks should come and see for themselves; they should’ve sent someone down to look. There were clothes in the cupboards, after all; they’d left clothes in every bedroom. What was she meant to do with them? The moth was in them—Mrs. Ramsay’s things. Poor lady! She’d never be wanting _them_ again. Dead, they said she was; years back, in London. Here was the old gray cloak she used to garden in (Mrs. McNab ran her fingers over it). She could see her now, as she came up the drive with the washing, bent over her flowers (a pitiful sight the garden was now, run wild, rabbits scuttling out at you from the beds)—could see her in that gray cloak with one of the children by her side. There were boots and shoes; there was a brush and comb left lying on the dressing table, for all the world as if she meant to be back tomorrow. (Went very sudden at the end, they said.) Once they’d been going to come, but they put it off, what with the war and traveling being so hard these days; and all these years they’d never come; only sent her money; never wrote, never came, and expected to find everything just as they left it, oh dear, dear! Why, the drawers in the dressing table were stuffed full (she pulled them open)—handkerchiefs, scraps of ribbon. Yes, she could see Mrs. Ramsay, as she came up the drive with the washing.
“Good evening, Mrs. McNab,” she’d say.

She had such a nice way with her. All the girls took to her. But dear me, a great deal had changed since those days (she shut the drawer); plenty of families had lost the ones they loved best. So she was dead; and Mr. Andrew killed; and Miss Prue gone too, so they said, with her first baby; but these years everybody had lost somebody. Prices had gone up something shocking, and they never came down again, neither. Oh, she remembered her well, in that gray cloak.

“Good evening, Mrs. McNab,” she’d said, and told cook to put by a plate of milk soup for her—quite sure she’d be wanting it, after lugging that heavy basket all the way up from town. Mrs. McNab could see her this minute, bent over her flowers. (And, faint and flickering, like a yellow beam of light or the circle at the far end of a telescope, a lady in a gray cloak, bent over her flowers, went drifting across the bedroom wall, up over the dressing table and across the washstand, while Mrs. McNab hobbled and shuffled about, dusting and tidying.)

And what was cook’s name, now? Mildred? Marian?—something of that sort. Ah, it had gone—she did forget things. A fiery one, the way red-haired women are. Many’s the laugh the two of them had had. There was always a welcome for her in the kitchen. She made them laugh, she did. Things were better then than they are now.

She sighed; it was too much work for one woman. She wagged her head from side to side. This room had been the nursery. Why, it was damp right through in here; the plaster was coming down. Whatever did they want with an animal’s skull hung up there? Gone all moldy, too. Rats in every attic, and all. The rain got in. But they never sent word; never came. Some of the locks had gone, so the doors kept banging. She didn’t care to be up here on her own at dusk, neither. It was too much for one woman—too much, too much. She creaked, she groaned. She banged the door shut. She turned the key in the lock and went, leaving the house shut up, locked, alone.

chapters.title: Time Passes · 9
paragraphs: The house had been left; the house stood deserted. Now that life had gone out of it, it was left like a shell on a sand dune, to fill up with dry grains of salt. The long night seemed to have begun; the trivial little airs that nibbled, the damp breaths that fumbled, seemed to have won the day. Rust had got into the saucepan, and the mat had rotted. Toads had nosed their way indoors. The shawl swung to and fro, idly, without purpose. In the larder a thistle forced its way up between the tiles. Swallows built nests in the drawing room; straw littered the floor; plaster came down by the shovelful; the beams showed through; rats carried off odds and ends to gnaw behind the wooden paneling. Tortoiseshell butterflies broke out of their chrysalises and beat their lives away against the windowpane. Poppies seeded themselves among the dahlias; long grass waved on the lawn; huge artichokes towered over the roses; a fringed carnation bloomed among the cabbages. And the soft tapping of a weed against the window had turned, on winter nights, into a drumming of sturdy trees and thorny briars, and in summer these made the whole room green.

What power was there now to stop the fertility of nature, its blind indifference? Mrs. McNab’s dream of a lady, a child, a plate of milk soup? That had flickered across the walls like a patch of sunlight and was gone. She had locked the door and left. One woman couldn’t manage it, she said. They never sent word. They never wrote. Up there, things were rotting in the drawers—a shame to leave them like that, she said. The whole place had gone to rack and ruin. Only the beam from the Lighthouse entered the rooms, for a moment at a time, throwing its sudden stare across bed and wall in the winter dark and gazing without concern at the thistle and the swallow, the rat and the straw. There was nothing left to stand against them, nothing to tell them no. So let the wind blow. Let the poppy sow itself, and the carnation mate with the cabbage. Let the swallow nest in the drawing room, the thistle shoulder the tiles aside, the butterfly sun itself on the faded chintz of the armchairs. Let the broken glass and china lie out on the lawn, overgrown and tangled with grass and wild berries.

For the moment had come—that pause when dawn trembles and night holds still, when a single feather dropped into the scale would tip it. One feather, and the house would have sunk and fallen, turning over and pitching down into the depths of darkness. Picnickers would have boiled their kettles in the ruined room; lovers would have taken shelter there, lying on the bare floorboards; the shepherd would have kept his dinner on the bricks, and the tramp would have slept there wrapped in his coat against the cold. Later the roof would have caved in. Briars and hemlock would have smothered path, step and window, growing unevenly but vigorously over the mound, until a trespasser who had strayed off his path could have guessed only from a red-hot poker lily among the nettles, or a fragment of china in the hemlock, that someone had lived here once; that there had once been a house.

Had the feather fallen, had it tipped the scale, the whole house would have plunged to the bottom and lain there on the sands of oblivion. But a force was at work—something not very conscious; something that leered, something that lurched; something with no inspiration to perform its task with dignified ritual or solemn chanting. Mrs. McNab groaned; Mrs. Bast creaked. They were old and stiff, and their legs ached. At last they arrived with their brooms and pails and set to work. Out of the blue, one of the young ladies had written: would Mrs. McNab see that the house was got ready? Would she see to this, and see to that—and all in a rush. They might be coming for the summer; they had left everything till the last minute; they expected to find things the way they had left them. Slowly, painfully, with broom and pail, mopping and scouring, Mrs. McNab and Mrs. Bast held off the decay and the rot. They snatched things back from the pool of Time that was quickly closing over them—a basin here, a cupboard there. One morning they dragged up out of oblivion all of Scott’s Waverley novels and a tea service; in the afternoon they brought a brass fender and a set of steel fire irons back into the sun and air. George, Mrs. Bast’s son, trapped the rats and mowed the grass. They had the builders in. To the creak of hinges and the shriek of bolts, and the slamming and banging of woodwork swollen with damp, some rusty, toilsome birth seemed to be under way, as the women bent and straightened, groaned and sang, slapping and slamming about, up the stairs one moment and down in the cellars the next. Oh, the work of it, they said!

Some days they had their tea in the bedroom, or in the study, stopping work at midday with their faces smudged and their old hands stiff and cramped from gripping the brooms. Slumped in their chairs, they looked over their achievements: at one moment the splendid conquest of the taps and the bath; at another the harder and less complete victory over the long rows of books, once black as ravens, now blotched with white, growing pale mushrooms and hiding secretive spiders. Once again, as the tea warmed her inside, the telescope settled itself over Mrs. McNab’s eyes, and in a ring of light she saw the old gentleman on the lawn, thin as a rake, wagging his head and talking to himself, she supposed, as she came up with the washing. He never took any notice of her. Some said he was dead; others said it was her that was dead. Which was it? Mrs. Bast couldn’t say for sure either. The young gentleman was dead. That she did know. She had seen his name in the papers.

Then there was the cook—Mildred, Marian, some name of that kind—a red-haired woman, with a quick temper, as they all have, but kind as well, if you knew how to take her. Many’s the laugh they’d had together. She always kept back a plate of soup for Maggie—Mrs. McNab herself; sometimes a bit of ham; whatever was going spare. They lived well, back then. They had everything they wanted. (Sitting in the wicker armchair by the nursery fender, with the hot tea inside her, she unwound her ball of memories, easily and merrily.) There was always something going on—people in the house, twenty to stay at a time, sometimes, and washing up going on till well after midnight.

Mrs. Bast had never known the family; she had been living in Glasgow in those days. Setting down her cup, she wondered what on earth they had hung that animal’s skull up there for. Shot abroad somewhere, no doubt.

Very likely, said Mrs. McNab, letting her memories run on as they pleased. They had friends out in eastern countries; there were gentlemen staying, ladies in evening dress; once she had seen them all through the dining-room door, sitting at dinner. Twenty of them, she’d be bound, all in their jewels, and she was asked to stay on and help with the washing-up, till past midnight as like as not.

Ah, said Mrs. Bast, they’d find it changed. She leaned out of the window and watched her son George scything the grass. Well might they ask what had been done to it. Old Kennedy was meant to be looking after it, and then his leg got so bad after he fell off the cart; and after that, maybe nobody for a year, or most of one; and then Davie Macdonald; and seeds might have been sent, but who was to say whether they ever went in the ground? Oh, they’d find it changed.
She watched her boy at his scything. A great one for work, he was—one of your quiet sort. Well, she supposed they’d best get on with those cupboards. Up they hauled themselves.

At last, after days of hard work indoors and of cutting and digging outdoors, the dusters were given a final flick out of the windows, and the windows were closed; all over the house keys were turned; the front door slammed; the job was done.

And now, as though all the cleaning and scrubbing, the scything and mowing, had been drowning it out, there rose up that half-heard melody, that broken, fitful music that the ear half catches and then lets slip. A bark, a bleat—irregular, now and then, yet somehow connected. An insect humming, cut grass quivering—separate, yet somehow belonging together. A dor beetle’s drone, a wheel’s squeak, loud, soft, but mysteriously related. The ear strains to bring them together, and is always just about to make them into a harmony; but they are never quite heard, never fully harmonized, and at last, in the evening, the sounds die out one by one, the harmony wavers, and silence falls. As the sun set, the sharp edges faded, and quiet rose like a mist and spread; the wind dropped; the world shook itself loosely down to sleep—dark here, with no light in it except what filtered green through the leaves, or lay pale on the white flowers by the window.
[Late one evening in September, Lily Briscoe arrived and had her bag carried up to the house. Mr. Carmichael had come on the same train.]

chapters.title: Time Passes · 10
paragraphs: Then, truly, peace had come. From the sea to the shore came breaths of peace, messages of it: never again to disturb its sleep, but to lull it into a deeper rest, and to confirm whatever the dreamers dreamed, in holiness and wisdom—what else could it be murmuring?—as Lily Briscoe laid her head on the pillow in the clean, quiet room and listened to the sea. In through the open window came the voice of the world’s beauty, murmuring too softly for its exact words to be made out—but what did that matter, if the meaning was clear? It pleaded with the sleepers (the house was full once more; Mrs. Beckwith was staying, and Mr. Carmichael as well) that if they would not actually come down to the beach, they should at least raise the blind and look out. Then they would see night flowing down in purple, his head crowned, his scepter set with jewels, and how a child might gaze into his eyes. And if they still held back (Lily, worn out by the journey, fell asleep almost at once, but Mr. Carmichael read a book by candlelight)—if they still refused, saying that this splendor of his was mere vapor, that the dew was stronger than he was, and that they would rather sleep—then the voice would sing its song gently, without complaint or argument. The waves would break gently (Lily heard them as she slept); the light fell tenderly (it seemed to come to her through her eyelids). And it all looked, thought Mr. Carmichael, closing his book and drifting off, very much the way it had looked years ago.

The voice might well take up its plea again, as the curtains of darkness folded themselves over the house, over Mrs. Beckwith, Mr. Carmichael and Lily Briscoe, until they lay with many layers of blackness pressed on their eyes. Why not accept this? Why not be content with it, yield, and be resigned? The sighing of all the seas breaking in rhythm around the islands soothed them; night wrapped them round; nothing disturbed their sleep. Then the birds started up, and dawn wove their thin voices into its whiteness; a cart went grinding by; somewhere a dog barked; the sun lifted the curtains and tore the veil from their eyes. And Lily Briscoe, stirring as she slept, clutched at her blankets the way a person falling clutches at the turf at the edge of a cliff. Her eyes flew open. So here she was again, she thought, sitting bolt upright in bed. Awake.

chapters.title: The Lighthouse · 1
paragraphs: So what does it mean, what can it all possibly mean? Lily Briscoe asked herself. She had been left on her own, and she was wondering whether she ought to go to the kitchen and get another cup of coffee, or stay where she was. What does it mean?—that was a stock phrase, picked up out of some book, and it only loosely fit what she was thinking. On this first morning with the Ramsays she could not pull her feelings together; all she could do was let a phrase ring out to cover the emptiness in her mind until these mists had cleared. Because really, what did she feel, returning after so many years to find Mrs. Ramsay dead? Nothing, nothing—nothing she could put into words at all.

She had got in late the night before, when everything was dark and mysterious. Now here she was, awake, sitting at her old place at the breakfast table, but by herself. It was very early as well, not even eight o’clock. There was this trip—Mr. Ramsay, Cam and James were going to the Lighthouse. They ought to have left by now; there was the tide to catch, or something of the kind. And Cam wasn’t ready, and James wasn’t ready, and Nancy had forgotten to order the sandwiches, and Mr. Ramsay had lost his temper and slammed out of the room.
“What’s the use of going now?” he’d raged.

Nancy had disappeared. And there he was, pacing back and forth along the terrace in a fury. You seemed to hear doors banging and people calling everywhere in the house. Then Nancy burst in and, glancing around the room in a strange, half-dazed, half-desperate way, asked, “What does one send to the Lighthouse?” She said it as if she were making herself do something she had no hope of ever managing.

What does one send to the Lighthouse, indeed! On any other day Lily could have given her a sensible answer: tea, tobacco, newspapers. But this morning everything felt so extraordinarily strange that a question like Nancy’s—What does one send to the Lighthouse?—flung doors open in your mind, doors that banged and swung back and forth, so that you kept asking, gaping and stupefied, What does one send? What does one do? Why is one sitting here at all?

Alone at the long table among the clean cups (Nancy had gone out again), she felt shut off from everyone else, fit only to keep on watching, asking and wondering. The house, the place, the morning all felt like strangers. She had no ties here, she felt, no connection with any of it; anything at all might happen. And whatever did happen—a footstep outside, a voice calling out (“It’s not in the cupboard, it’s on the landing!” somebody shouted)—came as a question, as if the thread that normally held things together had been snipped and they were drifting about, up here, down there, away, any old how. How pointless it all was, how chaotic, how unreal, she thought, gazing at her empty coffee cup. Mrs. Ramsay dead; Andrew killed; Prue dead as well—she could say it over as often as she liked and it woke no feeling in her. And here we all are, gathered in a house like this, on a morning like this, she said, looking out of the window. It was a lovely, still day.

All at once Mr. Ramsay, passing by, lifted his head and looked her straight in the face with that wild, distracted gaze of his that was also so piercing—as though he were seeing you, for a single second, for the first time and for ever. To get away from him, she pretended to sip from her empty coffee cup—to dodge his demand on her, to push that commanding need aside for one moment more. He shook his head at her and walked on (“Alone,” she heard him say; “Perished,” she heard him say), and, like everything else on this strange morning, the words turned into symbols and wrote themselves across the gray-green walls. If she could only fit them together, she felt, and write them out as a sentence, she would have reached the truth of things. Old Mr. Carmichael came padding quietly in, got his coffee, and carried his cup away to sit in the sun. The strange unreality of it all was frightening, but it was thrilling too. Going to the Lighthouse. But what does one send to the Lighthouse? Perished. Alone. The gray-green light on the opposite wall. The empty places. These were some of the pieces—but how could they be brought together? she asked herself. As though any interruption would shatter the delicate shape she was putting together on the table, she turned her back on the window in case Mr. Ramsay saw her. Somehow she had to get away, to find somewhere to be alone. Then suddenly she remembered. The last time she had sat here, ten years ago, there had been a small pattern of sprigs or leaves on the tablecloth, and she had looked at it in a moment of revelation. She had had a problem about the foreground of a painting. Move the tree to the middle, she had said. That picture she had never finished. All these years it had been knocking around in her head. Now she would paint it. Where had she put her paints? Yes, her paints. She had left them in the hall last night. She would begin right away. She got up quickly, before Mr. Ramsay could turn round.

She brought herself a chair. With her neat, precise, old-maidish movements she set up her easel at the edge of the lawn—not too near Mr. Carmichael, but near enough to be under his protection. Yes, this must have been the very spot where she had stood ten years ago. There was the wall, there the hedge, there the tree. It was a question of how those masses related to one another. She had carried that question in her head all these years. And now it seemed that the answer had come to her: she knew what she wanted to do.

But with Mr. Ramsay bearing down on her, she could do nothing at all. Each time he drew near—he was pacing up and down the terrace—ruin drew near, chaos drew near. Painting was impossible. She bent down; she turned away; she picked up this rag; she squeezed that tube. But all it did was keep him off for a moment. He made it impossible for her to get anything done. For if she gave him the slightest opening—if he caught her free for a moment, or glancing his way for a moment—he would be upon her, saying, as he had last night, “You find us much changed.” Last night he had stood up, come to a halt in front of her, and said just that. The six children, whom they used to nickname after the Kings and Queens of England—the Red, the Fair, the Wicked, the Ruthless—had all sat there, mute and staring, yet she had felt how furious they were underneath. Kind old Mrs. Beckwith had said something sensible. But it was a house full of passions that had nothing to do with one another—she had felt that the whole evening. And on top of all this chaos Mr. Ramsay had stood up, pressed her hand, and said, “You will find us much changed,” and not one of them had stirred or spoken; they had sat there as if they had no choice but to let him say it. Only James (certainly the Sullen one) glowered at the lamp, and Cam wound her handkerchief round and round her finger. Then he reminded them that tomorrow they were going to the Lighthouse. They were to be ready in the hall at half past seven sharp. Then, with his hand on the door, he paused and swung round on them. Didn’t they want to go? he demanded. If they had dared to say no (he had some reason for wanting it), he would have hurled himself tragically backward into the bitter waters of despair. He had such a talent for gesture. He looked like a king in exile. James said yes, doggedly. Cam faltered more miserably. Yes, oh yes, they would both be ready, they said. And it came to her that this was what tragedy was—not funeral palls, dust and the shroud, but children forced into things, their spirits subdued. James was sixteen, and Cam seventeen, perhaps. She had looked around for someone who was not there—for Mrs. Ramsay, presumably. But there was only kind Mrs. Beckwith, leafing through her sketches under the lamp. Then, tired as she was, her mind still rising and sinking with the sea, the taste and smell that a place has after a long absence taking hold of her, the candles flickering before her eyes, she had lost hold of herself and gone under. It was a marvelous starlit night; they heard the waves as they climbed the stairs; the moon took them by surprise, huge and pale, as they passed the landing window. She had fallen asleep at once.

She fixed her clean canvas firmly on the easel as a barrier—a fragile one, but solid enough, she hoped, to keep Mr. Ramsay and his demands at bay. Whenever his back was turned she did her best to look at her picture—that line there, that mass there. But it was hopeless. He might be fifty feet away, he might not say a word to you, might not so much as see you, yet he seeped into everything, he won out, he forced himself on you. He altered everything. The color was lost to her; the lines were lost to her; even with his back to her all she could think was, He’ll be on me in a moment, wanting—something she felt she was unable to give. She put down one brush and picked up another. When were those children going to come? When would they all be gone? she fretted. That man, she thought, her anger mounting, never gave anything; that man only took. Whereas she would be made to give. Mrs. Ramsay had given. Giving and giving and giving, she had died—and left all this behind. Honestly, she was angry with Mrs. Ramsay. Her brush trembling a little between her fingers, she looked at the hedge, the step, the wall. It was all Mrs. Ramsay’s doing. She was dead. And here was Lily, forty-four years old, wasting her time, unable to do anything, standing there pretending to paint—playing at the one thing that was not to be played at—and it was all Mrs. Ramsay’s fault. She was dead. The step she used to sit on was empty. She was dead.

But what was the good of repeating it again and again? Why keep straining after a feeling she simply didn’t have? There was something like blasphemy in doing that. It was all dry: all shriveled: all used up. They should never have invited her; she should never have come. At forty-four you can’t afford to waste your time, she thought. She hated playing at painting. A brush was the one reliable thing in a world of conflict, ruin and chaos—you had no business playing with it, even knowingly; the idea disgusted her. But he forced her to. You won’t lay a finger on that canvas, he seemed to say as he bore down on her, until you’ve given me what I want from you. And here he was, right beside her again, greedy and distraught. Well, thought Lily despairingly, letting her right hand sink to her side, then it would be easier just to get it over with. Surely she could copy from memory the glow, the rapture, the self-surrender she had seen on the faces of so many women (on Mrs. Ramsay’s, for one) when, on an occasion like this, they would blaze up—she could recall the look on Mrs. Ramsay’s face—into a transport of sympathy, of delight in their reward. Why they felt it she could not tell, but plainly it gave them the most perfect bliss that human nature was capable of. Here he was, come to a stop beside her. She would give him what she could.

chapters.title: The Lighthouse · 2
paragraphs: She seemed to have shriveled a little, Mr. Ramsay thought. She looked rather thin and wispy, but not unattractive. He liked her. There had been some talk once of her marrying William Bankes, but nothing had come of it. His wife had been fond of her. He had been a little bad-tempered at breakfast, too. And then, and then—this was one of those moments when an enormous need drove him, without his knowing what it was, to go up to any woman and force her, he did not care how, so great was his need, to give him what he wanted: sympathy.
Was anyone looking after her? he asked. Did she have everything she wanted?

“Oh, I have everything, thanks,” Lily Briscoe said nervously. No; she could not do it. She should have floated away at once on some wave of warm, expansive sympathy: the pressure on her was tremendous. Yet she stayed stuck. An awful pause followed. They both looked at the sea. Why, Mr. Ramsay thought, should she look at the sea when I am standing here? She said she hoped it would be calm enough for them to land at the Lighthouse. The Lighthouse! The Lighthouse! What has that got to do with anything? he thought impatiently. And instantly, with the force of some primeval gust (for really he could not hold it in any longer), a groan broke from him—such a groan that any other woman in the whole world would have done something, said something. Any woman except me, Lily thought, lashing out at herself bitterly: I am not a woman at all, presumably, but a peevish, bad-tempered, dried-up old maid.

Mr. Ramsay let out the fullest of sighs. He waited. Wasn’t she going to say anything? Couldn’t she see what he wanted from her? Then he told her he had a particular reason for wanting to go to the Lighthouse. His wife used to send things to the men there. The lighthouse keeper had a son, a poor boy with a tubercular hip. He gave a deep sigh. He gave a meaningful sigh. What Lily wished, and all she wished, was that this enormous flood of grief, this hunger for sympathy that could never be satisfied, this demand that she hand herself over to him completely—and even then he would have sorrows enough to keep her supplied forever—would leave her alone, would be turned aside (she kept looking at the house, hoping someone would interrupt) before its current swept her away.

“Trips like this,” said Mr. Ramsay, scraping the ground with the toe of his boot, “are very painful.” Still Lily said nothing. (She is a block of wood, she is a stone, he said to himself.) “They are very exhausting,” he said, looking at his beautiful hands with a sickly look that turned her stomach (he was acting, she felt; this great man was making a drama of himself). It was horrible, it was indecent. Would they never come? she asked herself, for she could not bear this enormous weight of sorrow, could not hold up these heavy drapes of grief (he had taken on a pose of extreme frailty; he even tottered a little as he stood there) a moment longer.

Still she could say nothing. The whole horizon seemed swept clean of things to talk about. She could only feel, in amazement, as Mr. Ramsay stood there, how his gaze seemed to fall mournfully over the sunny grass and stain it, and how it cast a veil of black mourning crape over the ruddy, drowsy, entirely contented figure of Mr. Carmichael, reading a French novel in a deck chair—as if such a life, flaunting its well-being in a world of sorrow, were enough to stir up the gloomiest thoughts of all. Look at him, he seemed to be saying, look at me; and in fact, all the time, what he was feeling was, Think of me, think of me. Oh, if only that bulk could be floated over beside them, Lily wished; if only she had set up her easel a yard or two closer to him! A man, any man, would stop this outpouring, would put an end to these laments. She was a woman, and she had provoked this horror; as a woman, she should have known how to deal with it. It counted immensely against her, as a woman, to stand there dumb. One said—what did one say?—Oh, Mr. Ramsay! Dear Mr. Ramsay! That was what that kind old lady who sketched, Mrs. Beckwith, would have said at once, and rightly. But no. They stood there, cut off from the rest of the world. His immense self-pity, his demand for sympathy, poured out and spread in pools at her feet, and all she did, miserable sinner that she was, was to draw her skirts a little closer around her ankles, so as not to get wet. She stood there in complete silence, gripping her paintbrush.

Heaven be praised, over and over! She heard sounds in the house. James and Cam must be coming. But Mr. Ramsay, as if he knew his time was running short, bore down on her lonely figure with the immense pressure of all his concentrated sorrow—his age, his frailty, his desolation—when suddenly, tossing his head impatiently, in his annoyance (for, after all, what woman could resist him?), he noticed that his bootlaces were untied. And remarkable boots they were, too, Lily thought, looking down at them: sculpted; colossal; like everything Mr. Ramsay wore, from his frayed tie to his half-buttoned vest, unmistakably his own. She could picture them walking to his room by themselves, expressing, even in his absence, his pathos, his surliness, his bad temper, his charm.

“What beautiful boots!” she exclaimed. She was ashamed of herself. To praise his boots when he had asked her to comfort his soul; when he had shown her his bleeding hands, his torn heart, and asked her to pity them—and then to say, cheerfully, “Ah, but what beautiful boots you wear!”—deserved, she knew, total annihilation in one of his sudden roars of temper. She looked up, expecting to get it.

Mr. Ramsay smiled instead. The pall, the drapes, the infirmities all dropped off him. Ah yes, he said, raising his foot so she could look, these were first-rate boots. Only one man in England could make boots like that. Boots, he said, were among the chief curses of the human race. “Bootmakers,” he exclaimed, “make it their business to cripple and torture the human foot.” No people on earth were more stubborn and contrary. He had spent the better part of his youth getting boots made as boots ought to be made. She would please notice (up went his right foot, then his left) that she had never before seen boots of quite that shape. And the leather was the finest in the world. Most leather was mere brown paper and cardboard. Pleased with himself, he gazed at his foot, which was still in the air. They had arrived, she felt, at a sunny island where peace made its home, where sanity was in charge and the sun never stopped shining: the blessed island of good boots. She felt a warmth toward him. “Now let’s see whether you can tie a knot,” he said. He brushed aside her feeble method with scorn and demonstrated his own invention. Tie it once and it would never come undone. Three times he knotted her shoe; three times he unknotted it.

Why, at this completely inappropriate moment, when he was bending over her shoe, should she be so tormented by sympathy for him? As she bent down too, the blood rushed to her face, and, thinking of how hard she had been (she had called him a playactor), she felt her eyes swell and sting with tears. Busy like this, he seemed to her a figure of infinite pathos. He tied knots. He bought boots. There was no helping Mr. Ramsay on the journey he was making. But now, just as she wanted to say something, could perhaps have said something, here they were—Cam and James. They appeared on the terrace. They came slowly, trailing side by side, a serious, melancholy pair.

But why did they have to come like _that_? She could not help feeling annoyed with them. They might have come more cheerfully; they might have given him what she, now that they were leaving, would have no chance to give him. For she felt a sudden emptiness, a frustration. Her feeling had come too late. There it was, ready, but he no longer needed it. He had turned into a very distinguished elderly man who had no need of her whatsoever. She felt snubbed. He slung a knapsack over his shoulders. He handed out the parcels—there were a number of them, badly tied, in brown paper. He sent Cam for a cloak. He looked every inch a leader getting ready for an expedition. Then, wheeling around, he led the way down the path with his firm military step, in those wonderful boots, carrying brown paper parcels, his children following him. They looked, she thought, as if fate had given them over to some stern undertaking, and they went to meet it, still young enough to be drawn along obediently in their father’s wake, but with a paleness in their eyes that made her feel they were silently suffering something beyond their years. So they passed the edge of the lawn, and it seemed to Lily that she was watching a procession go by, drawn on by some pressure of shared feeling which made it—faltering and flagging as it was—a little company bound together, and strangely impressive to her. Politely, but very distantly, Mr. Ramsay raised his hand and saluted her as they passed.

But what a face, she thought, and at once the sympathy she had not been asked to give began troubling her, looking for a way out. What had made it like that? Thinking, night after night, she supposed—about the reality of kitchen tables, she added, remembering the symbol Andrew had given her when she was vague about what Mr. Ramsay actually thought about. (He had been killed instantly by a splinter of shell, she reminded herself.) The kitchen table was something visionary and austere; something bare, hard, not decorative. There was no color to it; it was all edges and angles; it was uncompromisingly plain. But Mr. Ramsay always kept his eyes fixed on it, never let himself be distracted or fooled, until his face too became worn and ascetic and shared in this unadorned beauty which impressed her so deeply. Then, she recalled (standing where he had left her, holding her brush), worries had worn at it—less nobly. He must have had his doubts about that table, she supposed: whether the table was a real table; whether it was worth the time he gave it; whether he was able, after all, to find it. He had had doubts, she felt, or he would have asked less of people. That was what they talked about late at night sometimes, she suspected; and then the next day Mrs. Ramsay looked tired, and Lily flew into a rage with him over some absurd little thing. But now he had nobody to talk to about that table, or his boots, or his knots; and he was like a lion seeking whom he might devour, and his face had that touch of desperation, of exaggeration, which alarmed her and made her pull her skirts around her. And then, she recalled, there was that sudden revival, that sudden flare (when she praised his boots), that sudden return of energy and interest in ordinary human things. That too passed and changed (for he was always changing, and hid nothing) into that other, final phase which was new to her, and which had, she admitted, made her ashamed of her own irritability. It seemed then as if he had shed his worries and ambitions, and the hope of sympathy and the desire for praise; as if he had entered some other region and was being drawn on, as if by curiosity, in silent conversation, whether with himself or with someone else, at the head of that little procession, out of one’s reach. An extraordinary face! The gate banged.

chapters.title: The Lighthouse · 3
paragraphs: So they’re gone, she thought, sighing with relief and disappointment. Her sympathy seemed to fly back into her face, like a bramble springing back. She felt strangely divided, as if one part of her were drawn out there—it was a still, hazy day; this morning the Lighthouse looked immensely far away—while the other part had planted itself stubbornly, solidly, here on the lawn. She saw her canvas as if it had floated up and set itself, white and uncompromising, right in front of her. With its cold stare it seemed to scold her for all this hurry and agitation, this foolishness and waste of emotion. It called her back sharply, and it spread through her mind first a peace, as her disorderly feelings (he had gone, and she had been so sorry for him, and she had said nothing) marched off the field; and then emptiness. She looked blankly at the canvas, with its uncompromising white stare; from the canvas to the garden. There was something (she stood screwing up her little Chinese eyes in her small puckered face), something she remembered in the way those lines related, cutting across, slicing down, and in the mass of the hedge with its green cave of blues and browns, which had stayed in her mind. It had tied a knot in her mind, so that at odd moments, without meaning to, as she walked along the Brompton Road in London, as she brushed her hair, she found herself painting that picture, running her eye over it, and untying the knot in her imagination. But there was all the difference in the world between this airy planning away from the canvas and actually taking up her brush and making the first mark.

In her agitation at Mr. Ramsay’s being there, she had taken the wrong brush, and her easel, jammed into the ground so nervously, was at the wrong angle. And now that she had put that right, and in doing so had quieted the intrusions and irrelevances that tugged at her attention and reminded her that she was such-and-such a person, with such-and-such relations to people, she took her hand and raised her brush. For a moment it hung trembling in the air in a painful but exciting ecstasy. Where to begin?—that was the question; at what point should she make the first mark? One line placed on the canvas committed her to countless risks, to frequent decisions that could not be undone. Everything that seemed simple in the idea became complicated the moment she put it into practice—just as waves, seen from the top of a cliff, form themselves into symmetrical patterns, but to the swimmer among them are split by steep gulfs and foaming crests. Still, the risk had to be taken; the mark had to be made.

With a strange physical sensation, as if she were being pushed forward and at the same time had to hold herself back, she made her first quick, decisive stroke. The brush came down. It flickered brown over the white canvas; it left a running mark. She did it a second time—a third time. And so, pausing and flickering, she found a dancing, rhythmic movement, as if the pauses were one part of the rhythm and the strokes another, and all were connected. And so, lightly and swiftly pausing, striking, she scored her canvas with brown, running, nervous lines, which had no sooner settled there than they enclosed (she felt it looming out at her) a space. Down in the hollow of one wave she saw the next wave towering higher and higher above her. For what could be more formidable than that space? Here she was again, she thought, stepping back to look at it, drawn out of gossip, out of living, out of fellowship with people, into the presence of this formidable, ancient enemy of hers—this other thing, this truth, this reality, which suddenly seized her, rose up stark behind the appearance of things and demanded her attention. She was half unwilling, half reluctant. Why must she always be drawn out and dragged away? Why not be left in peace, to talk to Mr. Carmichael on the lawn? It was a demanding kind of relationship, anyway. Other objects of worship were content with worship; men, women, God, all let you kneel down flat before them. But this form, even if it was only the shape of a white lampshade looming on a wicker table, roused you to endless combat, challenged you to a fight you were bound to lose. Always (it was in her nature, or in her sex, she did not know which), before she traded the fluidity of life for the concentration of painting, she had a few moments of nakedness, when she seemed like an unborn soul, a soul torn from its body, hesitating on some windy pinnacle and exposed without protection to every blast of doubt. Why, then, did she do it? She looked at the canvas, lightly scored with running lines. It would be hung in the servants’ bedrooms. It would be rolled up and stuffed under a sofa. What was the good of doing it, then? And she heard some voice saying she couldn’t paint, saying she couldn’t create, as if she were caught up in one of those habitual currents which, after a while, form experience in the mind, so that you repeat words without being aware any longer of who first said them.

Can’t paint, can’t write, she murmured in a monotone, anxiously trying to decide on her plan of attack. For the mass loomed up before her; it stuck out; she could feel it pressing on her eyeballs. Then, as if some juice her faculties needed for oiling had squirted out all by itself, she began dipping, uncertainly, among the blues and umbers, moving her brush this way and that. But the brush was heavier now and slower, as though it had fallen in with some rhythm that what she saw was dictating to her (her eyes kept going from the hedge to the canvas), so that while her hand trembled with life, the rhythm was strong enough to carry her along on its current. She was certainly losing her awareness of things outside her. And as she lost awareness of outer things—of her name, her personality, her appearance, of whether Mr. Carmichael was there or not—her mind kept throwing up from its depths scenes and names and sayings and memories and ideas, like a fountain spurting over that glaring, horribly difficult white space, while she shaped it with greens and blues.

That was what Charles Tansley used to say, she remembered: women can’t paint, can’t write. He had come up behind her once and stood right beside her—she hated that—while she was painting here, on this very spot. “Shag tobacco,” he said, “fivepence an ounce,” making a show of his poverty and his principles. (But the war had taken the sting out of her sense of being a woman. Poor devils, you thought, poor devils of both sexes, getting into such messes.) He always had a book tucked under his arm—a purple one. He “worked.” She remembered him sitting at work in a blaze of sunshine. At dinner he would plant himself right in the middle of the view. And then, she reflected, there had been that scene on the beach. That had to be remembered. It was a windy morning, and they had all gone down to the beach. Mrs. Ramsay sat by a rock writing letters. On and on she wrote. At last she looked up at something floating in the sea. “Oh,” she said, “is it a lobster pot? Is it a boat turned upside down?” She was too nearsighted to see it, and at that Charles Tansley became as nice as he possibly could. He started playing ducks and drakes, skipping stones. The two of them picked out small flat black stones and sent them bouncing across the waves. From time to time Mrs. Ramsay looked up over her glasses and laughed at them. What they talked about, she could not remember—only herself and Charles throwing stones, suddenly getting along very well, and Mrs. Ramsay watching. She had been very aware of that. Mrs. Ramsay, she thought, stepping back and narrowing her eyes. (It must have made a big difference to the design when Mrs. Ramsay was sitting on the step with James. There must have been a shadow.) Mrs. Ramsay. Whenever she thought of Charles and herself skipping stones, and of that whole scene on the beach, it all seemed somehow to rest on Mrs. Ramsay sitting under the rock with a pad on her knee, writing letters. (She wrote endless letters, and now and then the wind snatched one, and she and Charles just managed to save a page from the sea.) What power there was in the human soul! she thought. That woman, sitting there writing under the rock, turned everything simple; made these angers and irritations fall away like old rags. She put this together with that, and then with this, and so, out of that wretched silliness and spite (she and Charles, squabbling and sparring, had been silly and spiteful), she made something—this scene on the beach, say, this moment of friendship and liking—that had lasted all these years, whole and complete, so that Lily dipped into it to remake her memory of him, and it stayed in the mind almost like a work of art.

“Like a work of art,” she repeated, looking from her canvas to the drawing-room steps and back again. She had to rest for a moment. And as she rested, looking vaguely from one to the other, the old question that was forever crossing the sky of the soul—the vast, general question which tended to take on a particular shape at moments like these, when she let go of faculties that had been under strain—stood over her, paused over her, darkened over her. What is the meaning of life? That was all—a simple question; one that tended to close in on you as the years went by. The great revelation had never come. Perhaps the great revelation never did come. Instead there were little daily miracles, illuminations, matches struck unexpectedly in the dark; here was one. This, that, and the other; herself and Charles Tansley and the breaking wave; Mrs. Ramsay bringing them together; Mrs. Ramsay saying “Life stand still here”; Mrs. Ramsay making something permanent out of the moment (just as Lily herself, in another sphere, tried to make something permanent out of the moment)—this had the nature of a revelation. In the midst of chaos there was shape; this eternal passing and flowing (she looked at the clouds going by and the leaves shaking) was struck into something stable. Life stand still here, Mrs. Ramsay said. “Mrs. Ramsay! Mrs. Ramsay!” she repeated. She owed this revelation to her.

Everything was silent. Nobody seemed to be stirring in the house yet. She looked at it, sleeping there in the early sunlight, its windows green and blue with the reflected leaves. The faint thought she was having about Mrs. Ramsay seemed in harmony with this quiet house, this smoke, this fine early-morning air. Faint and unreal, it was amazingly pure and exciting. She hoped nobody would open a window or come out of the house, but that she would be left alone to go on thinking, to go on painting. She turned to her canvas. But pushed by some curiosity, driven by the discomfort of the sympathy she was still holding in, unreleased, she walked a step or two to the end of the lawn to see whether, down there on the beach, she could see that little company setting sail. Down there among the little boats floating on the water, some with their sails furled, some moving slowly away, for it was very calm, there was one a little apart from the others. Its sail was being hoisted at that very moment. She decided that there, in that very distant and entirely silent little boat, Mr. Ramsay was sitting with Cam and James. Now they had got the sail up; now, after a little flagging and hesitation, the sails filled, and, wrapped in deep silence, she watched the boat make its way deliberately past the other boats and out to sea.

chapters.title: The Lighthouse · 4
paragraphs: Over their heads the sails flapped. Water chuckled against the boat and slapped its sides; the boat itself lay drowsing in the sun, not moving. Every so often a little breeze got into the sails and they rippled, but the ripple ran across them and died away. There was no motion at all. In the middle of the boat sat Mr. Ramsay. Any moment now he would get impatient, James thought, and so did Cam, both of them watching their father where he sat between them in the middle (James had the tiller; Cam was alone in the bow), his legs curled up tight. Hanging about was something he hated. And sure enough, after a second or two of fidgeting, he spoke sharply to Macalister’s boy, who brought out his oars and started rowing. But they knew their father would never be content until the boat was flying. He would go on watching for a breeze, fidgeting, muttering things that Macalister and Macalister’s boy would overhear, and both of them would be made horribly uncomfortable. He had made them come. He had forced them to. Angry, they hoped no breeze would ever rise, hoped he would be thwarted in every way possible, because he had forced them to come when they did not want to.

The whole way down to the beach the two of them had dragged along behind, together and silent, though he kept calling to them, “Walk up, walk up.” Their heads were bowed, pushed down as if by some relentless gale. Speak to him? That they could not do. Come they must; follow they must; walk behind him they must, loaded with brown paper parcels. Yet as they walked they made a silent vow: they would stand by each other and keep the great compact—to resist tyranny to the death. So they would sit there in silence, one at each end of the boat. Not a word would they say. They would only glance at him from time to time, sitting there with his legs twisted, frowning, fidgeting, pishing and pshawing, muttering to himself, impatient for a breeze. And they hoped for calm. They hoped for him to be thwarted. They hoped the whole trip would be a failure, and that they would have to go back to the beach, parcels and all.

But now, once Macalister’s boy had rowed them out a little way, the sails swung slowly round; the boat came alive, flattened itself, and shot away. Mr. Ramsay at once uncurled his legs, as though some great tension had been let go. He took out his tobacco pouch and, with a little grunt, passed it to Macalister, and they knew that he felt perfectly content, whatever they themselves might be suffering. For hours now they would sail along like this. Mr. Ramsay would put some question to old Macalister—probably about the great storm last winter—and old Macalister would answer, and the two men would puff away at their pipes, and Macalister would take up a tarry rope and work at some knot, tying or untying it, and the boy would fish without saying a word to anybody. It would be James’s job to watch the sail every moment. If he forgot, the sail puckered and shivered, the boat lost speed, and Mr. Ramsay would say sharply, “Look out! Look out!” and old Macalister would slowly turn round on his seat. Sure enough, they heard Mr. Ramsay ask something about the great storm at Christmas. “She comes driving round the point,” old Macalister said. He was describing last Christmas’s great storm, when eleven ships had been driven into the bay to shelter, and he had seen “one there, one there, one there” (pointing slowly round the bay, while Mr. Ramsay turned his head to follow). Three men he had seen, clinging to the mast. Then she was gone. “And at last we shoved her off,” he went on. (The children, though, caught only the odd word in their anger and silence, sitting at opposite ends of the boat, bound together by their compact to fight tyranny to the death.) At last they had shoved her off; the lifeboat was launched, and they had got her out beyond the point—so ran Macalister’s story. And though only a word here and there reached them, they were conscious of their father the whole time. They saw how he leaned in, how his voice fell into tune with Macalister’s; how he puffed at his pipe and looked this way and that where Macalister pointed, savoring the thought of the storm, the dark night, the fishermen struggling out there. He liked the idea of men laboring and sweating at night on a windy beach, setting muscle and brain against wind and waves; he liked men to work that way, and women to keep house and sit indoors beside sleeping children while out in the storm the men drowned. James could tell it, and so could Cam (they looked at him; they looked at each other). They could tell from the toss of his head, from how alert he was, from the ring in his voice and the faint Scottish accent that crept into it and made him seem a peasant himself, as he questioned Macalister about the ten ships driven into the bay by a storm. Three had gone down.

He gazed proudly where Macalister was pointing; and Cam, proud of him without quite knowing why, thought that if he had been there, he would have launched the lifeboat, he would have got to the wreck. He was so brave, Cam thought, so adventurous. But then she remembered. There was the compact: to resist tyranny to the death. Their grievance lay heavy on them. They had been forced; they had been ordered about. Once again he had flattened them with his gloom and his authority. On this fine morning he had made them do as he said—come, because he wanted it, with these parcels, to the Lighthouse—and join in those rituals he performed, for his own satisfaction, in memory of the dead. They hated them. So they trailed behind him, and the whole day’s pleasure was ruined.

Yes, the breeze was getting stronger. The boat heeled over; the water was cut sharply and fell away in green cascades, in bubbles, in waterfalls. Cam gazed down into the foam, into the sea and all the treasure it held, and its speed put her in a trance, and the bond between her and James went slack a little. It loosened slightly. How fast it goes, she began to think. Where are we going? The motion entranced her, while James steered grimly, his eye on the sail and the horizon. Yet as he steered, a thought began to come to him: he might get away; he might be done with all of it. They might land somewhere, and then be free. For a moment the two of them looked at each other and felt a lift of escape and exhilaration, from the speed and the change. But the breeze roused that same excitement in Mr. Ramsay, too. As old Macalister turned to cast his line over the side, he cried out loud, “We perished,” and then again, “each alone.” Then, in his usual spasm of shyness or remorse, he caught himself up and waved a hand at the shore.

“See the little house,” he said, pointing; he wanted Cam to look. Unwillingly she sat up and looked. But which one was it? Up there on the hillside, she could no longer tell which house was theirs. Everything seemed far off, peaceful, strange. The shore looked delicate, remote, unreal. The short way they had sailed had already set them at a great distance from it and given it that altered, settled look of something slipping away, something you no longer have any part in. Which house was theirs? She could not find it.

“But I beneath a rougher sea,” Mr. Ramsay murmured—a line from Cowper’s “The Castaway,” about a sailor drowned alone. He had found the house, and seeing it, he had seen himself there too, pacing the terrace alone. Up and down between the urns he was walking, and to himself he seemed very old and stooped. There in the boat he stooped, too, and hunched down, instantly playing his role—the role of a lonely man, widowed and bereft. That way he could summon up crowds of people who pitied him. Sitting in the boat, he put on a little play for himself, one that called for frailty and weariness and grief from him (he held up his hands and looked at how thin they were, to confirm the dream). Then, in abundance, women’s sympathy was handed to him, and he imagined how they would comfort him and feel for him. And catching in his dream some glimmer of the exquisite pleasure that women’s sympathy gave him, he sighed, and said softly and sadly,

But I beneath a rougher sea
Was whelmed in deeper gulfs than he,

so that every one of them heard the mournful words perfectly clearly. Cam gave a half start where she sat. It shocked her; it outraged her. Her movement woke her father out of it; he shuddered and stopped short, calling out “Look! Look!” so urgently that James, too, turned his head and looked back over his shoulder at the island. All of them looked. They looked at the island.

Cam, though, could see nothing. She was thinking how all those paths and the lawn, so thick and tangled with the lives they had lived there, were gone—rubbed out, over, unreal—and that this was what was real now: the boat, and the sail with its patch; Macalister with his earrings; the sound of the waves. All this was real. As she thought it, she was murmuring to herself, “We perished, each alone,” because her father’s words kept breaking in her mind and breaking again. Then her father saw her staring so vaguely and started to tease her. Didn’t she know the points of the compass? he asked. Couldn’t she tell north from south? Did she honestly think they lived way out there? He pointed once more and showed her where their house stood, there, beside those trees. He did wish she would try to be more precise, he said. “Tell me—which is east, which is west?” he said, half laughing at her and half scolding, for he simply could not grasp how anyone who was not a complete idiot could fail to know the points of the compass. But she did not know them. And when he saw her staring, her eyes vague and by now rather frightened, fixed on a spot where there was no house, Mr. Ramsay forgot his dream: the pacing up and down between the urns on the terrace, the arms held out to him. Women are always like that, he thought; their minds are hopelessly vague; he had never been able to understand it, but that was how it was. His wife had been like that too. Nothing would stay fixed clearly in their heads. But it had been wrong of him to get angry with her; and besides, didn’t he rather like this vagueness in women? It was part of their extraordinary charm. I will make her smile at me, he thought. She looks scared. She was so quiet. He gripped his fingers together and made up his mind that his voice and his face and all those quick, expressive gestures that for so many years had been at his command for making people pity and praise him should all be held in check. He would get her to smile at him. He would think of something simple and easy to say to her. But what? Wrapped up as he was in his work, he had forgotten the kind of thing people said. There was a puppy. They had a puppy. Who was taking care of the puppy today? he asked. Yes, thought James without pity, seeing his sister’s head against the sail, now she’ll give in. I’ll be left to fight the tyrant on my own. The compact would be his alone to keep. Cam would never resist tyranny to the death, he thought grimly, watching her face—sad, sulky, giving way. Sometimes a cloud settles on a green hillside and a heaviness comes down, and there, among all the hills around, is gloom and sorrow, and it seems as though the hills themselves must be brooding over the fate of the one that is clouded and darkened, either pitying her or maliciously enjoying her dismay. That was how overcast Cam felt now, sitting among calm, determined people, wondering how to answer her father about the puppy; how to hold out against his plea—forgive me, care for me—while James the lawgiver, the tablets of eternal wisdom open on his knee (to her, his hand on the tiller had become a symbol), said, Resist him. Fight him. And he was right to say it; he was just. For they must fight tyranny to the death, she thought. Of all human virtues, justice was the one she held most sacred. Her brother was the most godlike, her father the most imploring. And which of them was she yielding to, she wondered, sitting between the two, gazing at a shore whose landmarks were all strange to her, and thinking how the lawn and the terrace and the house were smoothed away now, and peace lived there.
“Jasper,” she said sulkily. Jasper would take care of the puppy.

And what name would she give him? her father kept on. When he was a small boy he had had a dog called Frisk. She’s going to give in, James thought, watching a certain look come over her face, a look he remembered. They look down at their knitting, or something, he thought. Then all at once they look up. He remembered a flash of blue, and then someone sitting with him laughed and gave in, and he was furious. It must have been his mother, he thought, in a low chair, with his father standing over her. He began to hunt through the endless series of impressions that time had laid down on his brain, softly, ceaselessly, leaf upon leaf, fold upon fold: scents, sounds; voices, harsh, hollow, sweet; lights going by, and brooms tapping; the wash and hush of the sea; how a man had marched up and down and stopped dead, standing upright over them. Meanwhile, he noticed, Cam was dabbling her fingers in the water, staring at the shore, saying nothing. No, she won’t give in, he thought; she’s not like that. Well, then, if Cam would not answer, he would leave her alone, Mr. Ramsay decided, and felt in his pocket for a book. But she did want to answer him. She longed, passionately, to shift whatever lay on her tongue and blocked it, and to say, Oh yes, Frisk. I’ll call him Frisk. She even wanted to ask, Was that the dog that found its own way across the moor? But however hard she tried, she could think of nothing like that to say—something fierce and faithful to the compact, yet which would pass her father, without James suspecting, a secret sign of the love she felt for him. For as she dabbled her hand (and just then Macalister’s boy caught a mackerel, and it lay kicking on the bottom of the boat with blood on its gills)—for as she looked at James, who kept his eyes on the sail without any feeling, or now and then glanced at the horizon for a second, she thought: you aren’t exposed to it—this pressure, this split feeling, this extraordinary temptation. Her father was searching his pockets; another second and he would have his book. For nobody drew her more than he did. His hands were beautiful to her, and his feet, and his voice, his words, his hurry, his temper, his strangeness, his passion, the way he would say straight out in front of everybody, we perish, each alone, and his remoteness. (He had opened his book.) But what was still unbearable, she thought, sitting up straight and watching Macalister’s boy pull the hook from another fish’s gills, was that crude blindness and tyranny of his. It had poisoned her childhood and stirred up bitter storms, so that even now she would wake at night shaking with rage, remembering some command of his, some insolence: “Do this,” “Do that”; his domination; his “Submit to me.”

So she kept silent, and looked at the shore stubbornly and sadly. It lay wrapped in its mantle of peace, as if the people there had fallen asleep, she thought—as if they were free like smoke, free to drift in and out like ghosts. There is no suffering there, she thought.

chapters.title: The Lighthouse · 5
paragraphs: Yes, that one is their boat, Lily Briscoe decided, as she stood at the edge of the lawn. It was the boat with the grayish-brown sails; she watched it flatten itself on the water now and shoot away across the bay. He’s sitting there, she thought, and the children still haven’t said a word. And she couldn’t reach him either. The sympathy she had held back from him lay heavy on her. It made painting hard.

She had always found Mr. Ramsay difficult. Never once, she remembered, had she managed to praise him to his face. Because of that, what was between them had been reduced to something neutral, lacking the element of sex that made him behave so gallantly, almost gaily, toward Minta. For Minta he would pick a flower, or hand over his books. But could he really have believed Minta read them? She used to drag them all over the garden, with leaves stuck in them for bookmarks.

“Do you remember, Mr. Carmichael?” Lily was tempted to ask, glancing at the old man. But his hat was pulled halfway down over his forehead. He was sleeping, she supposed, or dreaming, or just lying there catching words.

“Do you remember?” she was tempted to ask him as she went past, her mind going back again to Mrs. Ramsay on the beach: the cask bobbing up and down, the pages flying. After all these years, why had that scene lasted? There it was, ringed round and lit up, visible down to the smallest detail, while everything before it was blank and everything after it was blank, for miles and miles.

“Is it a boat? Is it a cork?” Mrs. Ramsay would say—Lily repeated the words as she turned back to her canvas, reluctant once more. Thank heaven the problem of space was still there, she thought, and took up her brush again. It glared at her. The entire mass of the picture balanced on that weight.
