The surface ought to be beautiful and bright, feathery and fleeting, each color melting into the next like the colors on a butterfly’s wing; but underneath, the fabric had to be clamped together with iron bolts. It should be something your breath could ruffle, and something a team of horses couldn’t shift. She began laying on a red, then a gray, and began shaping her way into the hollow there. At the same moment she seemed to be sitting next to Mrs. Ramsay on the beach.

“Is it a boat? Is it a cask?” Mrs. Ramsay asked, and started hunting about for her glasses. Once she had found them, she sat without a word, gazing out to sea. And as Lily painted steadily on, she had the feeling that a door had opened: you walked through it and stood looking silently about you in a lofty place like a cathedral, very dark and very solemn. Shouts reached them from a far-off world. On the horizon, steamers disappeared into stalks of smoke. Charles was throwing stones and making them skip.

Mrs. Ramsay said nothing. Lily thought she was glad to rest in silence, not talking; to rest in the deep obscurity of human relationships. Who knows what we are? What we feel? Even in a moment of intimacy, who can say, This is knowledge? Mrs. Ramsay might have asked (this silence beside her seemed to have happened so often) whether saying things didn’t spoil them. Weren’t we more expressive this way? At least the moment seemed extraordinarily fertile. She jabbed a little hole in the sand and then covered it over, as though burying the moment’s perfection there. It was like a drop of silver: you dipped into it, and it lit up the darkness of the past.

Lily took a step back to put her canvas—so—into perspective. This business of painting was a strange road to walk. You went out and out, farther and farther, until at last you seemed to be standing on a narrow plank over the sea, entirely alone. As she dipped her brush into the blue, she dipped into the past there as well. Now Mrs. Ramsay stood up, she remembered. Time to go back to the house—time for lunch. They all walked up from the beach together, with Lily behind beside William Bankes, and Minta ahead of them with a hole in her stocking. How that small round hole showing her pink heel seemed to flaunt itself at them! And how William Bankes disapproved of it, though as far as she could remember he never said a word! To him it stood for the end of womanhood—for dirt and mess, for servants giving notice and beds still unmade at noon—everything he hated most. He had a habit of shuddering and spreading his fingers wide as if to hide something ugly, and he did it now, holding his hand up in front of him. Minta walked on ahead, and Paul must have met her, and the two of them went off into the garden.

The Rayleys, Lily Briscoe thought, as she squeezed out her tube of green. She gathered together what she knew of them. She saw their lives as a string of scenes. One took place on the staircase at dawn. Paul had come home early and gone to bed; Minta was out late. And there she was on the stairs at around three in the morning, wreathed, made up, garish. Paul came out in pajamas with a poker, in case it was burglars. Minta stood halfway up by a window eating a sandwich in the deathly early light, and there was a hole in the carpet. But what did they say to each other? Lily wondered, as if looking hard enough would let her hear. Something violent. While he talked, Minta kept on eating her sandwich, which was maddening. His words were indignant and jealous; he abused her in a mutter so the children wouldn’t wake—the two little boys. He looked withered and drawn; she looked flamboyant and careless. After the first year or so, things had come loose; the marriage had turned out rather badly.

And this, Lily thought, loading her brush with green—this inventing of scenes about people—is what we call “knowing” them, “thinking” of them, “being fond” of them! None of it was true, not a word; she had invented it. Yet it was how she knew them, all the same. She kept tunneling on into her picture, into the past.

Then there was the time Paul said he “played chess in coffeehouses.” On that remark too she had built an entire structure of imagination. She remembered picturing it even as he spoke: he telephoned home, the maid answered, “Mrs. Rayley’s out, sir,” and so he made up his mind not to go home either. She saw him in the corner of some dismal place where smoke clung to the red plush seats and the waitresses came to know your face, playing chess with a small man in the tea trade who lived at Surbiton—and that was all Paul knew about him. Then Minta was out when he got home, and after that came the scene on the stairs, when he fetched the poker in case of burglars (and no doubt to scare her as well) and spoke so bitterly, telling her she had ruined his life. Anyway, when Lily went down to visit them at a cottage near Rickmansworth, the strain was horrible. Paul led her down the garden to see the Belgian hares he bred, and Minta came after them, singing, and laid her bare arm on his shoulder so that he wouldn’t tell Lily anything.

Hares bored Minta, Lily thought. But Minta never gave herself away. She would never say a thing like that about chess in coffeehouses; she was much too self-aware, much too careful. Still, to go on with their story—by now the dangerous stage was behind them. Lily had stayed with them for a while last summer, and the car broke down, and Minta had to pass him his tools. He sat in the road fixing it, and the way she passed him the tools—businesslike, direct, friendly—was proof that all was well now. They were not “in love” anymore. No: he had taken up with another woman, a serious woman who wore her hair in a braid and carried a briefcase (Minta described her with gratitude, almost with admiration). She went to meetings and shared Paul’s views, which had grown more and more pronounced, on taxing land values and on a capital levy. That alliance, far from wrecking the marriage, had put it right. Clearly they were excellent friends, he sitting in the road and she handing him his tools.

So that was the Rayleys’ story, Lily thought, smiling. She pictured herself telling it to Mrs. Ramsay, who would be eager to hear how the Rayleys had turned out. There would be a little triumph in it for Lily, telling Mrs. Ramsay that the marriage had not succeeded.

But the dead, Lily thought—she had hit some snag in her design that made her stop and consider, stepping back a foot or so—oh, the dead! she murmured. You pitied them, you pushed them aside, you even felt a little contempt for them. They are at our mercy. Mrs. Ramsay has faded away and gone, she thought. We can overrule her wishes and improve away her narrow, old-fashioned ideas. She draws further and further away from us. Mockingly, Lily seemed to see her at the far end of the corridor of years, saying the most unsuitable thing imaginable: “Marry, marry!” (sitting bolt upright early in the morning, as the birds began to chirp in the garden outside). And you would have to tell her, It has all gone against your wishes. They’re happy that way; I’m happy this way. Life has changed completely. At that, all of her, even her beauty, turned for a moment dusty and out of date. For a moment Lily, standing there with the sun hot on her back and the Rayleys summed up, triumphed over Mrs. Ramsay. Mrs. Ramsay would never know how Paul went to coffeehouses and kept a mistress; how he sat on the ground while Minta handed him his tools; how Lily stood here painting, and had never married—not even William Bankes.

It had been Mrs. Ramsay’s plan. Had she lived, she might have forced it to happen. Even that summer he was already “the kindest of men.” He was “the first scientist of his age, my husband says.” And he was “poor William—it makes me so unhappy, when I go to see him, to find nothing nice in his house—no one to arrange the flowers.” So the two of them were sent off on walks together, and Lily was told—with that slight touch of irony that let Mrs. Ramsay slip through your fingers—that she had a scientific mind, that she was fond of flowers, that she was so precise. Why this mania for marrying people off? Lily wondered, moving back and forth in front of her easel.

(All at once, as suddenly as a star slides down the sky, a reddish light seemed to blaze up in her mind; it covered Paul Rayley and poured out from him. It went up like a bonfire lit by savages on some faraway beach to mark a celebration. She heard it roar and crackle. For miles around, the whole sea ran red and gold. A smell like wine was mixed into it and went to her head, because she felt once more her own reckless longing to throw herself off the cliff and drown hunting for a pearl brooch on a beach. And the roar and crackle filled her with fear and disgust and drove her back. It was as if, even while she saw how splendid and powerful it was, she also saw how it fed on the treasure of the house, greedily and disgustingly, and she loathed it. Yet as a spectacle, as a glory, it outshone anything she had ever experienced; year after year it burned like a signal fire on a desert island at the sea’s edge, and you had only to say “in love” for Paul’s fire to leap up again at once, as it did now. Then it died down, and she said to herself with a laugh, “The Rayleys”—how Paul went to coffeehouses and played chess.)

Still, she thought, it had been a narrow escape. She had been looking at the tablecloth when it came to her in a flash that she would move the tree to the middle, and that she need never marry anyone, and she had felt tremendous exultation. She had felt she could stand up to Mrs. Ramsay now—which shows what astonishing power Mrs. Ramsay had over you. She said, Do this, and you did it. Even her shadow in the window with James carried authority. Lily remembered how it had shocked William Bankes that she disregarded the significance of mother and son. Didn’t she admire their beauty? he asked. But William had listened, she remembered, with his wise child’s eyes, as she explained that she meant no irreverence: a light here called for a shadow there, and so on. She had no wish to belittle a subject that Raphael, they both agreed, had painted divinely. She wasn’t cynical. Far from it. Because he had a scientific mind, he understood—proof of an impartial intelligence that had pleased and comforted her enormously. So it was possible, then, to talk seriously to a man about painting. In fact, his friendship had been one of the pleasures of her life. She loved William Bankes.

They used to go to Hampton Court, and he always gave her plenty of time to wash her hands, like the perfect gentleman he was, while he wandered along the river. Their whole relationship was like that; a great deal went unsaid. Afterward they strolled through the courtyards and, summer after summer, admired the proportions and the flowers. As they walked he would tell her about perspective and architecture, and he would stop to look at a tree, or at the view across the lake, or to admire a child (his great sorrow was that he had no daughter). He did it in the vague, detached way natural to a man who spent so long in laboratories that the world dazzled him when he came out. So he walked slowly, lifted a hand to shade his eyes, and stopped with his head thrown back just to breathe the air. Then he would mention that his housekeeper was away on vacation and he needed to buy a new stair carpet. Would she perhaps come with him to buy a new stair carpet? And once, for some reason, the talk turned to the Ramsays, and he told her that when he first saw Mrs. Ramsay she was wearing a gray hat; she could not have been more than nineteen or twenty. She was astonishingly beautiful. He stood there gazing down the avenue at Hampton Court as though he could see her among the fountains.

Lily looked at the drawing-room step now. Through William’s eyes she saw the shape of a woman, quiet and peaceful, her eyes cast down. She sat lost in thought, pondering (she was wearing gray that day, Lily thought). Her gaze was lowered. She would never raise it. Yes, thought Lily, looking hard, I must have seen her look that way—but not in gray, and not so still, or so young, or so peaceful. The figure came easily enough. She was astonishingly beautiful, William said. But beauty wasn’t everything. Beauty had this price: it came too easily and too completely. It stopped life still—froze it. You forgot the small agitations: the flush, the paleness, some strange twist, some light or shadow that made the face unrecognizable for an instant and yet added something you saw in it ever after. It was simpler to smooth all that away beneath beauty. But what did she look like, Lily wondered, when she clapped her deerstalker hat on her head, or ran across the grass, or scolded Kennedy, the gardener? Who could tell her that? Who could help her?

Without meaning to, she had surfaced and found herself half out of the picture, gazing a little dazed, as if at things that weren’t real, at Mr. Carmichael. He was lying in his chair, hands clasped on top of his belly—not reading, not asleep, but basking like some creature stuffed full of existence. His book had dropped onto the grass.

She wanted to walk straight over and say, “Mr. Carmichael!” He would look up kindly, as he always did, out of his vague, smoky green eyes. But you only woke people when you knew what you wanted to tell them. And what she wanted to say was not one thing but everything. Small words that chopped the thought up into pieces said nothing at all. “About life, about death; about Mrs. Ramsay”—no, she thought, you could say nothing to anybody. The urgency of the moment always missed. Words fluttered off to the side and struck inches below the target. Then you gave up, and the idea sank back down, and you turned into what most middle-aged people become: cautious, secretive, with lines between the eyes and a look of permanent anxiety. Because how could you put these feelings of the body into words? How could you express that emptiness there? (She was looking at the drawing-room steps. They looked extraordinarily empty.) It was the body that felt it, not the mind. The physical sensations that came with the bare look of those steps had all at once turned extremely unpleasant. Wanting and not having sent a hardness, a hollowness, a strain right through her body. And then wanting and not having—wanting and wanting—how it wrung the heart, over and over! Oh, Mrs. Ramsay! she cried out without a sound, to that essence sitting by the boat, that abstraction made out of her, that woman in gray—as if to scold her for having gone, and then, having gone, for coming back. Thinking of her had seemed so safe. Ghost, air, nothing, something you could toy with easily and safely at any hour of the day or night—that was what she had been. And then suddenly Mrs. Ramsay reached out her hand and wrung the heart like this. Suddenly the empty drawing-room steps, the frill of the chair inside, the puppy tumbling about on the terrace, the whole wave and whisper of the garden, turned into curves and arabesques flourishing around a center of total emptiness.

“What does it mean? How do you explain it all?” she wanted to ask, turning again to Mr. Carmichael. At this early hour of the morning the whole world seemed to have melted into a pool of thought, a deep basin of reality, and it was almost possible to imagine that if Mr. Carmichael spoke, a small tear would rip across the pool’s surface. And then what? Something would rise up out of it. A hand would push up; a blade would flash. Nonsense, of course.

She had an odd idea that he did hear, after all, the things she couldn’t say. He was an unreadable old man, with his yellow-stained beard and his poetry and his puzzles, sailing calmly through a world that met all his needs; it seemed to her that he had only to lower his hand where he lay on the lawn to fish up whatever he wanted. She looked at her picture. That, presumably, would have been his answer: how “you” and “I” and “she” pass and vanish; nothing lasts; everything changes; but not words, not paint. And yet it would be hung in the attics, she thought; it would be rolled up and tossed under a sofa. Even so, even of a picture like that, it was true. You could say of this scrawl—perhaps not of the actual picture, but of what it tried to do—that it “remained forever.” That was what she was going to say; or rather, since the words sounded too boastful even to her once spoken, she was going to hint it without words. But when she looked at the picture, she was surprised to find she couldn’t see it. A hot liquid filled her eyes (at first she didn’t think of tears); it left her lips firm, but it thickened the air and ran down her cheeks. In every other way she was in complete control of herself—oh yes! Was she crying for Mrs. Ramsay, then, without being aware of any unhappiness? She turned to old Mr. Carmichael again. What was it, then? What did it mean? Could things push their hands up and grab you? Could the blade cut, the fist clench? Was there no safety? No learning the world’s ways by heart? No guide, no refuge—was it all miracle, and leaping off the top of a tower into the air? Could it be that, even for older people, this was life?—startling, unexpected, unknown? For one moment she felt that if the two of them stood up, here and now on the lawn, and demanded an explanation—why was it so short, why so impossible to explain—and demanded it violently, the way two fully equipped human beings might speak who should have nothing hidden from them, then beauty would roll itself up; the space would fill; those empty flourishes would take shape; if they only shouted loudly enough, Mrs. Ramsay would come back. “Mrs. Ramsay!” she said out loud. “Mrs. Ramsay!” Tears were streaming down her face.

chapters.title: The Lighthouse · 7
paragraphs: “Mrs. Ramsay!” Lily cried. “Mrs. Ramsay!” Nothing happened. The pain only grew. How anguish could reduce you to such a level of foolishness! she thought. At any rate the old man hadn’t heard her. He stayed kindly and calm—even sublime, if you wanted to see him that way. Thank heaven nobody had heard that humiliating cry of hers: stop, pain, stop! At least she hadn’t visibly lost her mind. Nobody had watched her step off her narrow strip of board into the waters of annihilation. She was still just a skimpy old maid on the lawn with a paintbrush in her hand.

And now, little by little, the pain of wanting, and the bitter anger (at being called back just when she believed she would never grieve for Mrs. Ramsay again—had she missed her among the coffee cups at breakfast? Not at all), grew less. What their anguish left behind, as a remedy, was a relief that soothed in itself, and also, more mysteriously, a sense that someone was there—Mrs. Ramsay, freed for a moment of the weight the world had laid on her, lingering lightly beside Lily and then (for this was Mrs. Ramsay in all her beauty) lifting to her forehead a wreath of white flowers and going off with it. Lily squeezed her tubes again and attacked the problem of the hedge. It was odd how clearly she could see Mrs. Ramsay stepping, quick as always, across fields that were soft and purplish in their folds, full of flowers—hyacinths or lilies—among which she vanished. It was a trick of the painter’s eye. For days after hearing of her death, Lily had seen her like this, raising the wreath to her forehead and going off unquestioningly across the fields with her companion, a shadow. The sight, and the phrase, had power to comfort. Wherever she was—painting here in the country, or in London—the vision would come, and her eyes would half close, searching for something to rest the vision on. She would look down the railway carriage, or the bus; take a line from someone’s shoulder or cheek; look at the windows across the way; at Piccadilly strung with lamps at evening. All of it had been part of the fields of death. But there was always something—a face, perhaps, or a voice, or a newsboy calling the evening papers, _Standard, News_—that pushed through, snubbed her, woke her, and demanded, and in the end received, an effort of attention, so that the vision had to be made again and again. Now once more, driven by some instinctive need for distance and for blue, she gazed down at the bay, turning the blue bars of the waves into little hills and the more purple patches into stony fields. And once again, as always, something that didn’t belong startled her. In the middle of the bay was a brown speck. It was a boat—she saw that after a second. But whose? Mr. Ramsay’s, she answered. Mr. Ramsay: the man who had marched past her, aloof, with his hand raised, leading a procession, in those beautiful boots of his, asking for sympathy she had refused to give. By now the boat was halfway across the bay.

Apart from a streak of wind here and there, the morning was so fine that sea and sky seemed woven from a single fabric, as though sails were fixed high in the sky, or clouds had fallen into the sea. Far out, a steamer had drawn a huge scroll of smoke across the air, and it hung there, curling and circling ornamentally, as though the air were a delicate gauze that held things gently in its mesh and only rocked them softly this way and that. And, as sometimes happens in very fine weather, the cliffs seemed aware of the ships and the ships aware of the cliffs, as if they were passing some secret signal of their own between them. For though it was sometimes so near the shore, this morning in the haze the Lighthouse seemed immensely far away.

“Where are they now?” Lily wondered, gazing out to sea. Where was he—that very old man who had walked past her without a word, with a brown paper parcel under his arm? The boat had reached the middle of the bay.

chapters.title: The Lighthouse · 8
paragraphs: They feel nothing over there, Cam thought, watching the shore, which rose and fell and grew steadily further off and more peaceful. Her hand drew a furrow through the sea, while her mind turned the green swirls and streaks into patterns. Numb and muffled, she wandered in her imagination through that underwater world where pearls clung in clusters to white branches of spray, where, in the green light, your whole mind was changed, and your body glowed half transparent inside a green cloak.

Then the swirl around her hand died away. The water stopped rushing past; the world was full of small creaks and squeaks. You could hear the waves breaking and lapping at the side of the boat as if they lay at anchor in a harbor. Everything drew very near. James had kept his eyes on the sail until it had become like a person he knew, and now it sagged completely, so they came to a halt, flapping about and waiting for a breeze in the hot sun, miles from land, miles from the Lighthouse. The whole world seemed to stand still. The Lighthouse stopped moving, and the line of the far shore stayed fixed. As the sun grew hotter, they all seemed to draw very close together and to sense one another’s presence, which they had nearly forgotten. Macalister’s fishing line dropped straight down into the water. But Mr. Ramsay kept reading, his legs tucked up under him.

The book he was reading was a small, glossy one, its covers speckled like a plover’s egg. Every now and then, as they drifted in that dreadful calm, he turned a page. To James it seemed that every page was turned with a particular gesture meant for him—sometimes assertive, sometimes commanding, sometimes designed to make people feel sorry for him. And the whole time his father was reading and turning those little pages one after another, James was dreading the moment he would look up and say something sharp to him about one thing or another. Why were they hanging about here? he would ask, or something just as unreasonable. And if he does, James thought, I’ll take a knife and strike him to the heart.

This old symbol—taking a knife and striking his father to the heart—he had always kept. Only now that he was older, as he sat glaring at his father in helpless fury, it was not the man himself he wanted to kill, not that old man reading. It was the thing that came down on him—perhaps without his knowing: that fierce, sudden harpy with black wings, its claws and beak all hard and cold, which struck and struck at you (he could feel that beak on his bare legs, where it had struck him as a child) and then flew off; and there he was again, an old man, very sad, reading his book. That was what he would kill; that was what he would strike to the heart. Whatever he did with his life—(and he felt he might do anything, as he looked at the Lighthouse and the distant shore)—whether he went into business or a bank, or became a lawyer, or ran some enterprise, that was what he would fight, what he would hunt down and stamp out: tyranny, despotism, as he called it—forcing people to do what they didn’t want to do, taking away their right to speak. How could any of them say, But I won’t, when he said, Come to the Lighthouse. Do this. Fetch me that. The black wings spread; the hard beak tore. And then, a moment later, there he was, sitting reading; and he might look up—you never could tell—perfectly reasonably. He might chat with the Macalisters. He might be pressing a gold coin into the hand of some freezing old woman in the street, James thought; he might be cheering at some fishermen’s sports day; he might be flinging his arms about in excitement. Or he might sit at the head of the table without a word from one end of dinner to the other. Yes, James thought, while the boat slapped and lazed about in the hot sun: there was a wasteland of snow and rock, very lonely and stern; and there, he had begun to feel quite often lately, whenever his father said something that took the others by surprise, were only two sets of footprints—his and his father’s. Only they knew each other. Then what was this terror, this hatred? He turned back among the many leaves the past had folded inside him, peering into the heart of that forest where light and shadow so dapple each other that every shape is warped, and you stumble along, now with the sun in your eyes, now in dark shade. He was searching for an image that would cool his feeling, set it apart, and round it off into something solid. Suppose, then, that when he was a child sitting helpless in his baby carriage, or on somebody’s lap, he had seen a cart crush someone’s foot, without meaning to, innocently? Suppose he had seen the foot first, smooth and whole in the grass; then the wheel; then that same foot, purple and crushed. But the wheel was innocent. And so now, when his father came striding down the hall early in the morning, banging on their doors to get them up to go to the Lighthouse, it came down over his foot, over Cam’s foot, over anyone’s foot. You just sat and watched.

But whose foot did he mean, and in what garden had it all happened? Because these scenes had their settings: trees growing there; flowers; a particular light; a few figures. Everything tended to arrange itself in a garden free of all this gloom and all this flinging about of hands, where people talked in ordinary voices. All day long they went in and out. An old woman was gossiping in the kitchen; the breeze sucked the blinds in and out; everything was blowing and growing. And at night a very thin yellow veil, like a vine leaf, would be drawn over all those plates and bowls and the tall, waving red and yellow flowers. At night things grew quieter and darker. But the leaf-like veil was so delicate that lamps lifted it and voices wrinkled it; through it he could make out a figure bending down, and hear some dress rustling, some chain jingling, as it came near and went away.

It was in this world that the wheel had passed over the person’s foot. Something, he remembered, hung over him and darkened; it wouldn’t move. Something was brandished in the air; something dry and sharp came down, even there, like a blade, like a curved sword, cutting through the leaves and flowers of even that happy world and making them wither and drop.
“It’s going to rain,” he remembered his father saying. “You won’t be able to go to the Lighthouse.”
In those days the Lighthouse had been a silvery, misty tower with a yellow eye that opened, suddenly and gently, in the evening. Now—

James looked at the Lighthouse. He could make out the whitewashed rocks and the tower, bare and upright. He could see it was banded in black and white; he could see its windows; he could even see laundry laid out to dry on the rocks. So that was the Lighthouse, was it?

No—the other one was the Lighthouse as well. Nothing was ever just one thing. The other one was the Lighthouse too. At times you could barely make it out across the bay. In the evenings you would look up and see the eye open and close, and the light seemed to reach all the way to them in that airy, sunlit garden where they were sitting.

But he caught himself. Whenever he said “they” or “a person” and began to hear someone rustling in or tinkling out, he grew intensely aware of whoever might be in the room. Now it was his father. The tension became unbearable. Any moment now, if no breeze came, his father would clap his book shut and say, “What’s the matter now? Why are we dawdling about here, eh?”—just as once before he had brought his blade down among them on the terrace, and she had gone rigid, and if an axe had been within reach, or a knife, or anything sharp, James would have grabbed it and stabbed his father through the heart. His mother had gone rigid all over; then her arm had loosened, so that he felt she was no longer listening to him, and somehow she had got up and gone off and left him there—helpless, absurd, sitting on the floor gripping a pair of scissors.

There wasn’t a breath of wind. Water chuckled and gurgled in the bottom of the boat, where three or four mackerel flapped their tails up and down in a puddle too shallow to cover them. Mr. Ramsay (James hardly dared glance at him) might wake up at any moment, close his book, and say something sharp. But for now he was reading, and so James went on thinking, stealthily, as if he were tiptoeing barefoot down the stairs, afraid a creaking board would wake a watchdog: what was she like, and where had she gone that day? He started following her from one room to the next, until at last they reached a room where, in a bluish light, as though reflected off a great many china dishes, she was talking to someone, and he listened. She was speaking to a servant, just saying whatever came into her mind. “We shall need a big dish tonight. Where is it—the blue dish?” Only she told the truth; only to her could he tell it. Perhaps that was the source of her endless attraction for him: she was someone you could say anything to, whatever came into your head. But the whole time he was thinking of her, he could feel his father following his thought, shadowing it, making it tremble and stumble.

In the end he stopped thinking. He just sat there in the sun, his hand on the tiller, staring at the Lighthouse, unable to move, unable to brush off these grains of misery that kept settling on his mind one by one. It was as if a rope held him there, a rope his father had knotted, and the only way to escape was to take a knife and plunge it in. … But just then the sail swung slowly round and slowly filled; the boat seemed to shake herself, then to move off, half conscious, still in her sleep; and then she woke up and shot through the waves. The relief was enormous. They all seemed to move apart again and relax, and the fishing lines stretched tight at a slant over the side. But his father did not stir. He simply lifted his right hand high in the air, mysteriously, and let it drop back onto his knee, as if he were conducting some secret symphony.

chapters.title: The Lighthouse · 10
paragraphs: So this was the island, Cam thought, as she trailed her fingers through the waves again. Never before had she seen it from out at sea. So that was how it lay on the water: a dent in its middle, two sharp crags, the sea sweeping in there and stretching away for mile after mile on either side. It was tiny—shaped rather like a leaf standing on its end. So we took a little boat, she thought, and began telling herself an adventure story about escaping from a ship that was going down. But with the sea running through her fingers, and a sprig of seaweed disappearing behind them, she had no wish to tell herself a story in earnest. What she wanted was the feeling of adventure and escape. For as the boat sailed on she was thinking how everything had slipped away, passed, streamed off behind them: her father’s fury over the points of the compass, James’s obstinacy about their compact, her own misery. So what came next? Where were they heading? Out of her hand, icy cold, sunk deep in the sea, a fountain of joy shot up—joy at the change, the escape, the adventure (that she was alive, that she was here). And the drops from this sudden, thoughtless fountain fell here and there on the dark, drowsing shapes in her mind—shapes of a world she had not yet made real, turning in their darkness and catching a spark of light here and there: Greece, Rome, Constantinople. Tiny as it was, like a leaf on end, with the gold-flecked water flowing in and around it, did even that little island, she wondered, have its place in the universe? The old gentlemen in the study could have told her, she thought. Now and then she wandered in from the garden on purpose to catch them at it. There they would be (Mr. Carmichael, perhaps, or Mr. Bankes, very old and very stiff), facing each other in their low armchairs, crackling the pages of _The Times_ in front of them. She would come in from the garden with everything muddled in her head: something someone had said about Christ; a mammoth dug up in a London street; what had the great Napoleon been like? And they would take all this up in their clean hands (their clothes were gray; they smelled of heather), brush the scraps together, turn the paper, cross their knees, and every so often say something very short. As if in a trance, she would take a book off the shelf and stand watching her father write—so evenly, so neatly, from one edge of the page across to the other—coughing a little now and then, or saying something brief to the other old gentleman across from him. And standing there with her book open, she thought: here you could let any thought you had unfold like a leaf in water; and if it did well here, among the smoking old gentlemen and the crackle of _The Times_, then it was right. And as she watched her father writing in his study, she thought (sitting in the boat now) that he was utterly lovable and utterly wise; he was not vain, and he was no tyrant. Indeed, if he noticed her there with her book, he would ask her, as gently as anyone could, Was there nothing he could give her?

To make sure this was not wrong, she looked at him as he read the little book whose glossy cover was speckled like a plover’s egg. No; it was right. Look at him now, she wanted to say out loud to James. (But James was watching the sail.) He’s a sarcastic brute, James would answer. He always turns the conversation to himself and his books, James would say. His egotism is unbearable. And worst of all, he’s a tyrant. But look! she said, looking at him. Look at him now. She watched him reading, his legs curled up, the little book with the yellowish pages she knew so well without knowing a word of what was on them. It was a small book, in close print. On the flyleaf, she knew, he had noted down fifteen francs spent on dinner; so much for the wine; so much as a tip for the waiter; everything neatly totaled at the foot of the page. But what might be written inside—in a book whose corners had been worn round by his pocket—she had no idea. None of them knew what he thought. Yet he was so absorbed that when he glanced up, as he did now for a moment, it was not to look at anything; it was to pin some thought down more precisely. Once that was done his mind flew back and he dived into his reading again. He read, she thought, like someone steering something, or coaxing a great flock of sheep along, or forcing his way higher and higher up one narrow path. At times he went quickly and straight, breaking through the undergrowth; at times a branch seemed to lash at him, a bramble to blind him—but he would not let that defeat him; on he went, turning over page after page. And she kept telling herself her story about escaping from a sinking ship, for as long as he sat there she was safe—as safe as she felt when she slipped in from the garden and took down a book, and the old gentleman abruptly lowered his paper and said something very short over the top of it about Napoleon’s character.

She looked back across the sea toward the island. But the leaf was growing blurred at the edges. It was so small now, and so far off. The sea counted for more than the shore now. All around them waves were heaving and sinking; a log wallowed down one of them, a gull rode on another. Somewhere near here, she thought, dipping her fingers in the water, a ship had gone down; and dreamily, half asleep, she murmured how we perished, each alone.

chapters.title: The Lighthouse · 11
paragraphs: So a great deal depends, then, Lily Briscoe thought as she looked at the sea—hardly a stain on it, so soft that the sails and clouds seemed set into its blue—a great deal depends, she thought, on distance: on whether people are close to us or far away. For her feeling about Mr. Ramsay altered as he sailed farther and farther across the bay. It seemed to be drawn out, stretched thin; he seemed to recede more and more. He and his children seemed to be swallowed by that blue, that distance. But here on the lawn, right beside her, Mr. Carmichael gave a sudden grunt. She laughed. He clawed his book up off the grass and settled himself back in his chair, puffing and blowing like a sea monster. That was quite another matter, because he was so close. And then all was quiet again. Surely they were up by now, she thought, glancing at the house; but nobody showed. Then again, she remembered, they had always vanished the moment a meal ended, off on their own affairs. It all went with this silence, this emptiness, the unreal feeling of early morning. Sometimes things were like that, she thought, pausing for a moment to look at the long glittering windows and the blue plume of smoke: they turned unreal. It was the same when you came back from a journey, or got over an illness—before habit had spun its web across the surface again, you felt that same startling unreality; felt something rise up. Life was never more vivid than then. You could be at your ease. You did not, thank goodness, have to march briskly across the lawn to greet old Mrs. Beckwith as she came out looking for a corner to sit in—“Oh good morning, Mrs. Beckwith! What a lovely day! Are you going to be so bold as to sit in the sun? Jasper’s hidden the chairs. Do let me find you one!”—and all the rest of the usual small talk. You did not have to talk at all. You glided, you shook out your sails (the bay was busy now, with boats setting out), between things and beyond them. It was not empty; it was full to the brim. She seemed to be standing in some substance up to her lips, to move in it, float in it, sink in it—yes, for these waters had no bottom. So many lives had spilled into them. The Ramsays’, the children’s, and all kinds of strays and scraps of things as well. A washerwoman with her basket; a rook; a red-hot poker; the purples and gray-greens of flowers—some shared feeling that held the whole thing together.

Perhaps it was some such feeling of completeness that had made her say, ten years ago, standing nearly where she was standing now, that she must be in love with the place. Love took a thousand shapes. There might be lovers whose gift lay in picking out the elements of things and setting them side by side, giving them a wholeness they never had in life, and so making out of some scene, or some gathering of people (all gone now, all scattered), one of those rounded, solid things that thought lingers over and love plays upon.

Her gaze came to rest on the brown speck that was Mr. Ramsay’s boat. By lunchtime, she supposed, they would be at the Lighthouse. But the wind had got up, and as the sky shifted a little, and the sea shifted a little, and the boats moved to new positions, the view, which only a moment ago had looked miraculously fixed, no longer satisfied her. The wind had scattered the trail of smoke; something about where the ships sat was displeasing.

That lack of proportion out on the water seemed to disturb some harmony inside her. She felt a dim distress, and when she turned back to her picture it was confirmed. She had wasted her morning. For some reason she could not reach that knife-edge of balance between two opposing forces—Mr. Ramsay on one side, the picture on the other—and it was essential. Was the design wrong, perhaps? Did the line of the wall need breaking up, she wondered? Were the trees too heavy a mass? She gave an ironic smile; hadn’t she believed, when she started, that she had solved her problem?

Then what was the problem? She had to try to seize something that kept slipping away from her. It slipped away when she thought about Mrs. Ramsay, and it slipped away now when she thought about her picture. Phrases came to her; visions came to her. Beautiful pictures, beautiful phrases. But what she wanted to catch was that very jar to the nerves—the thing itself, before anything has been made of it. Catch that and begin again; catch that and begin again, she told herself desperately, planting herself squarely in front of the easel once more. The human apparatus for painting, or for feeling, was a wretched machine, she thought, an inefficient machine; it always broke down just when it mattered; you had to drive it on by sheer heroism. She stared, frowning. There, sure enough, was the hedge. But pleading urgently got you nowhere. All you got was a glare in your eyes from staring at the line of the wall, or from thinking—she wore a gray hat. She was astonishingly beautiful. Let it come, she thought, if it’s going to come. For there are moments when one can neither think nor feel. And if one can neither think nor feel, she thought, where is one?

Here on the grass, on the ground, she thought, sitting down and prodding a little colony of plantains with her brush, for the lawn was very rough. Here, sitting on the world, she thought. She could not rid herself of the sense that everything this morning was happening for the first time—perhaps for the last—just as a traveler on a train, even half asleep, knows as he gazes out of the window that he has to look now, because never again will he see that town, or that mule-cart, or that woman working in the fields. The lawn was the world; up here, on this high perch, the two of them were together, she thought, looking over at old Mr. Carmichael, who seemed to share her thoughts (though neither had said a word all this while). And perhaps she would never see him again. He was getting old. And he was getting famous too, she remembered, smiling at the slipper that hung from his foot. People said his poetry was “so beautiful.” They were bringing out things he had written forty years ago. There was a famous man now by the name of Carmichael, she thought with a smile—how many shapes one person could take on! In the newspapers he was that; here he was just as he had always been. He looked the same—a bit grayer, if anything. Yes, the same; and yet somebody had told her, she recalled, that when the news came of Andrew Ramsay’s death (a shell killed him in an instant; he would have been a great mathematician), Mr. Carmichael had “lost all interest in life.” What could that mean? she wondered. Had he gone marching through Trafalgar Square clutching a big stick? Had he sat alone in his room in St. John’s Wood turning page after page without reading a word? She had no idea what he had done when he heard that Andrew was dead, but she sensed it in him all the same. All they ever did was mumble to each other on the stairs, look up at the sky, and say it will be fine or it won’t be fine. Still, this was one way of knowing people, she thought: knowing the outline rather than the detail, the way you might sit in your garden and watch a hillside running purple down into the distant heather. That was how she knew him. She knew that something in him had changed. Not one line of his poetry had she ever read. Yet she felt she knew how it went: slow and sonorous, seasoned and mellow. It was about the desert and the camel, about the palm tree and the sunset. It was utterly impersonal; it had something to say about death and very little about love. He had a kind of aloofness. He asked very little of other people. Hadn’t he always lurched past the drawing-room window rather awkwardly, a newspaper under his arm, trying to dodge Mrs. Ramsay, whom for some reason he did not much like? Which was exactly why, of course, she always tried to make him stop. He would bow to her—pull up unwillingly and bow low. Irritated that he wanted nothing from her, Mrs. Ramsay would ask him (Lily could hear her) wouldn’t he like a coat, a rug, a newspaper? No, there was nothing he wanted. (Here he bowed.) Something in her did not appeal to him. Perhaps it was her masterful way, her certainty, a matter-of-fact streak in her. She was so direct.
(Her attention was caught by a sound from the drawing-room window—a hinge squeaking. The breeze was idly playing with the window.)

Some people must have disliked her intensely, Lily thought (Yes; she noticed the drawing-room step was empty, but it made no difference to her at all. She did not want Mrs. Ramsay now.)—people who found her too sure, too sweeping. Her beauty probably offended people as well. So monotonous, they would say—always the same! Their taste ran to another type, dark and vivacious. Then again, she was weak with her husband; she let him make those scenes of his. And she was reserved: nobody knew exactly what had happened to her. And (to return to Mr. Carmichael and his dislike) it was impossible to picture Mrs. Ramsay spending a whole morning on the lawn, standing at an easel or lying with a book. The idea was unthinkable. Saying nothing, with only the basket on her arm to show where she was going, she would set off for the town, to the poor, to sit in some airless little bedroom. How often Lily had watched her slip away without a word in the middle of a game or a discussion, basket on her arm, very upright. Lily had noticed her coming back. And she had thought, half laughing (she was so methodical about the teacups), half moved (her beauty took your breath away): eyes that are closing in pain have looked on you. You have been with them there.

And then she would be put out because somebody was late, or the butter was not fresh, or the teapot had a chip in it. And the whole time she was complaining about the butter, you would be thinking of Greek temples, and of how beauty had been with them there. She never spoke of it. She simply went, punctually, directly. Going was her instinct—an instinct like the swallows’ for the south or the artichokes’ for the sun—and it turned her unerringly toward the human race, to make her nest at its heart. And like every instinct, it was a little unsettling to those who lacked it: to Mr. Carmichael perhaps, and certainly to Lily herself. The two of them shared some idea about the uselessness of action and the supremacy of thought. Her going reproached them. It gave the world a different twist, so that they were moved to protest as they watched their own cherished assumptions fading, and to clutch at them as they vanished. Charles Tansley did that too; it was partly why you disliked him. He threw the proportions of your world out of true. And whatever had become of him? she wondered, idly stirring the plantains with her brush. He had got his fellowship. He had married, and lived at Golder’s Green.

During the war she had gone into a hall one day and heard him give a speech. He was denouncing something, condemning somebody. He was preaching brotherly love. And all she could feel was: how could he love humanity, this man who could not tell one picture from another—who had stood behind her smoking his shag (“fivepence an ounce, Miss Briscoe”) and made a point of telling her women can’t write, women can’t paint, not so much because he believed it as because, for some odd reason, he wanted it to be so? There he stood on a platform, lean and red and raucous, preaching love (among the plantains ants were crawling, and she disturbed them with her brush—red, busy ants, rather like Charles Tansley). From her seat in the half-empty hall she had watched him ironically as he pumped love into that cold space—and suddenly there was the old barrel, or whatever it had been, bobbing up and down in the waves, and Mrs. Ramsay hunting among the pebbles for her glasses case. “Oh dear! What a nuisance! Lost again. Don’t bother, Mr. Tansley. I lose thousands every summer.” At that he had pressed his chin back against his collar, as though afraid of seeming to approve such exaggeration—but he could put up with it from her, because he liked her—and had smiled very charmingly. He must have confided in her on one of those long excursions when people got separated and walked home alone. He was paying for his little sister’s education, Mrs. Ramsay had told her. It did him enormous credit. Her own picture of him was grotesque, Lily knew perfectly well, stirring the plantains with her brush. After all, half of what you thought about other people was grotesque. Such ideas served private purposes of your own. For her, he stood in for a whipping boy. When she was in a bad mood she caught herself flogging his lean flanks. If she wanted to take him seriously, she had to borrow Mrs. Ramsay’s sayings and see him through her eyes.
She heaped up a little mountain for the ants to climb over. Meddling like this in their cosmos, she drove them into a frenzy of indecision. Some scurried one way, some another.

You would need fifty pairs of eyes to see with, she reflected. Even fifty pairs would not be enough to get all the way around that one woman, she thought. And among them there ought to be one pair completely blind to her beauty. What you most needed was some secret sense, as fine as air, that could slip through keyholes and wrap itself around her as she sat knitting, or talking, or sitting alone and silent in the window—a sense that would gather up and store, the way the air held the steamer’s smoke, her thoughts, her fancies, her desires. What did the hedge mean to her? What did the garden mean? What did it mean to her when a wave broke? (Lily looked up, as she had seen Mrs. Ramsay look up; she too heard a wave fall on the beach.) And what then stirred and quivered in her mind when the children, playing cricket, shouted “How’s that? How’s that?” She would stop knitting for a second and look intent. Then she would sink back again—and suddenly Mr. Ramsay broke off his pacing and stopped dead in front of her, and some strange shock ran through her and seemed to rock her on its breast in deep agitation, as he stood still there above her and looked down at her. Lily could see him.

He reached out his hand and lifted her from her chair. Somehow it seemed he had done this before—as though once, long ago, he had bent over in just the same way and lifted her out of a boat lying a few inches off some island, where the ladies had to be handed ashore like this by the gentlemen. It was an old-fashioned scene; it almost demanded crinolines and peg-top trousers. As she let him help her, Mrs. Ramsay had thought (so Lily supposed): the time has come. Yes, she would say it now. Yes, she would marry him. And slowly, quietly, she stepped onto the shore. She probably said only a single word, her hand lying still in his. I will marry you, she might have said, her hand in his; nothing more. Again and again the same thrill had passed between them—obviously it had, Lily thought, clearing a path for her ants. She was not making it up; she was only trying to smooth out something handed to her folded, years ago—something she had seen. For in the rough and tumble of everyday life, with all those children around, all those guests, you had a constant sense of repetition: of one thing landing where another had landed before, and so starting an echo that chimed through the air and set it vibrating.

Yet it would be wrong, she thought, remembering how they would walk off together arm in arm past the greenhouse, she in her green shawl, his tie flying, to make their relationship too simple. It was no unbroken bliss—she with her impulses and her quickness, he with his shudders and his black moods. Far from it. Early in the morning the bedroom door would slam with a crash. He would spring up from the table in a rage and send his plate whizzing out of the window. Then the whole house would feel like doors banging and blinds flapping, as if a gusty wind were blowing through, and everyone rushed about trying to batten down the hatches and set things shipshape. That was how she had run into Paul Rayley one day on the stairs. The two of them had laughed and laughed like children, all because Mr. Ramsay had found an earwig in his milk at breakfast and hurled the whole lot through the air onto the terrace. “An earwig,” Prue whispered in awe, “in his milk.” Other people might find centipedes. But he had put up such a fence of holiness around himself, and filled the space inside it with such majesty, that an earwig in his milk became a monster.

But it wore Mrs. Ramsay out and cowed her a little, the whizzing plates and the slamming doors. And sometimes long, rigid silences would come down between them. At such times she was in a mood that irritated Lily—half plaintive, half resentful; she seemed unable to rise calmly above the storm, or to laugh as the rest of them laughed; yet perhaps in her weariness she was hiding something. She brooded and said nothing. After a while he would start hovering stealthily wherever she was, prowling under the window where she sat writing letters or talking; for she made sure to be busy when he went by, and slipped away from him, and pretended she had not seen him. Then he would turn as smooth as silk, genial and charming, and try to win her over like that. She would still keep her distance, and now, for a little while, she would take on some of the pride and grand manners that her beauty gave her a right to and that she almost never showed; she would turn her head, glance over her shoulder like that, always with some Minta or Paul or William Bankes beside her. In the end he would stand outside the group, the very image of a starving wolfhound (Lily got up from the grass and stood looking at the steps and the window where she had seen him), and say her name—just once, exactly like a wolf barking in the snow. Still she held back. Then he would say it again, and this time something in his voice would stir her, and all at once she would leave them and go to him, and the two of them would walk off together among the pear trees and the cabbages and the raspberry beds. They would have it out between them. But in what postures, and with what words? Their relationship had such dignity that she and Paul and Minta turned away, hiding their curiosity and their unease, and set about picking flowers, throwing balls, chattering, until dinnertime—and there the two of them were, as usual, he at one end of the table and she at the other.

“Why don’t some of you take up botany? … With all those legs and arms why doesn’t one of you…?” So they would chat, laughing, among the children, just as usual. Everything would be as usual—except for a kind of quiver, like a blade flashing in the air, that came and went between the two of them, as though the familiar sight of the children around their soup plates had been made new in their eyes by that hour among the pears and cabbages. Mrs. Ramsay, Lily thought, would look especially at Prue. Prue sat in the middle of her brothers and sisters, always so taken up, it seemed, with making sure nothing went wrong that she hardly said a word herself. How Prue must have blamed herself for that earwig in the milk! How pale she had turned when Mr. Ramsay flung his plate out of the window! How she wilted under those long silences between her parents! At any rate, her mother now seemed to be making it up to her—reassuring her that all was well, promising that some day that same happiness would be hers too. Yet she had had it for less than a year.

She had let the flowers drop from her basket, Lily thought, narrowing her eyes and stepping back as though to look at her picture, which she was not in fact touching; every faculty was in a trance, frozen over on top but racing underneath.

She let her flowers drop from her basket, spilled and tumbled them onto the grass, and—reluctantly, hesitantly, yet without question or complaint; wasn’t obedience a gift she had perfected?—she went too. Down across fields, through valleys, white and strewn with flowers—that was how she would have painted it. The hills were bare and severe. It was rocky and steep. Below, the waves sounded harsh on the stones. The three of them went together, Mrs. Ramsay walking quite fast in front, as though she expected to meet someone around the corner.

All at once the window she was watching went white with some light fabric behind it. So someone had come into the drawing room at last; someone was in the chair. For heaven’s sake, she prayed, let them stay sitting there, and not come blundering out to talk to her. Luckily, whoever it was stayed where they were inside, and by some fluke had sat so as to cast an oddly shaped triangular shadow across the step. It shifted the composition of the picture a little. That was interesting. It might be useful. Her mood was returning. You had to keep looking, without letting the intensity of feeling slacken for one second—the resolve not to be put off, not to be tricked. You had to grip the scene—like this—in a vise and let nothing get in to spoil it. What you wanted, she thought, dipping her brush with care, was to stay level with ordinary experience—to feel simply, that’s a chair, that’s a table—and yet, at the same moment, it’s a miracle, it’s an ecstasy. Perhaps the problem could be solved after all. Ah, but what had happened? A white ripple passed across the glass. The air must have stirred some frill of cloth in the room. Her heart leaped up at her, seized her, tortured her.

“Mrs. Ramsay! Mrs. Ramsay!” she cried, and felt the old horror return—wanting and wanting and not having. Could she still do that to her? And then, quietly, as if she were holding back, that too became part of ordinary experience, level with the chair and the table. Mrs. Ramsay—this was part of her perfect kindness toward Lily—simply sat there in the chair, flicking her needles to and fro, knitting her reddish-brown stocking, casting her shadow on the step. There she sat.

Her mind was so full of what she was thinking and seeing that she could hardly bear to leave her easel; yet, as if she had something she had to share, Lily walked past Mr. Carmichael to the edge of the lawn, her brush still in her hand. Where was that boat now? Mr. Ramsay? She wanted him.

chapters.title: The Lighthouse · 12
paragraphs: Mr. Ramsay was nearly at the end of his reading. One hand hovered above the page, poised to turn it the instant he reached the bottom. He sat there with no hat on, the wind tossing his hair about, extraordinarily exposed to everything. He looked very old. To James—who was lining his head up now with the Lighthouse, now with the empty stretch of water running off into the open—he looked like some old stone lying on the sand; as though his body had become the thing that always lay at the back of both their minds: that loneliness which was, for each of them, the truth about things.

He read very fast, as though impatient to reach the end. And they really were very near the Lighthouse now. There it rose up, bare and upright, glaring black and white, and you could see the waves smashing into white splinters, like broken glass, against the rocks. You could make out lines and creases in the rock. You could see the windows plainly—one of them with a dab of white on it—and a little tuft of green on the rock. A man had come out, looked at them through a spyglass, and gone back in. So that was what it was like, James thought—the Lighthouse you had watched across the bay all these years: a bare tower standing on a naked rock. That satisfied him. It bore out some obscure feeling he had about his own nature. The old ladies, he thought, remembering the garden at home, went dragging their chairs about the lawn. Old Mrs. Beckwith, say, was forever going on about how nice it was, how sweet it was, how proud and how happy they all ought to be; but in actual fact, James thought, looking at the Lighthouse planted there on its rock, it’s like that. He looked at his father, reading fiercely, his legs tightly curled. The two of them shared that knowledge. “We are driving before a gale—we must sink,” James began murmuring to himself, half aloud, exactly the way his father said it.

It seemed an age since anyone had spoken. Cam had grown tired of looking at the sea. Scraps of black cork had drifted by; in the bottom of the boat the fish lay dead. Her father went on reading, and James looked at him, and she looked at him, and they swore they would fight tyranny to the death; and he read on, with no idea at all of what they were thinking. That was how he got away, she thought. Yes, with that great forehead and great nose of his, holding his little speckled book firmly up in front of him, he got away. You might try to catch hold of him, but then he spread his wings like a bird and floated off, to land out of your reach, somewhere far off on some lonely stump. She stared out over the vast stretch of sea. The island had shrunk so much that it hardly looked like a leaf now. It looked like the tip of a rock that one big wave would cover. And yet, frail as it was, it held all those paths, those terraces, those bedrooms—all those countless things. But just as, on the edge of sleep, things grow simpler until only one detail out of thousands has the power to make itself felt, so, she felt, as she gazed drowsily at the island, all those paths and terraces and bedrooms were fading and vanishing, until nothing remained but a pale blue censer swinging rhythmically to and fro across her mind. It was a hanging garden; it was a valley full of birds and flowers and antelopes. … She was drifting off to sleep.
“Come along now,” said Mr. Ramsay, snapping his book shut all at once.

Come along where? To what extraordinary adventure? She woke up with a jolt. To land somewhere? To climb somewhere? Where was he taking them? After that enormous silence, his words gave them a start. But it was ridiculous. He was hungry, he told them; it was lunchtime. And besides—look, he said. That’s the Lighthouse. “We’re nearly there.”
“He’s doing very well,” Macalister said, in praise of James. “He’s holding her nice and steady.”
But his father never praised him, James thought grimly.

Mr. Ramsay undid the parcel and passed the sandwiches around. He was happy now, eating bread and cheese with these fishermen. What he would really have liked, James thought, watching him pare his cheese into thin yellow slices with his penknife, was to live in a cottage and loaf about the harbor, spitting, with the other old men.

This is right, this is it, Cam kept feeling while she peeled her hard-boiled egg. She felt now just as she did in the study when the old men sat reading _The Times_. Now I can go on thinking anything I please, and I won’t tumble off a cliff or drown, she thought, because there he is, keeping an eye on me.

All the while they were racing along so close to the rocks that it was thrilling—as if they were doing two things at the same time: sitting here in the sun eating lunch, and also fighting their way to safety through a great storm after a shipwreck. Would the water hold out? Would the food hold out? she asked herself—telling herself a story, yet knowing all along what the truth was.

Their own time would soon be over, Mr. Ramsay was telling old Macalister, but their children would live to see some strange things. Macalister said he had turned seventy-five in March; Mr. Ramsay was seventy-one. Macalister said he had never once been to a doctor, and never lost a tooth. And that’s how I’d like my children to live—Cam felt sure her father was thinking that, because when she was about to throw a sandwich into the sea he stopped her and told her, as if he had the fishermen and their way of life in mind, that if she didn’t want it she should put it back in the parcel. She mustn’t waste it. He said it so wisely, as though he understood so well everything that went on in the world, that she put it back straight away. Then from his own parcel he handed her a gingerbread nut, like some grand Spanish gentleman, she thought, offering a flower to a lady at a window (his manner was so courteous). Yet he was shabby and plain, eating his bread and cheese; and all the same he was leading them on a great expedition in which, for all she knew, they would drown.
“That’s where she went down,” Macalister’s boy said suddenly.

“Three men drowned right where we are now,” said the old man. He had seen them clinging to the mast with his own eyes. And Mr. Ramsay glanced at the spot, and James and Cam were afraid he was about to burst out:
But I beneath a rougher sea,

and if he did, they could not bear it; they would scream; they could not take one more eruption of the passion that seethed in him. But to their surprise all he said was “Ah”—as though he were thinking to himself, Why make a fuss about that? Of course men drown in storms, but it’s a perfectly simple matter, and the depths of the sea (he shook the crumbs from his sandwich paper over them) are nothing but water, after all. Then he lit his pipe and took out his watch. He studied it closely; perhaps he worked out some mathematical sum. At last, triumphantly, he said:
“Well done!” James had steered them like a born sailor.

There! Cam thought, speaking to James without a sound. You’ve got it at last. She knew this was what James had been longing for, and she knew that now that he had it he was so pleased he would not look at her, or at their father, or at anybody. There he sat, bolt upright, his hand on the tiller, looking a bit sulky and frowning a little. He was so pleased that he would not let anyone rob him of one grain of his pleasure. His father had praised him. They must all think he didn’t care in the slightest. But you’ve got it now, Cam thought.

They had tacked, and now they were running fast and lightly along beside the reef on long rocking waves that passed them from one to the next with a wonderful lilt and thrill. To the left a line of rocks showed brown through the water, which grew thinner and greener; and on one of them, a taller rock, a wave kept breaking without pause, throwing up a little spout of drops that came down in a shower. You could hear the slap of the water, the patter of drops falling, and a sort of hushing, hissing sound from the waves as they rolled and romped and slapped at the rocks, like wild creatures that were perfectly free and would toss and tumble and play like this forever.
They could see two men on the Lighthouse now, watching them and getting ready to meet them.

Mr. Ramsay buttoned up his coat and rolled up his trouser legs. He took the big, clumsily wrapped brown paper parcel that Nancy had put together and sat holding it on his knee. Sitting like this, all ready to land, he gazed back at the island. With his long sight he could perhaps see quite plainly that shrunken leaf-shape standing on end on a plate of gold. What could he see? Cam wondered. To her it was only a blur. What was he thinking now? she wondered. What was he searching for, so fixedly, so intently, so silently? The two of them watched him as he sat there hatless with his parcel on his knee, staring and staring at the fragile blue shape, which looked like the vapor of something that had burned itself away. What do you want? both of them wanted to ask. Both of them wanted to say, Ask us for anything and we’ll give it to you. But he did not ask them for anything. He sat looking at the island, and he might have been thinking, We perished, each alone, or he might have been thinking, I have reached it. I have found it; but he said nothing.
Then he put on his hat.

“Bring those parcels,” he said, nodding toward the things Nancy had wrapped for them to take to the Lighthouse. “The parcels for the Lighthouse men,” he said. He stood up in the bow of the boat, very straight and very tall—exactly, James thought, as though he were saying, “There is no God,” and exactly, Cam thought, as though he were leaping into space—and they both stood up to follow him as he sprang onto the rock, lightly, like a young man, holding his parcel.

chapters.title: The Lighthouse · 13
paragraphs: “He must have reached it,” Lily Briscoe said aloud, and suddenly she felt utterly exhausted. For the Lighthouse had almost disappeared; it had dissolved into a blue haze. And the strain of looking at it, together with the strain of thinking of him landing there—which seemed to be one and the same strain—had pulled her body and her mind as far as they would go. Ah, but what relief she felt. Whatever it was she had wanted to give him when he left her that morning, she had given it to him at last.

“He has landed,” she said aloud. “It is finished.” Then old Mr. Carmichael heaved himself up, puffing a little, and stood beside her like some old pagan god, shaggy, weeds in his hair and the trident (it was only a French novel) in his hand. He stood next to her at the edge of the lawn, his great bulk swaying slightly, and, shading his eyes with his hand, said, “They will have landed,” and she felt she had been right. They had had no need to speak. They had been thinking the same things, and he had answered her without her asking him anything. There he stood, spreading his hands over all the frailty and suffering of mankind; she thought he was looking out, tolerantly, compassionately, over their final fate. Now he has crowned the occasion, she thought, as his hand slowly dropped—as though she had watched him let fall from his great height a wreath of violets and asphodels, which drifted slowly down and came to rest at last on the earth.

Quickly, as though something over there had called her back, she turned to her canvas. There it was—her picture. Yes, with all its greens and blues, its lines running upward and across, its attempt at something. It would be hung up in the attic, she thought; it would be destroyed. But what did that matter? she asked herself, and took up her brush once more. She looked at the steps: they were empty. She looked at her canvas: it was blurred. With a sudden intensity, as though for one second she saw it clearly, she drew a line there, in the center. It was done; it was finished. Yes, she thought, laying down her brush in extreme fatigue, I have had my vision.
